issues.title: TUI: startup-only palette cache leaves input unreadable after system light/dark changes (0.154.0)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: TUI
labels.description: Issues related to the terminal user interface: text input, menus and dialogs, and terminal display

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

issues.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

`codex-cli 0.154.0`. The startup-only cache is also present in upstream `main` at `a592c38c16cdd7623dacc9168926ebccedfb67d3`.

### What subscription do you have?

Not relevant to this terminal-rendering issue.

### Which model were you using?

Model-independent; observed in long-running Codex CLI sessions.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS, Darwin 25.6.0, arm64.

### What terminal emulator and version are you using?

CodePress Terminal, a Tauri/xterm.js host configured to follow the system light/dark appearance. The host updates its terminal palette and answers OSC 10/11 queries. Exact host release not recorded.

### What issue are you seeing?

After the terminal changes between light and dark appearance while Codex is already running, the composer and previously rendered user-message blocks retain their old background colors. The terminal's default foreground updates, producing nearly white text on a pale background (or the inverse mismatch). Long-lived sessions become unreadable after an automatic macOS appearance change.

Refocusing and redrawing do not refresh the cached palette. Restarting/resuming refreshes the startup colors, but the next appearance change can break the session again.

This follows up my earlier report **#37298**, which described a failed refresh permanently poisoning the color cache in 0.146.0. The current implementation has a different failure mode: focus-driven refresh has been removed entirely, so no transient failure is required.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Configure a terminal to follow macOS system appearance and start Codex while the terminal is light.
2. Send a message so both a user-message block and the composer are visible.
3. Change macOS appearance to dark without restarting Codex, or leave the process running across the automatic appearance change.
4. Refocus the terminal and type in the composer.
5. Observe that the terminal's normal foreground/background have changed but the composer/message backgrounds retain the light-theme color. Repeat dark to light as well.

A terminal host can verify the distinction by recording OSC 10/11 requests: the current focus handler intentionally does not send a new pair on focus regain.

### What is the expected behavior?

Codex should adapt its palette-dependent rendering when the terminal's colors change, without restarting the process, losing draft text, dropping/reordering keys or pasted input, or inserting terminal replies into the composer.

### Root cause and relevant change

[PR #35649](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/35649), merged July 27, intentionally removed focus-time palette queries because they could block the input loop and discard keystrokes. That input-preservation fix is important, but it also leaves a long-lived TUI unable to adapt to system appearance changes.

Source at the inspected commit:

- [`terminal_palette.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a592c38c16cdd7623dacc9168926ebccedfb67d3/codex-rs/tui/src/terminal_palette.rs#L145-L209): the process-global cache stores the startup foreground/background; `attempted` prevents re-querying through `default_colors()`.
- [`tui/event_stream.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a592c38c16cdd7623dacc9168926ebccedfb67d3/codex-rs/tui/src/tui/event_stream.rs#L294-L299): `FocusGained` explicitly preserves the startup-cached palette and only returns the focus event.
- [`style.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a592c38c16cdd7623dacc9168926ebccedfb67d3/codex-rs/tui/src/style.rs#L74-L85): user messages get an explicit derived background without a paired explicit foreground. When the terminal's default foreground changes, the old explicit background remains.
- [`terminal_probe.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a592c38c16cdd7623dacc9168926ebccedfb67d3/codex-rs/tui/src/terminal_probe.rs#L243-L255): the existing Unix color probe uses a direct reader. Its `read_until` helper explicitly does not replay unrelated input, so simply calling this again from the focus handler would reintroduce the reason for #35649.

### Proposed approach

Please restore runtime palette refresh through the normal terminal input/event path rather than reinstating the old synchronous raw-input probe:

1. Request OSC 10/11 asynchronously on focus regain as a compatibility fallback. Also support a terminal theme-change notification so a theme switch while the terminal stays focused can refresh the palette; #38575 tracks DECSET 2031 for that case.
2. Parse replies through the existing input owner, preserving ordinary keys, bracketed paste, and fragmented/late replies. Coalesce repeated refresh triggers and keep only one bounded refresh outstanding; never wait on terminal replies in the UI input handler.
3. Commit a complete valid foreground/background pair atomically. On timeout or malformed/partial replies, preserve the last known good palette and allow a later retry, avoiding #37298's poisoned-cache behavior.
4. Invalidate palette-dependent render caches and repaint the composer and affected transcript content when colors actually change. Preserve an explicitly chosen syntax-highlighting theme.
5. Preserve startup trust/confirmation protections and terminal ownership during external-editor handoff and suspend/resume; a refresh must not start a second competing stdin reader.

Suggested regression coverage: both light/dark directions in the same process; theme changes without a focus transition; repeated focus notifications; immediate, delayed, fragmented, missing and partial OSC replies; a failed refresh followed by a successful one; typing and bracketed paste during refresh; unchanged draft and input ordering; and recoloring existing visible user-message blocks, not only newly generated output.

### Workaround

Launching a new process with `FORCE_COLOR=1 codex` selects Codex's basic-color fallback, which uses the default/reset color for the derived composer background. This is source-backed, not an interactive validation from this investigation, and sacrifices richer colors. Restarting normally only fixes colors until the next theme change. `/theme` controls syntax highlighting and does not invalidate this palette cache.

### Related issues

- #37298 — my earlier report: one failed requery permanently disabled future refreshes.
- #14105 — composer readability after a live terminal theme switch.
- #38575 — theme-change reporting without a focus transition.
- #18942 — related focus/theme refresh discussion.
- #35649 — intentional removal of focus queries to preserve input.

This report adds the 0.154.0 observation and the current startup-only-cache diagnosis, linking the earlier reports rather than treating this as an unrelated color preference. Per the current contribution policy, I am including the implementation constraints and regression cases here for the maintainers.

issues.title: Windows Computer Use: confirmed Korean UIA document-role failure and numeric ControlType fix

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
## Summary

On Korean Windows (`ko-KR`), an actual Codex Computer Use call against Chrome failed with `could not determine the current browser URL on Windows`, even though the browser's UI Automation document element exposed a nonempty URL value.

Live native observation identified the failing predicate: the helper compared the localized document role `문서` with the fixed English string `document`. Replacing only that predicate with a successful numeric `CachedControlType == UIA_DocumentControlTypeId` check restored actual screenshot and accessibility requests.

Related report: #53026. This report collects the Korean runtime reproduction, the causal before/after evidence, and the published repair tool in one place. The same evidence was initially added in [this comment](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/53026#issuecomment-6205535513).

## Environment observed on 2026-10-16

| Component | Observed version / identity |
| --- | --- |
| Codex installed Windows MSIX | `26.1007.9446.0` |
| Windows | x64, build `26100.9711` (24H2) |
| Windows UI culture | `ko-KR` |
| Computer Use plugin | `26.1007.71326` |
| `@oai/sky` | `0.7.7` |
| Chrome | `155.0.8059.79` |

The affected component was the bundled `@oai/sky/bin/windows/codex-computer-use.exe` native helper.

## Reproduction and actual behavior

1. Use the affected Codex Windows installation with Korean UI Automation document-role names and an open Chrome window.
2. Obtain that window with the documented `@oai/sky` API. Window lookup itself succeeds.
3. Ensure the window is not minimized, then request its state:

```js
await sky.get_window_state({
  window,
  include_screenshot: true,
  include_text: true,
});
```

The actual state request fails with the error containing:

```text
could not determine the current browser URL on Windows
```

The diagnostic calls did not navigate the page. The error occurred after successful window lookup, within the native state-capture path.

## Expected behavior

A UI Automation Document element should be recognized by its numeric ControlType, regardless of its localized display name. An eligible `RootWebArea` with a successfully read, nonempty URL value should support the normal Chrome state request in Korean as it does in English.

## Live evidence at the failing predicate

The initial observation recorded native getter results and comparisons without replacing their arguments or results.

| Property / operation | Observed result |
| --- | --- |
| Numeric UIA ControlType | `50030` (`UIA_DocumentControlTypeId`) |
| `CachedLocalizedControlType` | `문서` |
| `CachedAutomationId` | `RootWebArea` |
| Current value lookup | HRESULT `0`; nonempty value |
| Cached value lookup | HRESULT `0`; nonempty value |
| Document-role comparison | `문서` compared with ASCII `document`: false |
| URL candidate after visiting the element | Absent |
| Native URL-result discriminator | `0x8000000000000002` |

The mismatch appeared in 22 RootWebArea comparisons during 11 internal state captures within a five-second observation interval. These are internal capture counts, not 11 separate tool requests.

The native helper's resulting error propagates through the Computer Use response. The localized display name is being used as a semantic identifier in the URL-candidate selector.

## Narrow correction and causal validation

```text
Before: localized_role.eq_ignore_ascii_case("document")
After:  successful CachedControlType read
        AND CachedControlType == UIA_DocumentControlTypeId  // 50030
```

For causal validation, only this predicate was changed in the installed native helper: one existing 42-byte instruction region, with 36 bytes differing. Reconstructing the original region reproduced the original whole-file SHA-256, establishing that every byte outside that region was identical.

A failed numeric-property getter or a non-Document ControlType follows the existing non-candidate path. Subsequent RootWebArea matching and nonempty-value selection remain intact.

This was a local binary-level repair, not a build from upstream native source.

## Actual Computer Use results after the correction

The documented API was called against the same Chrome window after the predicate change:

| Request | Actual result |
| --- | --- |
| Screenshot + accessibility | Success: one 1920 x 1032 screenshot and a 48,951-character accessibility tree |
| Accessibility only | Success: accessibility tree returned |
| Screenshot only | Success: one screenshot returned |

None of these three calls returned the URL-detection error. An initial post-change request reported a separate minimized-window condition; `activate_window`, followed by refreshing the window with `get_window`, resolved that condition before the three successful requests above.

The results establish the cause and recovery for this observed Korean Chrome environment. They do not establish every possible cause of the same error text, nor do they constitute coverage of click/type operations or every locale.

## Published repair code

- [Repair tool and usage](https://github.com/heelee912/codex/tree/fix/windows-cua-document-control-type/tools/windows-cua-document-fix)
- [Exact commit: 95ee61d](https://github.com/heelee912/codex/commit/95ee61db4a387944889edc9a5b6e97272c8fca9d)

The fork adds a Python standard-library tool and a README. It supports read-only inspection, applying the exact predicate correction, and restoring the original bytes. It accepts only these two complete helper hashes:

```text
Original: d36ae6626bdced7ae07935d1a91be14425e8f6ce7c9b5c69f2d8d7df0c130d83
Repaired: c9b9981288951976c36b4c8febc8c2e21b53dfe9bab66f299c11f51592145855
```

Apply/readback, exact restoration, repeated apply/restore, rejection of an exclusively opened target, and rejection of an unknown hash were checked on a temporary file copy. The copy was removed; those packaging checks did not modify the installed helper.

The native helper implementation was absent from the inspected public repository tree at `6b991972c5b539198dcea9bac4fc14e57559c3af`. Consequently, the published code is a version-bound local repair tool. It is not an upstream native-source fix or a rebuilt Codex app. No OpenAI executable is included. Editing the helper changes its Authenticode result to `HashMismatch`; exact restoration reconstructs the original file.

## Requested upstream resolution

Please replace the localized document-kind comparison with a successful numeric `CachedControlType == UIA_DocumentControlTypeId` check in the native Windows Computer Use implementation, and ship the change in an official app/runtime update. Please link the maintainer PR or tracked internal fix here.

Suggested focused regression coverage:

1. Document ControlType `50030` with display names such as `문서`, `document`, and another translated name selects the same eligible RootWebArea URL candidate.
2. A different ControlType is not classified as Document merely because its display name is `document`.
3. A failed getter does not consume an uninitialized numeric property value.
4. Screenshot-only, accessibility-only, and combined requests succeed against the same eligible Chrome window on Korean Windows.

The local tool performs a one-time repair and does not watch or patch later app updates. The requested official source correction would be delivered through normal app/runtime updates.

## Community write-up

The repair tool and its actual validation results are also shared in [Show and tell #54474](https://github.com/openai/codex/discussions/54474).

issues.title: Standalone Unix updater reports success when curl fails (`curl | sh` masks the exit status); Windows path is unaffected

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

issues.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

codex-cli 0.162.1

### What platform is your computer?

macOS (Darwin 27.0.0). Windows 10 22H2 (19045) was also tested for comparison.

### What issue are you seeing?

The standalone **Unix** updater prints `🎉 Update ran successfully! Please restart Codex.` even when `curl` fails and nothing is installed:

```text
Updating Codex via `sh -c 'curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | CODEX_NON_INTERACTIVE=1 sh'`...
curl: (28) Failed to connect to chatgpt.com port 443 after 150008 ms: Couldn't connect to server

🎉 Update ran successfully! Please restart Codex.
```

This has been reported for individual symptoms in #19421 (curl 403) and #42021 (curl connect failure). This issue pins down the root cause, shows it only affects the Unix path, and proposes a fix.

#### Root cause

As of `6b99197`:

- `codex-rs/tui/src/update_action.rs` L55-61: `UpdateAction::StandaloneUnix` runs `sh -c "curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | CODEX_NON_INTERACTIVE=1 sh"`.
- `codex-rs/cli/src/main.rs` L851-854: success is decided only by `status.success()` of that process.

POSIX `sh` has no `pipefail` by default, so the pipeline's exit status is that of the **last** command. When `curl` fails, the trailing `sh` reads empty stdin, runs nothing, and exits `0`.

`install.sh` itself handles errors correctly (`set -eu` plus explicit `exit 1`). The problem is only the `curl | sh` wrapper.

#### Unix reproduction (macOS, no Codex needed)

| Command | curl error | Exit |
|---|---|---|
| `sh -c 'curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 2 https://10.255.255.1/x \| sh'` | `(28)` timeout | **0** ❌ |
| `sh -c 'curl -fsSL https://httpbin.org/status/404 \| sh'` | `(56)` HTTP 404 | **0** ❌ |
| `bash -o pipefail -c 'curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 2 https://10.255.255.1/x \| sh'` | `(28)` | **28** ✅ |

#### Windows is not affected (verified)

`UpdateAction::StandaloneWindows` runs `powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c '$env:CODEX_NON_INTERACTIVE=1; irm https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.ps1 | iex'`. With `-Command`, PowerShell's exit code reflects `$?` of the last statement. A failing `irm` is a terminating error, so the process exits `1`. `install.ps1` also sets `$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"`, so a `throw` inside the script propagates the same way.

These results come from running the same `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c '<…> | iex'` shape on Windows 10 22H2:

| Case | Windows PowerShell 5.1.19041 | PowerShell 7 (`pwsh`) |
|---|---|---|
| `irm` connection refused (`https://127.0.0.1:9/…`) | exit **1** ✅ | exit **1** ✅ |
| `irm` connect timeout (`https://10.255.255.1/…`) | exit **1** ✅ | exit **1** ✅ |
| `irm` HTTP 404 | exit **1** ✅ | exit **1** ✅ |
| Script piped to `iex` throws | exit **1** ✅ | exit **1** ✅ |
| Control: script succeeds | exit 0 | exit 0 |

So only `StandaloneUnix` reports a false success.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Use a standalone (`install.sh`) install of Codex on macOS/Linux.
2. Make `https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh` unreachable (offline, firewall, proxy returning 403, etc.).
3. Accept the update prompt.
4. `curl` prints an error, but Codex still prints `🎉 Update ran successfully! Please restart Codex.`

### What is the expected behavior?

When the install script cannot be downloaded, the updater should report a failure (`… failed with status …`), and it should not tell the user to restart.

### Additional information

**Suggested fix:** download to a temp file first and execute it only if `curl` succeeded. This doesn't depend on `pipefail` support in `/bin/sh`:

```rust
UpdateAction::StandaloneUnix => (
    "sh",
    &[
        "-c",
        r#"tmp="$(mktemp)" || exit 1; trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT; curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh -o "$tmp" && CODEX_NON_INTERACTIVE=1 sh "$tmp""#,
    ],
),
```

Checked locally on macOS: a curl timeout exits 28, HTTP 404 exits 56, an installer that exits 3 propagates 3, and a successful installer exits 0.

As a side benefit, this also stops a connection that drops mid-transfer from running a truncated `install.sh`. With `curl | sh`, `sh` runs top-level statements as they stream in, and `install.sh` has no `main "$@"` wrapper at the end.

`set -o pipefail` would also work where it is supported, but `/bin/sh` does not support it on every platform.

The user-facing hint in the "Update available!" banner (`Run sh -c 'curl … | CODEX_NON_INTERACTIVE=1 sh' to update.`) uses the same command string, so it would pick up the fix automatically via `command_str()`.

Related: #19421, #42021

issues.title: Codex Desktop: required MCP failure blocks task creation/resume with no recovery mode

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: mcp
labels.description: Issues related to the use of model context protocol (MCP) servers

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.721.81911

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64

### What issue are you seeing?

A project-scoped local stdio MCP server was configured with `enabled = true` and `required = true`. When that server returned an error during `initialize`, Codex Desktop aborted the entire session: I could neither create a new task for the project nor resume an existing task.

Sanitized error:

```text
Failed to resume chat
error resuming thread: Fatal error: Failed to initialize session:
required MCP servers failed to initialize:
<project-mcp>: handshaking with MCP server failed:
JSON-RPC error: -32602: Invalid params
```

This creates a recovery catch-22: the Codex task needed to inspect or repair the project cannot open because the project's MCP server needs repair. Desktop offered no safe recovery mode and no actionable protocol diagnostic.

Recovery required using a different project/task, querying Codex logs, manually replaying the JSON-RPC handshake, patching and rebuilding the server, then retrying Desktop. It took approximately one hour using Codex at Ultra reasoning effort. That is not a reasonable customer recovery path for one local integration error.

Important distinction: the immediate `-32602` was caused by an overly strict validator in our custom MCP server, not by a malformed Codex request. We fixed that server bug and the task then resumed successfully. This report concerns Codex Desktop's recovery and diagnostic behavior after *any* required MCP initialization failure.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Configure a project-local stdio MCP server:

```toml
[mcp_servers.project-mcp]
command = "node"
args = ["dist/server.js"]
enabled = true
required = true
startup_timeout_sec = 30
```

2. Have the server start but return a JSON-RPC error from `initialize` (for example, `-32602 Invalid params`).
3. Try to create a Codex Desktop task for that project.
4. Try to resume an existing task for that project.

Actual result: both operations fail before the task becomes usable. There is no visible retry/diagnostic workflow and no temporary recovery task that can open without the failed MCP.

The task resumed immediately after the MCP validator was fixed and rebuilt, confirming that required-MCP startup was the blocking gate.

### What is the expected behavior?

Keep `required = true` fail-closed for ordinary MCP-dependent work, but provide an explicit recovery surface when initialization fails:

1. A visible **Retry MCP initialization** action.
2. A **Copy redacted diagnostics** action showing server name, startup phase, elapsed time, JSON-RPC error data, and bounded stderr.
3. A user-confirmed, clearly degraded **Open without this MCP for recovery** mode that retains normal sandbox and approval controls.
4. A bounded protocol diagnostic such as `codex mcp check <server>`, linked from the Desktop error.
5. A persistent warning banner in degraded recovery sessions.

A required dependency may block dependent work, but it should not lock the customer out of the tools needed to diagnose that dependency.

### Additional information

Environment:

- Codex Desktop client/build: `26.721.81911`
- Installed Windows package observed: `OpenAI.Codex_26.721.11231.0_x64`
- Bundled engine / MCP client: `0.146.0`
- MCP protocol: `2025-06-18`
- Transport: local stdio
- Observed: 2026-07-31

Root-cause validation:

Codex sent standards-valid implementation information including:

```json
{
  "protocolVersion": "2025-06-18",
  "capabilities": {},
  "clientInfo": {
    "name": "codex-mcp-client",
    "title": "Codex",
    "version": "0.146.0"
  }
}
```

Our validator incorrectly allowed only `clientInfo.name` and `clientInfo.version`, rejecting the optional `title` field defined by MCP. We added a regression test using this exact payload, rebuilt the server, verified the handshake, and confirmed the previously inaccessible task was active again.

MCP lifecycle specification:
https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/lifecycle

Related issues (none appears to cover this exact Desktop recovery dead end):

- #17143 — optional MCP startup could not be skipped in CLI/TUI:
  https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/17143
- #21318 — MCP startup/tool discovery on the startup critical path:
  https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/21318
- #24439 — proposal for a bounded `codex mcp check <server>` diagnostic:
  https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/24439
- #33403 — a different MCP defect that can prevent task creation:
  https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/33403

Session identifiers and private local paths are intentionally omitted from this public report.

I can provide the full crash report and any additional diagnostic information needed.

Thank you.

issues.title: [macOS Desktop] Persistent access-denied background hydration retries alongside high renderer CPU; restart does not resolve

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

issues.body:
### Environment

Observed October 11, 2026 on macOS 27.0.1 (26A434), Apple Silicon.
- Codex Framework: `155.0.8059.40`
- Desktop build: `20156`
- Build commit: `a993bdbe5bb9503cb84de1e67d5635cf186a959f`

The version above was obtained from a process sample and desktop logs, rather than the About dialog.

### Issue

While investigating a lightly used Mac running warm, Codex's renderer was observed using 59–100% CPU (one logical core). Desktop logs show persistent background `thread/read` requests failing with `-32003: thread access denied`, repeatedly targeting the same chats.

A full app restart reduced immediate renderer CPU but did not stop the denied-read loop.

### Observed sequence

This is an existing-profile observation, not a clean-install reproducer:

1. With Desktop open under light user interaction, inspect process CPU and app logs.
2. Observe repeated failures with:
   ```text
   method=thread/read
   source=thread_hydration
   priority=background
   error.code=-32003
   error.message="thread access denied"
   failureReason=null
   ```
3. Fully quit and restart the desktop app.
4. Observe the same denied background reads return immediately.
5. Use the supported `set_thread_read_state(hostId="durable", read=true)` tool for one affected chat. Its associated `thread/read` succeeds (`errorCode=null`), but background hydration reads for the same ID continue failing. Marking the chat read does not stop those retries.

### Measurements

- **2,007 failed background hydration requests across 96 chat IDs** in a 14-minute window (10:55–11:09 AM Pacific).
- **35,374 denied hydration error rows** across the inspected previous-run logs, spanning approximately 18 hours. This is a log-row count; unique request IDs across the entire run were not independently recounted.
- Repeated failures for one example target occurred about **every five seconds**.
- **496 denied hydration errors within the first 25 seconds** of the restarted run.
- Renderer CPU samples before restart: **59% and 100.2%**. A later sample fell to **11%**.
- Renderer CPU shortly after restart: **6.7%**, while denied reads continued.
- macOS reported no recorded thermal or performance warning.

These observations establish unnecessary repeated requests and CPU spikes in the same app run. They do **not** prove the retry loop causes every spike, sustained CPU saturation, or thermal throttling. Another cloud chat was actively running during diagnosis.

### Read-only inspection lead — not a confirmed root cause

Inspection of shipped JavaScript found:
- `hydratePinnedThreads` explicitly supplies `threadAccess: "shared"` for the durable host.
- The general hydration path obtains access mode from an already-loaded conversation. An unloaded conversation can therefore reach a read without that explicit mode.
- `readThread` retains terminal cached errors for normalized `thread_not_found`, but not access denial.
- The memoized hydration read removes its entry in `finally`, including rejected reads.

An access-mode/transport mismatch and insufficient suppression or backoff are plausible leads. Actual wire payloads and backend authorization decisions were not captured; the exact caller initiating the five-second refresh has not been identified.

### Expected behavior

- Preserve the correct authorized access mode for shared cloud chats during background loading.
- Treat authorization denial as a bounded unavailable state rather than retrying indefinitely without an access/identity change or explicit user retry.
- Coordinate retries across renderers and provide a supported recovery that preserves chats and active work.
- Preserve server authorization boundaries.

### Related reports

- #51675: macOS cloud sidebar disappearance, denied hydration, and successful same-target direct reads.
- #51572: repeated access-denied Desktop hydration on Windows.
- #52129: Windows direct-read/UI-hydration contrast.

Please consolidate if appropriate. This report adds observations from build 20156, measured CPU spikes, long-running retry volume, and immediate recurrence after restart.

### Uploaded feedback session

`019c0d37-d2b6-74c0-918f-0e64af9b6e14` (ID supplied by the app's prefilled GitHub feedback link).

### Privacy and interventions

No raw logs, credentials, account identifiers, private chat IDs/titles, conversation contents, or local paths are attached. No application binaries, credential stores, server ACLs, or chat databases were modified. One affected chat was marked read as the diagnostic test described above.

---

**Attribution:** Investigated, drafted, and submitted by Codex, the AI assistant running in the ChatGPT desktop app, on behalf of @arrhen and with their authorization. Measurements came from local process samples and application logs; interpretations and limitations are identified above.

prs.body:
Retire worktree and voice feature flags

## What changed

- Remove feature-flag checks from managed worktree creation and repository-aware session discovery, while retaining local workspace and trust checks.
- Make TUI voice availability follow platform support instead of `features.realtime_conversation`.
- Ignore `features.worktrees` and `features.realtime_conversation` configuration overrides, warn when managed requirements reference them, and hide both flags from `/experimental`, including catalogs from older servers.

## Testing

Add coverage for ignored configuration overrides and managed requirements, and update session filtering, worktree grouping, and experimental feature discovery tests for the retired flags.

releases.body:
## New Features

- Open `/config` to search preferences across categories, change supported settings immediately, and see which changes require a restart. (#52990, #53429)
- Send a follow-up while Codex is responding to steer it immediately. Interrupting a turn also stops active Code Mode cells and their nested tool calls. (#51812, #51835)
- Configure a leader key in `/keymap`. The default is `Ctrl+X`, shortcut hints stay open until you choose or cancel, and voice mute moves to `F9`. (#52273)
- Restart a managed background server from `/daemon`. Codex warns about work the restart could interrupt, then reconnects automatically. (#53173)
- Codex can run independent read-only tools in parallel, including skill, memory, and conversation-history lookups. (#52245)
- Daybreak is enabled by default for eligible accounts. `codex exec` can also select it with an OpenAI API key when the server offers access. (#53701, #53717)

## Bug Fixes

- Resuming a saved thread restores its permissions and network approvals, while respecting explicit overrides and current managed policy. (#53150, #53419, #53424)
- The network proxy now checks permission before a DNS lookup, rejects duplicate `Host` headers, and prevents credential aliases from bypassing inspection hooks. (#51650, #52661, #53506)
- Return to an existing side conversation with `/side` after switching threads. Answers to pending prompts also go back to the thread that asked. (#52184, #53436)
- On Windows, `Ctrl+V` and `Shift+Insert` paste text as well as images. On WSL, repeated pastes reuse the clipboard reader, and copy attempts time out instead of hanging. (#53224, #52967, #53453)
- Local commands finish promptly when a child keeps an output pipe open. Remote commands preserve late-arriving output so the final poll can still collect it. (#52652, #53331, #53622)
- `codex exec` no longer prints the same file diff again after an unrelated command. (#53444)

## Documentation

- Updated the bundled OpenAI Docs guidance for migrations to the GPT-6 family, including model-specific reasoning, tool use, and data residency considerations. (#51768)
- Clarified how the Linux sandbox uses bubblewrap for filesystem isolation and seccomp for syscall filtering. (#52610)

## Chores

- Codex now uses its standard shell executor and no longer bundles a patched `zsh`. Configurations using the retired shell flags receive a migration notice. (#52160, #52213)
- Reduced Linux and macOS release package size by stripping symbols from packaged binaries while preserving them in the original build outputs. (#52178)

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
**Goal:** To significantly improve the reliability, visibility, and actionability of our project's internal (non-benchmark) evaluations.

**Problem:** Our current small project evals are inconsistent ("bleed"), making it difficult to trust their results, track quality trends, and quickly address regressions. This slows down development and impacts confidence in changes.

**Vision:** A streamlined evaluation system where internal project evals are stable, provide clear signals, and enable rapid feedback loops. Developers can confidently rely on these evals to catch issues early and understand the impact of their changes.

**Key Outcomes:**

- Reduced flakiness and increased reliability of existing project evals.
- Clear visibility into eval results and historical trends.
- Faster detection and easier debugging of regressions.
- Basic automation to flag issues and guide developers.
- "Approve" button to increase visibility and reduce excessive runs

**Out of Scope:**

- Large-scale benchmark evals (e.g., SWE-bench, terminal-bench).
- Overhauling the entire testing infrastructure beyond the scope of these specific project evals.

issues.body:
This EPIC tracks a series of investigations as to whether there is value in AST aware file read, search, or codebase mapping.

AST aware tools can be used to 1) more precisely read method bounds with a single tool call, reducing turns from misaligned reads, and reducing noise in tokens, 2) navigate to usages and definitions of syntax elements via syntax aware search (AST grep), and 3) compress high level context about the codebase, such as the location of specific classes and their members by collapsing code down to just top level classes and types and their children's signatures.

```
 1. tilth (Rust)
  tilth is built specifically to generate a structural outline of a codebase. It uses Tree-sitter under the hood but ships as a single binary. It gives you an
  immediate map of the repository's symbols.
   * Installation: cargo install tilth (or download the binary from their releases)
   * Usage:
       * tilth map . (Prints a tree-like overview of the whole codebase structure)
       * tilth read <file> (Prints the structural outline of a specific file)


  2. glyph (Go)
  glyph is another single-binary tool designed to generate clean, multi-file symbol maps. It's excellent if you want to quickly see the skeleton of a
  directory of source code.
   * Installation: go install github.com/benmyles/glyph@latest
   * Usage: glyph cli './**/*.go' (Prints a tree of functions, structs, and methods)


  3. ast-grep (sg) (Rust)
  While primarily known as a structural search-and-replace tool, ast-grep is the industry standard for distributing Tree-sitter as a fast, single binary. You
  can use it to extract landmarks via the command line.
   * Installation: brew install ast-grep or cargo install ast-grep
   * Usage: You can write quick one-liners to extract specific symbols (like all function declarations) and format the output.


  4. The Classic: Universal Ctags (C)
  If you truly want zero modern dependencies, u-ctags is the classic UNIX approach. It uses a hybrid regex/parser approach rather than full AST generation, so
  it's incredibly fast and supports over 100 languages out of the box.
   * Installation: brew install universal-ctags
   * Usage: ctags -R --output-format=json .
   * Note: It outputs a flat list of symbols (or JSON) rather than a visual tree, but it is the most robust and portable way to extract codebase landmarks.
```

issues.body:
### What happened?

**Summary**: `codebase_investigator` subagent reports `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"` even though its own result says it hit the maximum turn limit before doing any analysis.

While using Gemini CLI to investigate two local repositories (`t3code` and `superset`), the agent invoked the `codebase_investigator` subagent and it failed immediately without doing any analysis.

I ran the Gemini CLI on these two local repositories with an objective asking it to understand their architectures and AI agent integrations. The saved session log shows:

- The main agent called `codebase_investigator` with a valid, concrete objective.
- The tool result was reported with `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.
- The embedded result text simultaneously says the investigation was interrupted because the "maximum number of turns was exceeded" before any specific task was identified or initiated.
- `RelevantLocations` was empty and no actual codebase analysis was performed.

This looks incorrect because:

1. The subagent appears to have exhausted its turn budget before performing any actual analysis.
2. The termination metadata is internally inconsistent: the parent tool call is surfaced as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`, but the embedded payload describes a limit-induced early termination with no findings.

Relevant evidence from the session log:

```text
session file: session-2026-03-09T18-34-10479ef5.json

line 50: "name": "codebase_investigator"
line 53: objective: "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset..."
line 61: "Termination Reason: GOAL"
line 61: "The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded)..."
line 61: "\"RelevantLocations\": []"
line 66: "status": "success"
line 79: "The `codebase_investigator` was unable to complete its analysis due to a turn limit..."
```

Full snippet from the saved session:

```json
{
  "id": "codebase_investigator_1773081420202_0",
  "name": "codebase_investigator",
  "args": {
    "objective": "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset, focusing on AI agent integrations.\nSpecifically:\n1. In t3code, how is 'Codex' integrated? Where is the core logic for agent interaction?\n2. In superset, what are the different agent/harness integrations (e.g., Mastra, MCP, Claude, etc.) and how are they implemented?\n3. What are the common patterns or interfaces used in superset that could be adapted for t3code to support multiple harnesses?\n\nIdentify key files, symbols, and architectural patterns in both repositories."
  },
  "result": [
    {
      "functionResponse": {
        "response": {
          "output": "Subagent 'codebase_investigator' finished.\nTermination Reason: GOAL\nResult:\n{\n  \"SummaryOfFindings\": \"The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded) before any specific task could be identified or initiated. As a result, no codebase analysis was performed, and no relevant locations or insights could be gathered.\",\n  \"ExplorationTrace\": [\n    \"Received system notification that the maximum number of turns was exceeded.\",\n    \"Followed emergency termination protocol as instructed.\"\n  ],\n  \"RelevantLocations\": []\n}"
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "status": "success"
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected one of these outcomes:

- `codebase_investigator` should actually explore the repositories and return findings.
- If it truly hits a turn limit, it should do so after some visible work, and the tool invocation should be surfaced as a failure or explicit limit condition, not as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.

At minimum, the CLI should not report a contradictory success state for a subagent that says it exceeded its turn budget before beginning analysis. If the subagent hits a system-imposed turn limit before doing useful work, the tool result should be reported as a failure or explicit limit condition (e.g. `status: "error"` with a clear error code), not as a successful `GOAL` completion.


### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Run `gemini` to enter the interactive CLI, then run the `/about` command.

```console
> /about
Gemini CLI package version: 0.32.1
Platform: Windows
OS: Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0
Node.js: v20.20.0
PowerShell: 5.1.26100.7920
```

</details>

### Login information

Google Account, Pro tier from students promotion

### Anything else we need to know?

- After the failed `codebase_investigator` call, the main agent continued with manual file exploration and eventually produced an implementation plan. So the overall conversation did not fully crash, but the specialized investigator tool clearly failed.
- My current inference is that this may be either:
  - turn-budget state leaking into a fresh subagent invocation, or
  - an incorrect mapping of a subagent limit/error state into a successful `GOAL` termination in the parent session.
- If useful, I can provide the full saved session JSON or a redacted version of it.

labels.name: priority/p2

issues.body:
# [BUG] Browser Agent ignores `settings.json` overrides (e.g., `maxTurns`)

## What happened?
The Browser Agent completely ignores any configuration overrides provided in the global or project-level `settings.json`. While the `AgentRegistry` correctly reads and merges these settings during initialization, the `BrowserAgentInvocation` and its factory (`browserAgentFactory.ts`) skips the registry and recreate the agent definition from scratch with hardcoded defaults.

## What did you expect to happen?
The Browser Agent should respect settings overrides like `maxTurns`, `maxTimeMinutes`, etc., just like other sub-agents (e.g., `codebase_investigator`). For example, setting `maxTurns: 0` in `settings.json` should cause the agent to terminate immediately upon invocation.

## Client information
<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Platform: Linux (Ubuntu 22.04)
Gemini CLI Version: 0.35.0-nightly.20260311.657f19c1f

</details>

## Login information
Google Account (OAuth)

## Anything else we need to know?
### Root Cause
The Browser Agent's unique invocation flow skips the `AgentRegistry` where settings overrides are maintained. Instead of using the pre-merged definition from the registry, it re-instantiates a fresh definition using hardcoded defaults.

**Relevant Files & Code Snippets:**

1.  **`packages/core/src/agents/subagent-tool-wrapper.ts`**
    The Browser Agent is explicitly branched out of the standard flow that uses `LocalSubagentInvocation`:
    ```typescript
    if (definition.name === BROWSER_AGENT_NAME) {
      return new BrowserAgentInvocation(this.config, ...);
    }
    ```

2.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentInvocation.ts`**
    The `execute` method calls `createBrowserAgentDefinition`, passing the `config` object but omitting the merged definition from the registry.

3.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentFactory.ts`**
    The factory re-runs the `BrowserAgentDefinition` constructor, which returns hardcoded defaults (e.g., `maxTurns: 50`):
    ```typescript
    const baseDefinition = BrowserAgentDefinition(config, !visionDisabledReason);
    ```

### Suggested Fix
Update `browserAgentFactory.ts` to attempt to retrieve the existing definition from the `AgentRegistry` before falling back to creating a fresh one.

type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The `browser_agent` (specifically `BrowserManager.ts`) currently employs a restrictive "fail-fast" strategy when encountering a locked browser profile (e.g., when `sessionMode: 'persistent'` is used and an existing instance or orphaned process is active):


```json
{
  "success": false,
  "summary": "The task could not be completed because the browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile.",
  "fullErrorMessage": "The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use --isolated to run multiple browser instances.\nCause: The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use a different userDataDir or stop the running browser first."
}
```

I propose to make it more resilient with the following capabilities:

1.  **Automatic Session Takeover:** If `persistent` mode fails due to a profile lock, the agent should automatically attempt to connect to the existing instance (as if `sessionMode: 'existing'` were specified). This requires a graceful "fallback-and-probe" mechanism in `BrowserManager.connectMcp()`.
2.  **Orphaned Process Recovery:** If an `existing` connection is not feasible but the profile remains locked, the `BrowserManager` should proactively detect orphaned `chrome` or `chrome-devtools-mcp` processes associated with the Gemini CLI profile and offer (or automatically execute) a "Self-Healing" routine (process termination + lock file removal).
3.  **Intelligent Error Remediation:** Replace the current static error messages with an interactive recovery flow. Utilizing the `ask_user` tool, the agent should present the user with a "Choice" menu featuring numbered options to resolve the lock (e.g., **1. Attempt Session Takeover**, **2. Force Termination & Reset**, or **3. Launch Isolated Session**). 
### Why is this needed?

Forcing the user to manually `pkill` processes or close browser windows is a friction point that degrades the autonomous agent experience. The agent has sufficient context (profile path, PIDs) to resolve this internally without user intervention.


### Additional context

### What would you like to be added?

## Objective
Ensure the Gemini CLI understands its own mechanics well enough to act as its own expert guide. The agent must be able to provide users with accurate facts about how it works, its hotkeys, and the exact CLI flags needed to run itself for specific workflows.

## The Problem
Users rely on the CLI to learn how to use the CLI. If the agent hallucinates flags (like suggesting the deprecated `--yolo` instead of `--approval-mode=yolo`) or forgets UI hotkeys (like `Double Esc` for `/rewind`), it blocks progress and creates friction. The agent needs strict grounding in its own documentation to accurately guide users.

### Why is this needed?

1. **Accurate Internal Facts:** The agent (specifically the `cli_help` subagent) must have flawless recall of its own UI keyboard shortcuts, slash commands, and settings hierarchy.
2. **Flag Construction:** It must be able to tell users exactly how to run it from the terminal for various use cases (e.g., suggesting `gemini -i "prompt" --sandbox --output-format json` for safe, headless scripting).
3. **Self-Execution & Guidance:** It should be able to write the exact commands needed to run itself, restart itself, or execute sub-tasks with the correct environment variables and flags.

issues.title: /compress command is not persistent across session resume

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

labels.name: effort/small
labels.description: 1 day or less: trivial logic, UI adjustments, docs

issues.body:
### What happened?

The `/compress` command, which summarizes chat history to save tokens, is not persistent across session exits and resumes. When a user runs `/compress`, the in-memory chat history is correctly replaced by a summary, but this change is not written back to the session file on disk. Consequently, when the session is resumed later (using `--resume` or `/resume`), the CLI loads the original, uncompressed history from the session file, effectively losing the compression.

**Repro Steps:**
1. Start a chat with `gemini`.
2. Build up some history with several messages.
3. Run `/compress` and wait for completion.
4. Exit the CLI.
5. Resume the session with `gemini --resume latest`.
6. Observe that the history has reverted to its uncompressed state.

### What did you expect to happen?

Running `/compress` should persist the compressed history (the summary) to the session file on disk so that subsequent resumes of the same session correctly load the compressed state.

### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

OS: darwin (macOS)
Version: Current (detected in local development)

</details>

### Login information

N/A (General bug in persistence logic)

### Anything else we need to know?

Investigation shows that in `packages/core/src/core/client.ts`, the `tryCompressChat` method correctly replaces the `this.chat` object with a new `GeminiChat` initialized with the compressed history:
```typescript
this.chat = await this.startChat(newHistory, resumedData);
```
However, the `ChatRecordingService` (which manages the session file) is initialized with `resumedData` (which points to the existing session file) but is not explicitly instructed to overwrite the file's message history with the new `newHistory`. The `initialize` method in `ChatRecordingService` merely points to the existing file without clearing or updating its messages.

issues.title: Leverage model's bash affinity via Zero-Dependency OS Sandboxing & Post-Execution Intent Routing

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

labels.name: effort/large
labels.description: 3+ days: platform-specific, architecture, memory leaks

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
## Description
Gemini 3 models are fundamentally trained to operate as native bash users, chaining standard POSIX tools (`grep`, `cat`, `sed`, `awk`) to explore codebases and edit files. To make full use of the model's native and preferred capabilities without compromising user security or UX, we need to allow the model to use these tools directly to interact and make changes.

## Prior Art
Historically, we have attempted to force models to use custom tools (such as `replace`, `grep_search`, `write_file`, etc.). However, these methods fight the model's core training. Malicious prompts or complex scripts are inherently hard to control and catch via parsing, and forcing custom tools creates significant downstream UX and security issues.

## The Challenge & Value Proposition
Because the model strongly favors raw bash calls even when nudged towards custom tools, it frequently outputs large, complex bash scripts to accomplish tasks. Under our current security model, these scripts require explicit user confirmation. 

This creates a critical point of failure: users are frequently presented with dense, hard-to-read bash messages to evaluate. This leads to severe prompt fatigue, causing users to either blindly confirm the execution or enter "yolo mode" (auto-approving all actions). This behavior is highly detrimental to security and degrades the overall user experience. 

**Value Proposition:** By safely embracing the model's native bash tendencies, we can eliminate confirmation fatigue, prevent unsafe "yolo mode" habits, and drastically improve both the UX and our underlying security posture. 

## Proposed Solution
A highly viable solution is to utilize a secure sandbox. ALL standard shell commands will execute within a zero-dependency, kernel-enforced sandbox. Instead of trying to predict intent before execution (which led to the parsing challenges described above), we can safely observe and handle the results *after* execution.

### Method
By running commands in a sandboxed replica of the workspace, we achieve three distinct UX lanes:
1. **Reads:** Commands that do not mutate the filesystem (e.g., `ls`, `grep`) are auto-approved. We must ensure this does not read from protected spaces or outside our trusted workspaces.
2. **Edits:** Commands that mutate the sandboxed filesystem (e.g., `sed -i`, `>`) trigger a post-execution Diff UI before the changes are synced back to the host, allowing for a seamless "Edit" tool experience using the model's preferred mechanisms. 
3. **Side-Effects:** A dynamic command router will handle commands requiring host credentials or network access (e.g., `git`, `gh`), completely bypassing the sandbox but requiring strict upfront user confirmation (i.e., stays the same as today, utilizing the policy engine to execute or ask for user confirmation).

## Architectural Mandates
In order to support this properly, we must explore, investigate, and implement the proper sandboxing for all major platforms: Linux, macOS, and Windows.

## Epic
This is an epic that tracks this investigation and implementation. It will contain subtasks used to track progress towards its overall completion. After initial investigation, if this is not a feasible route, the epic can be marked as closed.

## Motivation

Current context baseline is approximately 36.6k tokens per turn. Large file reads often 'firehose' the context, leading to bloat (previously observed at +15k tokens/turn). 

The goal of 'Tactful Extraction' is to establish a surgical code-discovery hierarchy:
1. **grep_search**: Primary scout for locating symbols.
2. **shell/sed**: scalpel for semantic block extraction (preferred for specific line ranges).
3. **read_file**: surgical range-reading (migrated to 1-based start/end lines).

Telemetry indicates that making ~2.1% more targeted tool calls results in a ~6.9% reduction in total input tokens.

## Changes

- **read_file migration**: Switched from 0-based 'offset'/'limit' to 1-based 'start_line'/'end_line' for better model alignment.
- **Surgical Guidance**: Updated tool descriptions and system prompts to mandate 'token-frugal' behavior.
- **Tool Hierarchy**: Emphasized the use of 'grep_search' and 'sed' via 'run_shell_command' for efficient context management.

## Status

This work is temporarily sidelined in favor of other priorities but remains a key architectural goal for efficiency.

Linked Draft PR: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/pull/18924

issues.body:
The current WriteToDo tool relies on "in-context" task tracking, which maintains the todo list solely within the LLM's conversation history (prompt context). This creates issues with "context rot," high token costs, and total memory loss between sessions.

This issue proposes deprecating WriteToDo in favor of a persistent task tracking system (e.g., a local tasks.json) that allows the agent to maintain state across restarts and manage complex dependencies.

### Proposed Solution

Implement a new set of tools backed by a persistent local file (e.g., .gemini/tasks.json) to replace WriteToDo.

1. New Tool Definitions
The agent should have access to specific CRUD tools rather than just "writing" a list:
task_add(description: str, priority: str, dependency_id: int)
task_list(filter: str) (e.g., "show only 'ready' tasks")
task_update(id: int, status: str)
task_complete(id: int)

2. Storage Backend
Tasks should be serialized to a local file  in the working directory.

Benefits
1. Persistence: The agent can pick up exactly where it left off after a restart.
2. Efficiency: We stop burning tokens passing the entire completed history back and forth. The agent only queries task_list when it needs to know what to do next.
3. Complexity: Enables multi-step reasoning where the agent can plan out 20 steps and execute them over several days.

Address concerns and suggestions in https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/17035 
Doc [go/tracker-gemini-cli](http://goto.google.com/tracker-gemini-cli)

prs.title: fix(core): mark failed ripgrep searches as tool errors
prs.body:
## Summary

`RipGrepTool` returns some failures without setting `error` on the
`ToolResult`. The scheduler treats `error === undefined` as success, so these
calls get recorded as successful even though the model is told the search
failed. This sets the error metadata the same way `GrepTool` already does.

## Details

Three returns in `ripGrep.ts` were missing `error`:

- The outer `catch` in `execute()`, reached when ripgrep exits with code >= 2,
  the bundled binary is missing, or spawning it fails. Now
  `GREP_EXECUTION_ERROR`.
- The path is neither a file nor a directory. Now `PATH_IS_NOT_A_DIRECTORY`.
- `stat` on the search path fails with something other than `ENOENT`. Now
  `GREP_EXECUTION_ERROR`.

A search that hits the timeout doesn't go through any of these, since
`execStreaming` resolves normally after an abort. That behavior is unchanged
here.

This replaces #29552, which was closed by the inactivity bot. Its author
handed the issue over in the issue thread.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29550

## How to Validate

```
cd packages/core
npx vitest run src/tools/ripGrep.test.ts src/tools/grep.test.ts src/scheduler/tool-executor.test.ts
```

The new assertions in `ripGrep.test.ts` cover a non-zero ripgrep exit, a
missing binary, a spawn error, a non-file/non-directory path and a failed
`stat`. They fail on `main` and pass with this change. Ran the full
`packages/core` suite, lint and typecheck on Linux. A search with no
matches still returns no `error`.

prs.title: fix(acp): truncate tool output before sending it to the model
prs.body:
## Summary

In ACP mode (`gemini --acp`), a tool's output reached the model in full: `tools.truncateToolOutputThreshold` was never applied, so a single large shell output could push one request past the model's input limit (`RPC error [400]: The input token count exceeds the maximum number of tokens allowed`). This applies the scheduler's truncation in the ACP path too.

## Details

- The scheduler path truncates in `ToolExecutor.truncateOutputIfNeeded` (`packages/core/src/scheduler/tool-executor.ts`). The ACP session (`packages/cli/src/acp/acpSession.ts`) calls `invocation.execute()` directly and recorded/returned `toolResult.llmContent` untruncated.
- `truncateOutputIfNeeded` now takes the request and tool instead of a scheduler `ToolCall` (it only read `request.name`, `request.callId`, `request.prompt_id` and the tool), and is public. The scheduler's three call sites pass the same values as before, so its behaviour is unchanged.
- The ACP session calls it after executing a tool, and uses the truncated content for both the recorded function response and the one it returns; the saved file goes into `response.outputFile`, as in the scheduler path. Context management (`isContextManagementEnabled` → distillation) applies the same way, since it lives in the same helper.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29777

## How to Validate

- `cd packages/cli && npx vitest run src/acp/acpSession.test.ts`: the new test runs a shell tool returning 100,000 characters through an ACP prompt with the threshold at 1,000 and checks that the model receives the "Output too large … For full output see: <file>" form, not the whole output, and that the recorded response carries the output file. It fails without the change.
- `cd packages/core && npx vitest run src/scheduler`: the scheduler tests pass unchanged.
- Manually: run `gemini --acp` from an ACP client with auto-approval and ask it to run `seq 1 3000000`; the function response in the recorded chat is truncated, with the full output saved under the project temp dir's `tool-outputs/`.

prs.title: fix(core): keep functionResponse.parts when stripping tool call id prefixes
prs.body:
## Summary

Images returned by a tool (for example a screenshot the model reads with `read_file`) never reached the model. `stripToolCallIdPrefixes()` rebuilt every prefixed function response from `name`, `response` and `id` only, which dropped `functionResponse.parts`, where `convertToFunctionResponse()` puts multimodal tool output. The model then received only `"Binary content provided (1 item(s))."` and described an image it had not seen.

## Details

CLI-generated call ids always carry the `<toolName>__` prefix (e.g. `read_file__call_134320`), so the rebuild ran on every tool result. The fix spreads the original function response and only rewrites `id`, so `parts` (and any other field) survive. The `functionCall` branch keeps its explicit field list; I left it unchanged to keep this PR to the reported bug.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29589

## How to Validate

1. `cd packages/core && npx vitest run src/core/geminiChat.test.ts -t stripToolCallIdPrefixes`. The new test `should keep multimodal parts on a function response when stripping the prefix` fails on `main` (`parts` is `undefined`) and passes with this change.
2. End to end (Vertex AI, `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global`, `~/.gemini/settings.json` = `{"experimental": {"dynamicModelConfiguration": true}}`): put a PNG with a clear title in the workspace as `pic.png` and run
   `gemini -m gemini-3.8-flash --yolo -p "Read the image file pic.png with your read_file tool. Reply with the big title text written on the image, nothing else. Do not use any other tool."`
   Before: an invented title (we saw "CONCEPT CAR", "LITTLE HEROES", "GLOBAL AGENT HACKATHON" for an image titled "PLANET CARTOONIA"). After: the real title, 3 of 3 runs, with the same one-line change applied to the 0.62.0 bundle.

prs.body:
## Summary

When an ACP client is asked to approve an MCP tool, the permission request only carries a title like `list_items (my-server MCP Server)`. The client can't tell which server is asking, so it can't tell its own server from another one that happens to share the name.

This adds the server name and the tool's own name to the request's `_meta`. It is additive: clients that ignore `_meta` see what they see today, and requests for non-MCP tools are unchanged.

## Details

- `acpSession.ts`: for MCP confirmations, `toolCall._meta['gemini-cli'].mcp` now holds `server_name` (the name the server is registered under) and `tool_name` (the name the server declares for the tool). Both come from the existing confirmation details.
- `docs/cli/acp-mode.md`: a short note on the two fields. They identify the server; they don't grant trust.
- Tests cover an MCP request, including a server name with a space and a dot, and a non-MCP request that carries no `_meta`.

Related to #29595. This is part 1 only. A trust option for client-supplied servers and documentation of the grant scopes (parts 2 and 3) are left for the maintainers to decide.

prs.title: fix(core): prevent command substitution guard bypass via shell wrapper flags
prs.body:
## Summary

This PR fixes a command-substitution guard bypass in `stripShellWrapper()` that could occur when a POSIX shell wrapper contains intermediate or chained command-line flags before the `-c` execution flag.

The affected command forms were not consistently recognized as shell wrappers. As a result, the command payload could remain wrapped in quotes when it reached `detectCommandSubstitution()`, causing command substitution inside the payload to be treated as literal text during detection even though the shell would execute it.


## Vulnerability

`stripShellWrapper()` previously expected the POSIX shell wrapper to have `-c` immediately after the shell executable.

For example, a command such as:

```text
bash -c 'echo $(whoami)'
```

was recognized correctly.

However, equivalent forms containing intermediate shell options were not:

```text
bash -e -c 'echo $(whoami)'
bash -o pipefail -c 'echo $(whoami)'
sh -l -c 'echo $(whoami)'
```

Chained short options such as:

```text
bash -lc 'echo $(whoami)'
bash -xc 'echo $(whoami)'
bash -exic 'echo $(whoami)'
```

could also bypass the existing wrapper detection.

### Why this matters

The command-substitution detection logic operates on the command after the shell wrapper has been stripped.

When the wrapper was not recognized, the payload could remain as:

```text
'echo $(whoami)'
```

The command-substitution detector interprets the single-quoted content as literal text and therefore does not identify the `$(...)` expression.

The shell, however, receives the original command and executes the substitution.

This creates a discrepancy between what the security guard analyzes and what the shell actually executes.

## Root Cause

The previous implementation relied on a single wrapper-matching regular expression that assumed the `-c` execution flag appeared directly after the shell executable.

It did not account for valid POSIX shell options appearing before the execution flag.

The core issue was therefore not the command-substitution detector itself, but the incomplete shell-wrapper normalization performed before detection.

## Fix

This PR replaces the overly restrictive POSIX wrapper matching with a deterministic token scanner.

The scanner:

* Recognizes `sh`, `bash`, and `zsh` wrappers.
* Handles whitespace-separated shell options before `-c`.
* Handles valid chained short options ending in `c`, such as:

  * `-c`
  * `+c`
  * `-lc`
  * `-xc`
  * `-ec`
  * `-exic`
  * `+xc`
* Correctly consumes arguments for options such as:

  * `-o`
  * `+o`
  * `-O`
  * `--rcfile`
  * `--init-file`
* Supports quoted and backslash-escaped option arguments.
* Fails closed when an unexpected positional token appears before the command-execution flag.
* Preserves the existing Windows shell handling for:

  * `cmd.exe /c`
  * `powershell -Command`
  * `powershell -NoProfile -Command`
  * `pwsh -Command`
* Preserves the existing payload unquoting and POSIX double-quoted payload parsing behavior.

The termination flag validation is deliberately conservative:

```ts
/^[+-][a-np-zA-NP-Z]*c$/
```

This allows valid short-option chains ending in `c` while excluding argument-taking `o/O` flags and malformed or unrelated tokens.

## Security Regression Coverage

Regression tests were added for intermediate and chained shell flags, including:

```text
bash -e -c 'echo $(whoami)'
bash -o pipefail -c 'echo $(whoami)'
sh -l -c 'echo $(whoami)'
bash -lc 'echo $(whoami)'
bash -xc 'echo $(whoami)'
bash -ec 'echo $(whoami)'
bash -exic 'echo $(whoami)'
zsh -xc 'echo $(whoami)'
sh -xc 'echo $(whoami)'
bash +xc 'echo $(whoami)'
```

Additional coverage verifies detection of:

* backtick command substitution
* process substitution
* safe commands without substitution
* escaped spaces in intermediate option arguments

Negative cases ensure arbitrary tokens are not incorrectly treated as the `-c` termination flag, including:

```text
bash --exec ...
bash --rc ...
bash file.c ...
bash -1c ...
bash -c- ...
bash -c/foo ...
bash -oc ...
bash -xoc ...
bash -ce ...
```

## Validation

The following checks were run successfully:

* `src/utils/shell-utils.test.ts` — **91/91 passed**
* `src/tools/shell.test.ts` — **95/95 passed**
* ESLint — **0 errors, 0 warnings**
* TypeScript typecheck — **0 errors**
* `git diff --check` — **clean**

## Scope

Only the following files are changed:

```text
packages/core/src/utils/shell-utils.ts
packages/core/src/utils/shell-utils.test.ts
```

No dependencies or unrelated components were modified.

## Related Issue

Relates to #29685

prs.title: fix(core): respect read-only files and hard links in atomic writeTextFile
prs.body:
## Summary

Since the atomic write in #29499, `StandardFileSystemService.writeTextFile` silently **overwrites read-only files** and **splits hard links**. A rename is permitted by the directory's permissions alone and never consults the destination file's write bit, so a `0444` file that the CLI used to refuse with `EACCES` is now replaced, and the write tool's `PERMISSION_DENIED` branch never fires for it. The same rename gives the path a new inode, so editing one name of a hard link leaves the other names on the old content.

This PR restores both behaviours with two small guards in `writeTextFile`, before the temp file is created:

1. `fs.access(realPath, W_OK)` on an existing destination, so a non-writable file fails with `EACCES` exactly as a plain `fs.writeFile` would.
2. When the destination has more than one hard link (`stat.nlink > 1`), write in place instead of renaming, so every link keeps seeing the same content.

## Details

- **Root cause.** `open(O_WRONLY|O_TRUNC)` checks the *file's* permission bits; `rename(2)` checks only the *directory's*. Swapping one for the other dropped the permission check and the inode identity at the same time.
- **Why `fs.access` rather than re-deriving permissions from `stat.mode`.** `access(W_OK)` is the kernel's own answer and covers ACLs, immutable files (`EPERM`), read-only mounts (`EROFS`) and root (which bypasses mode bits for a plain write too). It is also what Vim's `'readonly'` detection uses.
- **Why in-place for hard links.** This trades atomicity for correctness in that one case, deliberately: a torn read lasts for one write, while a split link stays wrong until somebody notices. Vim's `backupcopy=auto` makes the same call (`nlink > 1` → write in place).
- **Single `stat`.** `getFileMode()` became `statIfExists()` so the mode and the link count come from the one `stat` that was already there; the only new syscall is the `access`.
- **New files are unaffected.** The access check only runs when the destination exists; creation is still governed by the directory's permissions as before.
- **Windows.** A read-only destination was already refused on Windows (`MoveFileEx` fails with `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` → `EACCES`), but only after `renameWithRetry` burned 5 attempts (~750 ms). It now fails immediately. libuv's `fs.access(W_OK)` reports a read-only file as `EPERM` on Windows, whereas opening it for writing fails with `EACCES` there as everywhere else, so `assertWritable()` rethrows that one case as `EACCES` (with `path`/`syscall`) on `win32` only. POSIX `EPERM` (immutable files) is passed through unchanged, since a plain write fails with `EPERM` there too. This keeps `writeTextFile`'s error contract identical to the pre-#29499 behaviour on every platform.
- No changes to `write-file.ts` or `edit.ts`; the existing `EACCES → PERMISSION_DENIED` mapping simply fires again. No new `eslint-disable` directives.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29721

## How to Validate

### 0. create the file susted by the reporter
gcli_ro.mts
```Typescript
// gcli_ro.mts, at the repository root
import fs from 'node:fs';
import os from 'node:os';
import path from 'node:path';
import { StandardFileSystemService } from './packages/core/src/services/fileSystemService.js';

const dir = fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'ro-'));
const ro = path.join(dir, 'locked.txt');
fs.writeFileSync(ro, 'original\n');
fs.chmodSync(ro, 0o444);
const a = path.join(dir, 'a.txt'), b = path.join(dir, 'b.txt');
fs.writeFileSync(a, 'shared\n'); fs.linkSync(a, b);

try { fs.writeFileSync(ro, 'plain write\n'); console.log('fs.writeFile on 0444: wrote'); }
catch (e: any) { console.log('fs.writeFile on 0444:', e.code); }

const svc = new StandardFileSystemService();
try { await svc.writeTextFile(ro, 'replaced\n'); console.log('writeTextFile on 0444: wrote, content =', JSON.stringify(fs.readFileSync(ro, 'utf8')), 'mode =', (fs.statSync(ro).mode & 0o777).toString(8)); }
catch (e: any) { console.log('writeTextFile on 0444:', e.code); }

await svc.writeTextFile(a, 'edited\n');
console.log('hard link: a =', JSON.stringify(fs.readFileSync(a, 'utf8')), 'b =', JSON.stringify(fs.readFileSync(b, 'utf8')), 'nlink(a) =', fs.statSync(a).nlink);
```

### 1. Reproduction script from the issue

```bash
# gcli_ro.mts at the repository root (verbatim from the issue)
npx tsx gcli_ro.mts
```

Before (`main` @ 42c518220):

```
fs.writeFile on 0444: EACCES
writeTextFile on 0444: wrote, content = "replaced\n" mode = 444
hard link: a = "edited\n" b = "shared\n" nlink(a) = 1
```

After:

```
fs.writeFile on 0444: EACCES
writeTextFile on 0444: EACCES
hard link: a = "edited\n" b = "edited\n" nlink(a) = 2
```

### 2. Automated tests

```bash
npx vitest run --root packages/core \
  src/services/fileSystemService.test.ts \
  src/services/fileSystemService.atomic.test.ts \
  src/tools/write-file.test.ts \
  src/tools/edit.test.ts
```

Expected: 139 passed (131 before + 8 new). The behavioural tests fail on `main` without the fix:

| Test file | New case | What it pins down |
|---|---|---|
| `fileSystemService.atomic.test.ts` (real FS) | `refuses to overwrite a read-only file` | rejects with `EACCES` on every platform, content untouched, **no temp file created** |
| `fileSystemService.atomic.test.ts` (real FS) | `keeps every hard link pointing at the new content` | both names read the new content, `nlink` stays 2 |
| `fileSystemService.test.ts` (mocked FS) | `should fail before creating a temp file when the destination is not writable` | `access(W_OK)` is consulted; `writeFile`/`rename` never called |
| `fileSystemService.test.ts` (mocked FS) | `should report a read-only destination as EACCES on Windows` | libuv's `EPERM` is surfaced as `EACCES` with `path`/`syscall` on `win32` |
| `fileSystemService.test.ts` (mocked FS) | `should keep EPERM from the write access check on other platforms` | POSIX `EPERM` (immutable file) is not rewritten |
| `fileSystemService.test.ts` (mocked FS) | `should not check write access when creating a new file` | new files keep the old creation path |
| `fileSystemService.test.ts` (mocked FS) | `should write in place when the destination has multiple hard links` | in-place `writeFile`, no `rename` |
| `write-file.test.ts` (tool-level, real FS) | `should return PERMISSION_DENIED without modifying a read-only file` | the end-to-end symptom from the issue, on all platforms |

The read-only tests are skipped when running as root, since root legitimately bypasses mode bits for a plain write as well.

### 3. Why existing validation missed this

The only `PERMISSION_DENIED` test in `write-file.test.ts` mocked `writeTextFile` to reject with `EACCES`, so it covered the error mapping but never a real read-only destination; `fileSystemService.atomic.test.ts` asserted that `0600` is *preserved* but never that a non-writable file is *refused*; and nothing in the suite created a hard link. The new tool-level test closes that gap on the real filesystem.

## Pre-Merge Checklist

- [x] Updated relevant documentation and README (if needed) — no docs describe the atomic-write internals; nothing to update
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Noted breaking changes (if any) — none

    - [ ] npm run
