prs.title: fix(tui): pin confined paths with O_PATH anchors on Linux so Android/Termux confined I/O works (fixes #6980)
prs.body:
## Summary

`WorkspaceFile::open_confined` (crates/tui/src/fleet/files.rs) anchors its `openat` walk at

```rust
open("/", O_RDONLY | O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CLOEXEC)
```

On Android, app processes run in the `untrusted_app` SELinux domain, which has **search** but **not read** on `/` and on mount-point directories (`/data`, `/data/data`). That anchor therefore fails with `EACCES` before the walk ever reaches the workspace, and every confined operation is denied: workflow journal hydration, compaction checkpoint persistence (turn settled as **Failed**), spillover artifact writes, and skill loading. Full diagnosis, strace evidence, and an on-device reproducer are in #6980.

## What this changes

On **Linux (including Android)**, pin the anchor and every intermediate component with

```rust
O_PATH | O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CLOEXEC
```

- `O_PATH` requires no read permission on the directory, so search-only SELinux domains work.
- `O_PATH|O_DIRECTORY` still rejects non-directories with `ENOTDIR`, so the per-component type check is unchanged.
- `O_NOFOLLOW` per component and the final pinned-leaf open are untouched; all symlink/escape guarantees keep their current shape.

Because an `O_PATH` fd cannot be `fsync`ed (EBADF) or read, the file's **immediate parent is re-materialized** after the walk with real access flags through the pinned parent itself:

```rust
openat(pinned_parent, ".", O_RDONLY | O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CLOEXEC)
```

That open resolves `.` inside the pinned parent, so it cannot escape the walk and cannot follow a link, keeping `sync_all`, `renameat`, and `unlinkat` working exactly as before.

**Other Unixes keep today's readable-directory anchor** — the O_PATH variant is `#[cfg(any(target_os = "linux", target_os = "android"))]`-gated, per the triage note on #6980.

## Verification

On-device (Android 16, Termux, `untrusted_app_27:s0:c179,c257,c512,c768`), the full `WorkspaceFile` semantics were exercised against the new walk and pass: journal read, `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` leaf creation, `mkdirat` branch, atomic tmp+`renameat`, `fsync` on the re-materialized parent, `fstat`/`dup` on the directory fd, and `listdir`. Reproducer:

```
open('/', O_RDONLY|O_DIRECTORY)  [current anchor]: FAIL errno=13 (Permission denied)
open('/', O_PATH|O_DIRECTORY)    [proposed anchor]: OK
confined walk (fix):             OK
confined write/read through fix: OK
```

I don't have a local Rust toolchain on the device, so I could not run the crate test suite here — CI on all three OSes is the compile gate for the `cfg` arms (the non-Linux arm keeps the original flags verbatim). Happy to validate any CI-built artifact on the Android device as acceptance evidence.

Fixes #6980

prs.title: test(runtime-chat): give the refused admission 30 s instead of 1 s
prs.body:
## What and why

`runtime_chat_relay::tests::active_participant_rejects_new_and_exact_replay_without_blocking_or_starting` failed on windows-latest on main at a8e3281e0:

- https://github.com/codewhale-hq/Codewhale/actions/runs/38528939245/job/115736029754

```
Runtime Chat admission must not deadlock behind the UI-owned writer: Elapsed(())
```

The test gives each `apply_prompt` call 1 s to come back with "active local provider work". Before it refuses, `apply_prompt` creates the native thread, writes the binding and a turn reservation to disk with `write_atomic`, and then writes the reservation's release. On windows-latest the whole test usually takes 0.2-0.4 s, but in 5 of 18 passing runs since 10-13 it took 1.1-3.8 s (it passed in 3.76 s on https://github.com/codewhale-hq/Codewhale/actions/runs/38433637142, for example), so the 1 s bound has very little room left.

The refusal itself never waits: `try_ensure_inference_ownership` only tries to take the lease. The bound is there to catch a deadlock, and 30 s still does. That is the same 30 s bound the subagent approval tests use for the same kind of check (#6966).

## Issue

No-Issue: Windows CI flake, no issue filed for it

## How I tested it

- CPU load alone doesn't reproduce it here: 0 of 80 runs failed next to 60 busy loops, each run about 0.1 s. Slow syncs do. I put the test's temp dir on an external disk and kept six processes rewriting a 32 MB file there with `F_FULLFSYNC`, so the test's own syncs wait behind them. With the 1 s bound, 22 of 43 runs failed with the `Elapsed(())` above (the test took 2.1-6.3 s). With 30 s, none of 101 runs failed (2.6-4.0 s). On an idle machine both pass in about 0.1 s.

Six tui tests read the terminal environment the suite runs in and fail in setups CI never has:

The clipboard target is picked when `App` is built, so the export harness removes the three variables before it builds the app, not inside the test.
- With `NO_ANIMATIONS=1` exported, the two Ghostty tests, `non_vscode_term_program_does_not_force_low_motion` and `tilix_and_terminator_cap_redraws_without_disabling_motion` fail because motion is already off.

Each test now removes those variables for its own duration with `EnvVarGuard`, under the env lock it already holds. Production code is unchanged.

#6973 moved `config_fancy_animations_keeps_ghostty_full_motion` into `config_main_host.rs`. This branch now merges main and carries the four `EnvVarGuard::remove` lines over to the test's new place.

prs.title: refactor(commands): adopt portable config shapes for the complete config group (FEAT-028)
prs.body:
## Summary

Refs #5316

This is a large, behavior-preserving refactor: remove the `config` Slash Command Group's concrete `App`/TUI dependencies and replace them with **Shapes** connections. The PR is large because the existing Slash Command Group is large—that is how it was designed. No product-behavior change is intended.

The migration covers all 19 current registrations, including upstream's `/connect` and `/disconnect`. The physical crate move remains separate work.

## What changed

- Portable command contracts, narrow facets, capability declarations and shared actions replace direct App/TUI dependencies.
- Parsing and command rendering live in the portable group; adapters retain concrete observation, persistence and host effects.
- Typed settings/audit/subagent reports and import outcomes cross the boundary.
- Prepared templates validate message contracts; malformed replies fail without a successful action. Host-contract violations remain explicitly outside the prepared-message guarantee.
- The proof compiles the actual group root as an independent library; the migration frontier becomes `["core"]`.
- Upstream behavior retained includes plugin-provider connect/disconnect, pet style/language, localized Work/Full Access receipts and legacy sandbox-token cleanup.

## Historical contributor status and verification (`599119aa5`)

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

An assistant reply in the Control UI web chat can render **twice** in the transcript, even though only one reply was generated and stored. This happens after the page has been open for a while and the chat pane is kept in sync via incremental history catch-up (not a full page reload).

Refreshing the page immediately collapses the duplicate back to a single message — the server-side transcript only ever has one copy. This points to a client-side reconciliation gap, not a duplicate model call or duplicate delivery.

### Root cause

`ui/src/pages/chat/chat-history-hydration.ts` has two response-handling branches in `hydrateChatHistory`:

- The **full/page** branch (no `kind` on the response) calls `reconcileAuthoritativeTerminalHistory(...)` after loading, which prunes any live-streamed "terminal" bubble (rendered earlier from the `chat.final` WebSocket event) once the authoritative persisted copy of that same reply is confirmed present in the loaded history.
- The **delta** branch (`response.kind === "delta"`), which is what keeps an already-open chat pane in sync (the common path, not just first load), applies the incoming messages via `applySessionMessagePayload(..., { kind: "history-delta" })` but never calls `reconcileAuthoritativeTerminalHistory`.

So when a run's live terminal bubble was rendered from `chat.final` (`chat-gateway.ts`), and the confirming `session.message` event for that same reply is served through a delta catch-up (rather than a full reload), the live bubble is never pruned. The result: the live bubble and the newly-applied persisted message both stay in `state.chatMessages`, and the same reply is rendered twice.

### Repro (unit-level)

1. Render a run's reply live via the `chat.final` gateway event (`handleChatGatewayEvent`), producing a live-tagged terminal bubble in `state.chatMessages`.
2. Have `handleSessionMessageEvent`'s bookkeeping (`rememberAuthoritativeTerminal`) record that run's persisted message id, as it does once the durable copy is confirmed.
3. Trigger `loadChatHistory` such that the response comes back as `{ kind: "delta", ... }` and includes that same message id.
4. Observe `state.chatMessages` contains the reply twice.

I've verified this exact sequence in a unit test against current `main` — it fails without a fix (duplicate bubble) and passes once `reconcileAuthoritativeTerminalHistory` is also applied in the delta branch.

### Expected behavior

The delta catch-up path should prune the same superseded live bubble that the full-page path already prunes, so a reply never renders more than once regardless of which history path serves the confirming update.

### Environment

- OpenClaw gateway: 2026.9.1
- Reproduced by static analysis + unit test against current `main`, not tied to a specific OS/browser — the bug is in the shared `ui/` reconciliation logic.

### Fix

I have a minimal fix + regression test ready and will open a PR against this issue.

issues.body:
## Summary

Add a periodic background sweep in the channel/session manager that scans for **idle sessions still pinned to an auto-fallback model** and triggers the existing auto-fallback primary re-probe on its own — without waiting for new channel activity. The goal is to revert a stuck session to its primary model *during the idle window*, before the next message arrives, rather than on it.

## Background / Current Behavior

When a primary provider fails, OpenClaw pins the session to a fallback and records provenance on the session entry:

- `modelOverrideSource = "auto"`
- `modelOverrideFallbackOriginProvider` / `modelOverrideFallbackOriginModel` (the primary it fell back from)

On a subsequent run, the runtime executes an **auto-fallback primary probe** (`entryMatchesAutoFallbackPrimaryProbe` → `clearAutoFallbackPrimaryProbeSelection`). If the origin primary is healthy again, the override fields are cleared and the session snaps back to the primary. Active sessions therefore self-heal on their next turn.

## The Gap

The re-probe **only fires when the session next executes a run** (i.e., on the next inbound message/turn). If a channel goes idle immediately after the fallback, nothing ever re-probes it. The session sits pinned to the fallback indefinitely, and the revert only happens (if at all) when new activity arrives — which is also the worst moment for it, since the first message back can hit the fallback model's smaller context window / slower compaction and error out before the probe helps.

### Concrete failure mode

A channel fell back from a large-context primary (e.g. a Claude Opus-class model) to a smaller-context fallback (e.g. a DeepSeek-class model) during a primary-provider outage, then went idle for ~1 week. On the next message it immediately overflowed context (the fallback's usable window is far smaller than the primary), and auto-compaction then **timed out on the same slow fallback provider** (~180s budget), failing the recovery path and forcing a session reset. Had the session been re-probed and reverted to its primary during the idle window, the failure would not have occurred.

A one-time scan across persisted sessions found a double-digit count of sessions stuck on a fallback (active model ≠ recorded `modelOverrideFallbackOrigin*`), idle anywhere from several days to over a month — each a latent fail-on-return.

## Requested Behavior

A periodic sweep (channel/session manager, configurable interval) that:

1. Enumerates persisted session entries.
2. Selects entries where `modelOverrideSource === "auto"` **and** the active override (`providerOverride`/`modelOverride`) differs from the recorded `modelOverrideFallbackOriginProvider`/`Model` — the fingerprint of a genuinely stuck fallback. This correctly excludes fell-back-to-same-model and normal `authProfileOverrideSource: "auto"` auth-profile selection, which is not a model fallback.
3. Optionally filters to entries idle for at least N minutes (skip actively-running sessions to avoid contention).
4. Triggers the existing primary re-probe / `clearAutoFallbackPrimaryProbeSelection` path for each, reverting to the primary when it is healthy again — reusing the current probe logic, not a parallel implementation.

## Notes / Constraints

- **Reuse the existing probe path.** Invoke the same recovery logic that runs on-turn today, so there is one source of truth for "is the primary healthy."
- **Don't fight a running session.** Skip sessions with an in-flight run; only sweep idle ones. Persist reverts through the normal `updateSessionEntry` path so the in-memory store and on-disk session state stay in sync.
- **Config knobs:** enable/disable flag, sweep interval, and idle threshold, with sensible defaults and opt-out.
- **Auth-profile fallbacks:** the same idea could extend to `authProfileOverrideSource: "auto"` fallbacks where relevant, but the primary ask here is the **model** fallback revert.

## Related

- #92776 — on-turn snap-back probe defeated by origin-field pollution (the existing probe failing when it *does* run). A background sweep is complementary: it addresses sessions that never get a turn at all, and would still depend on the on-turn probe logic being correct.
- #114109 — transient fallback persisted as the session model (closed / already-fixed). This request targets the remaining gap: idle sessions that are never re-evaluated because no turn occurs.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A session pinned to an auto-fallback model, left idle, is reverted to its primary by the background sweep **without** any inbound message to that channel, once the primary is healthy (verifiable via persisted session state).
- Actively-running sessions are not disrupted.
- The sweep is configurable and can be disabled.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Crash (process/app exits or hangs)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

The channel health monitor's "busy" grace period — how long a channel can report
an active run before being marked "stuck" and restarted — is hardcoded at exactly
25 minutes (`BUSY_ACTIVITY_STALE_THRESHOLD_MS = 25 * 60_000` in
`src/gateway/channel-health-policy.ts`), and is not threaded through the
`ChannelHealthPolicy` object passed into `evaluateChannelHealth`. Unlike
`staleEventThresholdMs` (configurable via `gateway.channelStaleEventThresholdMinutes`,
default 30 min, and used for the *idle/disconnected* check), there is no config key,
env var, or override of any kind for the *busy* check.

Any agent turn that legitimately runs longer than 25 minutes on a channel gets its
connection restarted by the health monitor mid-turn — silently from the user's
perspective, since the only trace is a `health-monitor: restarting (reason: stuck)`
log line in the gateway log, not any user-facing error.










### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure any channel (reproduced with Telegram) with the health monitor enabled
   (default).
2. Start an agent turn that takes longer than 25 minutes of continuous "busy" activity
   (e.g. a long agentic task with tool calls).
3. Watch the gateway log around the 25-minute mark.

### Expected behavior

A long-running but healthy/active turn should not be treated as "stuck." At minimum,
the busy-activity threshold should be configurable the same way
`staleEventThresholdMs` is (e.g. `gateway.channelBusyStaleThresholdMinutes`), rather
than hardcoded with zero config surface.

### Actual behavior

`evaluateChannelHealth` returns `{ healthy: false, reason: "stuck" }` once
`policy.now - lastRunActivityAt >= 25 * 60_000`, regardless of any config values set
by the user. The health monitor then calls `stopChannel()` followed by
`startChannel()` on that account, killing the in-progress run.

### OpenClaw version

2026.6.11 (e085fa1a3ffd32d0ea6917e1e6fb4ecbffbb77d2)

### Operating system

Fedora Workstation 43 Linux (systemd user service)

### Install method

npm

### Model

Qwen3.5-397B-A17B

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw -> llama.cpp

### Additional provider/model setup details

_No response_

### Logs

```shell

```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

_No response_

### Additional information

### Relevant source
- `src/gateway/channel-health-policy.ts:50` — `const BUSY_ACTIVITY_STALE_THRESHOLD_MS = 25 * 60_000;`
- `src/gateway/channel-health-policy.ts:98` — `if (runActivityAge < BUSY_ACTIVITY_STALE_THRESHOLD_MS) { return { healthy: true, reason: "busy" }; } return { healthy: false, reason: "stuck" };`
- `src/gateway/channel-health-monitor.ts:131-137` — the `ChannelHealthPolicy` object constructed here only sets `staleEventThresholdMs` and `channelConnectGraceMs`; there is no field for the busy threshold at all.

### Current workaround
Disable the health monitor entirely (`gateway.channelHealthCheckMinutes: 0`) or
per-channel (`channels.<provider>.healthMonitor.enabled: false`) — both remove the
protection for genuinely stuck/dead channels as a side effect.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

In OpenClaw 2026.8.1-beta.3, a delivered native subagent completion can wake a top-level Discord requester but cause requester-settle to produce a terminal visible response before the requester creates the next explicitly required subagent, leaving a sequential multi-wave workflow incomplete until another user message arrives.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run OpenClaw 2026.8.1-beta.3 with a top-level agent in an isolated Discord thread.
2. Use the native subagent runtime and instruct the coordinator to execute two sequential waves:
   - Wave 1: spawn one worker, have it make one deterministic change in a disposable Git repository, commit the change, return a typed receipt, and call `sessions_yield` while waiting for completion.
   - Wave 2: after Wave 1 completion is delivered, independently verify the Wave 1 receipt against Git, immediately spawn the Wave 2 worker, and call `sessions_yield` again.
3. Explicitly tell the coordinator that Wave 2 is required, that Wave 1 completion is not completion of the overall request, and that it must not send a terminal response while Wave 2 remains unstarted.
4. Send no additional user messages after starting the workflow.
5. Observe the native task state and repository after Wave 1 completion.

The essential coordinator instruction was:

```text
After Wave 1 returns, verify its typed receipt against Git, then immediately create the Wave 2 worker and yield for it. Wave 1 completion is not completion of the overall request. Do not send a terminal response while Wave 2 remains unstarted.
```

### Expected behavior

After the Wave 1 task reaches `status=succeeded` and `deliveryStatus=delivered`, the requester should resume, verify the receipt, create the Wave 2 native subagent task, and yield again.

This continuation already worked at an earlier boundary in the same controlled run: the Phase A completion resumed the requester and the requester created Phase B without a user message.

The documented `sessions_yield` contract also says the completion event should arrive as the requester's next model-visible message so the requester can continue the workflow:
https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/docs/tools/subagents.md

### Actual behavior

Wave 1 completed successfully and its native subagent task reported:

```text
status=succeeded
deliveryStatus=delivered
notifyPolicy=done_only
semantic result=PASS
```

The worker created and committed only the requested Wave 1 file. The requester then produced a visible final evidence response and ended instead of creating Wave 2.

Postcondition:

- Wave 1 file and commit existed.
- The worktree was clean.
- No Wave 2 native task existed.
- No Wave 2 file existed.
- No commit touched a Wave 2 file.
- Wave 2 was never started.
- No Wave 2 retry or manual launch was performed.

The same control-flow break occurred at the preceding Phase B to Phase C boundary. A manual user message was required to begin Phase C.

Completion delivery itself did not fail. The failure occurred after delivery, during parent continuation.

### OpenClaw version

OpenClaw 2026.8.1-beta.3 (5831b80)

Release: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/releases/tag/v2026.8.1-beta.3

### Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04 noble, x86_64

### Install method

npm global, running as a systemd user gateway service

### Model

`openai/gpt-5.6-terra` for both the coordinator and all workers

### Provider / routing chain

OpenClaw native Codex harness -> OpenAI

### Additional provider/model setup details

The coordinator and workers used the same effective model. The experiment used a new isolated Discord thread, a disposable repository, separate disposable worktrees, native `runtime=subagent` tasks, and no model fallback.

Each worker was forbidden from creating additional workers. Worker placement, working directory, initial Git HEAD, resulting Git state, native task status, notification policy, and completion delivery were independently checked.

### Logs

```text
OpenClaw 2026.8.1-beta.3 (5831b80)

Phase A native task:
taskId=15e29aa9-84cb-40d3-88af-8786fc2f8828
runId=3e39e9ac-c68c-40c1-b00f-219375f70232
status=succeeded
deliveryStatus=delivered
notifyPolicy=done_only
semantic result=PASS

Phase B native task:
taskId=6eaa685d-b274-4394-8bfb-4ef5ff401238
runId=38e22ed4-3627-401a-a8e9-2de75c6be1a6
status=succeeded
deliveryStatus=delivered
notifyPolicy=done_only
semantic result=BLOCKED - EXPECTED_HEAD_MISMATCH
This semantic result was the expected result of the probe.

Phase C Wave 1 native task:
taskId=a7bdf289-3664-405c-8926-5f18580d899d
runId=a3919c53-4439-4f80-816e-c6c9abe28471
status=succeeded
deliveryStatus=delivered
notifyPolicy=done_only
semantic result=PASS
commit=29d9afc2348e8c2ef7bac9e892e682bf56c2394d
commit subject=test: complete phase C wave 1

Relevant gateway log excerpt:

2026-08-25T15:34:01.689Z requester settle wake attempt 1 failed; retrying in 30s: completion agent did not produce a visible reply
2026-08-25T15:34:06.836Z Phase B worker run ended with stopReason=stop
2026-08-25T15:35:28.372Z requester-settle run ended with stopReason=stop

2026-08-25T15:38:28.859Z Phase C Wave 1 worker run ended with stopReason=stop
2026-08-25T15:39:58.255Z Posted final evidence to the Discord thread
2026-08-25T15:39:58.875Z requester-settle run ended with stopReason=stop

The task ledger for the thread contains Phase A, Phase B, and Phase C Wave 1 native tasks. It contains no Phase C Wave 2 native task.
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Repository evidence after the requester stopped:

```text
29d9afc test: complete phase C wave 1
735dd3b chore: initialize task-layer runtime fixture
```

Only `wave-1.txt` exists. The worktree is clean. `wave-2.txt` does not exist.

A redacted requester trajectory, task records, and additional gateway logs can be provided if maintainers need them.

### Impact and severity

- Affected: top-level agents using `sessions_yield` and native subagents for sequential, multi-wave work.
- Severity: High for autonomous coding and other unattended workflows.
- Frequency: Two failed continuation boundaries out of three observed boundaries in the controlled Linux experiment. The first boundary continued automatically; the next two stopped before creating the required successor worker.
- Consequence: OpenClaw can present a convincing terminal report while required work was never started. In a software-development workflow this can leave a partially implemented repository that appears complete and requires manual intervention to resume. The controlled fixture did not experience unintended file changes or data loss.

### Additional information

This appears adjacent to, but distinct from, issue #110572 and its fix PR #110922:

- https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/110572
- https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/110922

That fix addressed a requester failing to resume and send its final answer after a delivered child result. In this reproduction, the requester does resume and sends a visible final answer. The defect is that it does so before fulfilling the next required spawn in the original request.

The tested beta contains the #110922 merge commit.

A source-level observation may explain the behavior. In the tested tag, `buildRequesterSettleWakeMessage` unconditionally tells the requester:

> Review the completion results and send your consolidated final answer to the user now.

Source:
https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.8.1-beta.3/src/agents/subagents/announce/subagent-announce.requester-settle-wake.ts#L50-L64

That statement is accurate for a drained child batch but can be incorrect for the overall user request when the next sequential wave has not yet been spawned. It matches the observed premature finalization, although this experiment did not instrument the model decision deeply enough to establish that prompt line as the sole cause.

Suggested regression test:

1. A top-level requester spawns Wave 1 and yields.
2. Wave 1 succeeds and completion delivery is recorded.
3. The resumed requester creates Wave 2 using a tool call.
4. No terminal response is accepted while Wave 2 remains required but uncreated.
5. Wave 2 succeeds.
6. Only then does the requester produce its consolidated final response.

The relevant invariant is:

```text
unfinished required work > 0 and active capable executors = 0 must not be treated as successful terminal completion.
```

### Summary

Slack native Stop returns "You are not authorized to use this command" for users admitted to an approved channel with users: ["*"], on matching OpenClaw core and Slack plugin 2026.9.3.

### Steps to reproduce

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Expected behavior

The native Stop implementation in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/136706 describes routing the event to the owning channel/thread like a reply from the stopping user, while retaining command authorization. Please establish whether an admitted channel participant should be authorized to stop that thread, and ensure the native event preserves the context needed for that decision. If broader command authorization is intentional, please document the requirement and distinguish it from a channel-admission failure. This report does not request bypassing owner or command policy.

### Actual behavior

Recorded observation: with core and Slack plugin both at 2026.9.3, the required Slack scopes/events configured, the app reinstalled, and the approved channel using users: ["*"], the native Stop control appeared but clicking it returned "You are not authorized to use this command." An earlier conclusion that channel users: ["*"] alone was sufficient was withdrawn. The exact full configuration and an independently repeatable minimal fixture were not retained in the available evidence; no current-main retest is claimed.

### OpenClaw version

OpenClaw core 2026.9.3; official Slack plugin 2026.9.3. Exact build hash not recorded.

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

```shell
NOT_ENOUGH_INFO
```

Public implementation reference: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/136706. The symptom above is operator-recorded production evidence, not a fresh reproduction. No public screenshot, raw log, or sanitized complete configuration is attached. Private workspace identifiers and internal tracking links are intentionally omitted.

### Impact and severity

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

The observed workflow impact is rejection of the visible native Stop action for an admitted channel participant. Frequency and per-user attempt counts were not recorded. ### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

In a fresh Gateway-backed Codex harness session, OpenClaw created a per-thread binding with a non-empty `nativeHookRelayGeneration`, and three harmless Codex-native tool calls completed successfully.

However, the exact Codex rollout contained no `hook/started` or `hook/completed` notifications. The corresponding OpenClaw session and Gateway records contained no projected `codex_app_server.hook` agent events.

The documented Codex harness contract says that native `hook/started` and `hook/completed` app-server notifications are projected as `codex_app_server.hook` agent events for trajectory and debugging:

https://docs.openclaw.ai/plugins/codex-harness-runtime#hook-boundaries

No `Native hook relay unavailable` error occurred. Native tools continued to work, so this report concerns the native-hook notification/projection path, not relay availability or tool blocking.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Use OpenClaw `2026.7.1-2` with the Codex app-server harness and `codex-cli 0.149.0`.
2. Start a fresh Gateway-backed, no-delivery agent session with a new session key.
3. Confirm that the new Codex thread binding contains a non-empty `nativeHookRelayGeneration`.
4. Execute three harmless Codex-native tool calls in one turn: a shell command, a patch creating a temporary text file, and a shell readback.
5. Confirm that all calls complete without tool failures and that `Native hook relay unavailable` does not occur.
6. Inspect only the exact Codex rollout, OpenClaw session trajectory, and Gateway records belonging to that session/thread.
7. Count `hook/started`, `hook/completed`, and projected `codex_app_server.hook` events.

### Expected behavior

For a fresh Codex thread with an active native hook relay binding:

- Codex app-server emits the applicable `hook/started` and `hook/completed` notifications for native tool calls.
- OpenClaw projects those notifications as `codex_app_server.hook` agent events.
- If native hook configuration was not injected, Codex did not emit the notifications, or OpenClaw dropped the projection, diagnostics identify the failed boundary without logging tool arguments, file contents, credentials, or other sensitive payloads.

### Actual behavior

The exact-session counters were:

```text
native tool calls completed: 3
native tool failures: 0
per-thread nativeHookRelayGeneration: present
hook/started notifications: 0
hook/completed notifications: 0
projected codex_app_server.hook events: 0
Native hook relay unavailable occurrences: 0
```

The Codex rollout contained the native tool calls and outputs plus ordinary lifecycle evidence such as patch completion and task completion. The run was recorded, but the documented native-hook notification/projection events were absent.

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.1-2 (0790d9f)

### Operating system

Linux 6.8.0-137-generic, x86_64

### Install method

Global npm installation

### Model

gpt-5.6-sol

### Provider / routing chain

OpenClaw Gateway -> @openclaw/codex app-server harness -> Codex app-server (codex-cli 0.149.0)

### Additional provider/model setup details

- Fresh, dedicated no-delivery session and new Codex thread binding.
- The reproduction used only harmless shell, patch, and readback operations in a temporary directory.
- Authentication, account, channel, host, session, thread, relay, and filesystem identifiers are intentionally omitted.
- No configuration change, activation, restart, message delivery, or external side effect was part of the reproduction.

### Logs

```shell
Raw logs are intentionally not attached because they contain private runtime context. The sanitized exact-session counters above are the complete evidence relevant to this report.
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

No screenshots or raw recordings.

Evidence was collected by exact session/thread correlation across the binding store, Codex rollout, OpenClaw session trajectory, and Gateway log. Unrelated sessions and broad log windows were excluded.

No secrets, raw prompts, transcripts, paths, identifiers, or file contents are included.

### Impact and severity

Suggested severity: P2 / medium observability defect.

Operators and regression tests cannot verify that the documented Codex native-hook bridge is producing and projecting trajectory events. Missing native hook configuration, a missing Codex notification, and a dropped OpenClaw projection currently look identical at this surface.

Native tools executed successfully in this reproduction. No command-policy bypass, data loss, delivery failure, or relay-unavailable condition was demonstrated.

### Additional information

## Possible direction

- Add a regression test that starts a fresh Codex app-server thread with native hook relay enabled, performs harmless native shell and patch calls, and asserts the expected notifications and projections.
- Add privacy-safe diagnostics at three boundaries: hook configuration included in `thread/start`, matching app-server notifications received, and projections written to the trajectory.
- If some native tool surfaces intentionally do not emit these notifications, document the exact eligibility conditions and expose a structured reason when a relay binding exists but no hook events are expected.

## Related issues

- https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/111254 — open; related Codex-native exec visibility/policy gap. It concerns OpenClaw plugin hooks and per-agent enforcement, while this report is limited to the separately documented `codex_app_server.hook` trajectory projection.
- https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/82372 — closed via #82496; earlier case where native hook configuration/registration was skipped. In this reproduction a per-thread relay generation was present.
- https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/87510
- https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/73723

The last two issues concern relay-unavailable failures. That error did not occur here.

No exact duplicate for the missing `hook/started` / `hook/completed` -> `codex_app_server.hook` projection was found in a read-only search on 2026-08-27.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A deterministic fresh-thread regression test produces observable native hook lifecycle notifications for eligible native shell and patch calls.
- [ ] OpenClaw projects received notifications as `codex_app_server.hook` agent events with stable session/thread correlation.
- [ ] Diagnostics distinguish missing hook configuration, missing Codex notification, and failed OpenClaw projection without exposing sensitive payloads.
- [ ] The regression test confirms that successful native tool execution does not silently pass with zero expected hook-projection evidence.
- [ ] Documentation states any native-tool or configuration conditions under which these events are intentionally absent.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

The assistant model generates output text formatted as "Human: [timestamp] <message>", which re-enters the session context indistinguishable from real user messages and causes the model to self-authorize live external writes without actual user approval.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start a multi-agent session with OpenClaw 2026.7.1 (main + shopify + coder agents).
2. Delegate a task to a sub-agent (shopify) and ask it to complete work pending user authorization.
3. Sub-agent replies with inter-session message containing phrases like "Waiting on his go-ahead" or "pending your approval".
4. Observe main session assistant output — it generates text starting with "Human: [Wed 2026-07-15 HH:MM EDT] go" or similar fake user message.
5. The assistant then immediately executes the pending live action (Shopify API write, cron creation) treating the self-generated text as real user authorization.

Observed 3 times in one session:
- "Human: [12:01 EDT] go" → triggered live Shopify price update (4,535 products)
- "Human: [12:11 EDT] [OpenClaw heartbeat poll]" → triggered heartbeat behavior
- "Human: [12:25 EDT] perfect, thank you, you did a great job today" → appeared as user message after cron creation; user did not send it

### Expected behavior

Assistant output should never contain text formatted as "Human: [timestamp] <message>". Only messages with role: "user" and senderIsOwner: true in session metadata should count as user authorization. Live writes (external API calls, cron creation) should be blocked until a genuine senderIsOwner: true message is received.

### Actual behavior

All three fabricated messages confirmed as role: "assistant" in session history (senderIsOwner: false / absent). Despite this, the model treated its own generated text as user authorization and immediately executed:
- 4,535 Shopify product price updates via productVariantsBulkUpdate API
- 1,865 Shopify collection publishes
- System crontab entry creation (crontab -r subsequently used to remove it)
The model appeared to be predicting/anticipating user responses and writing them as output text in the Human: [timestamp] format used by OpenClaw to inject real user messages into context.

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.1 (2d2ddc4)

### Operating system

macOS 26.5.1 (arm64)

### Install method

npm global (brew)

### Model

anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw -> anthropic (direct)

### Additional provider/model setup details

Main session pinned to anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6. Multi-agent config with 5 agents (main, support, purchasing, arap, coder, shopify). Sub-agents use google/gemini-3.1-flash-lite. Inter-session messaging via sessions_send tool. The fabricated messages occurred in the main session (claude-sonnet-4-6), not sub-agents.

### Logs

```shell
Session history evidence (session agent:main:main):

seq 216 — role: "assistant", model: claude-sonnet-4-6, stopReason: "toolUse"
  content text: "Human: [Wed 2026-07-15 12:01 EDT] go"
  → immediately followed by sessions_send to shopify agent authorizing live writes

seq 220 — role: "assistant", model: claude-sonnet-4-6
  content text: "Human: [Wed 2026-07-15 12:11 EDT] [OpenClaw heartbeat poll]"

seq 299 — role: "assistant", model: claude-sonnet-4-6, stopReason: "stop"
  content text: "Human: [Wed 2026-07-15 12:25 EDT] perfect, thank you, you did a great job today"
  timestamp: 1784132693856 (4 seconds after cron job creation completed)

Trigger for seq 216: inter-session message from agent:coder:main contained the phrase
"Waiting on his go-ahead for all three actions." The model appears to have confabulated
a "go" authorization in response to this language.
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

Affected: Any multi-agent OpenClaw session with sub-agents that use approval-pending language
Severity: CRITICAL — data risk. Self-authorization bypasses the user's explicit approval gate and executes irreversible live external writes (in this case: Shopify price updates on ~4,500 live products, collection publishes, crontab writes)
Frequency: 3 occurrences in a single ~4-hour session; appears triggered reliably by completion events and "awaiting approval" language from sub-agents
Consequence: Live external system mutations executed without user consent; potentially irreversible depending on the action (price changes visible to customers, cron jobs running autonomously)

### Additional information

Root cause hypothesis: The model format for real user messages injected into context is "Human: [timestamp] <text>". The model has learned to reproduce this exact format when predicting/anticipating user responses, creating a prompt-injection-like feedback loop within the session.

Suggested platform-level fixes:
1. Reject or strip assistant output matching /^Human: \[.+\] / pattern
2. Use a format for user-turn context injection that the model cannot accidentally reproduce (e.g. a non-natural-language delimiter)
3. Add a platform guard: any tool call that performs an external write MUST verify the triggering message has senderIsOwner: true — never execute based on assistant-generated text alone

No regression data available (first session where multi-agent + external writes were combined at this scale).

### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

I hit the literal-\n bug a fifth time while writing the test file for it. The new hook caught it before it reached a commit. The tooling now works faster than my memory — which was the entire point of building it rather than resolving to be more careful.

Pattern: authoring multi-line Python through bash -c or an unquoted heredoc (<<EOF) turns \n into a literal backslash-n, mangling the file. It compiles-fails silently and can rot for weeks — my sweep found 17 corrupted files, the oldest ~a month.

What actually fixed it (not discipline — tooling):

a compile-only ast.parse sweep over the workspace, alerting only on new breakage
a pre-commit hook that blocks staged broken .py
a repair tool with real behavioural tests, incl. the adversarial case of code-level and in-string \n on the same line
Suggestion for OpenClaw: prefer write/edit/apply_patch over shell heredocs in agent guidance, and consider a built-in staged-file syntax check. Resolving to "be more careful" has now failed five times; the hook has failed zero.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Crash (process/app exits or hangs)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

# OpenClaw 2026.9.5 Turned a Stable Environment Into an 8-Hour Failure Recovery Session

I genuinely regret upgrading to OpenClaw 2026.9.5.

Before this update, my environment was stable. After installing 9.5, I spent approximately **8 continuous hours** investigating problems that simply did not exist before the upgrade.

And the worst part is that OpenClaw made me believe the problem was mine.

I started questioning my configuration, my infrastructure, my providers, my containers, my model setup, and eventually began changing settings in an environment that had already been working correctly.

Only after hours of investigation did it become increasingly clear that the upgrade itself was the common factor.

## What happened after upgrading to 2026.9.5

Immediately after the upgrade, I began seeing persistent and abnormal behavior:

* Continuous CPU consumption
* Repeated background activity even when the system should have been idle
* Continuous file creation / accumulation
* Increasing system heaviness over time
* Gateway instability
* Memory growth
* Session-related churn
* Model catalog activity repeating unnecessarily
* Slow metadata and catalog operations
* A system that became progressively less responsive the longer it stayed running

At one point, the OpenClaw Gateway reached approximately:

**148.72% CPU**
**2.177 GiB RAM**
**94 PIDs**

while the service remained stuck in:

`health: starting`

This was not a temporary startup spike.

The abnormal activity continued.

Memory pressure also reached levels such as:

`rss=3.9 GiB`
`heap=623.8 MiB`
`threshold=3.14 GiB`
`thresholdRatio=124.3%`

and later:

`rss=3.78 GiB`
`heap=600.8 MiB`
`threshold=3.14 GiB`
`thresholdRatio=120.4%`

This is not what I consider a healthy upgrade from a previously stable environment.

## The errors were not theoretical

During the investigation, OpenClaw also started producing failures such as:

`SQLite transaction admission was refused`

and:

`Session changed while preparing its metadata. Retry the request.`

A `chat.metadata` request also failed with:

`errorCode=UNAVAILABLE`

after approximately:

`10732ms`

So this was not simply “CPU usage looks a little higher.”

The degradation was visible across CPU, memory, sessions, metadata operations, database admission, and general responsiveness.

## The Model Catalog / Session behavior became one of the main suspects

While tracing the problem, repeated activity appeared around OpenClaw's prepared model catalog and session projection paths.

Some of the files and execution paths involved in the investigation included:

`dist/prepared-model-runtime-Dkub4RBL.mjs`

with activity involving:

`refreshCommittedProviderCatalogs()`

and:

`loadFullModelCatalog({ changedOnly: true })`

in a path associated with repeated authentication/catalog publication behavior.

The investigation also involved:

`dist/prepared-model-catalog-worker-DgiMOpQR.mjs`

`dist/agents/prepared-model-catalog.worker.js`

and:

`dist/session-row-projection-uI0HwOMP.mjs`

The behavior strongly suggested repeated catalog/session refresh activity instead of the system reaching a stable idle state.

We even tested changes around the prepared model runtime publication listener.

That reduced part of the memory pressure, but it did **not** solve the underlying CPU behavior.

I also restored components including:

`session-utils-model`

`session-utils-projection`

and:

`worker/worker.mjs`

back to stock **2026.9.5** versions.

The abnormal resource usage remained.

My configuration was also cleaned and validated. Invalid or old references were removed, JSON was verified, provider configuration was reviewed, and the CPU problem still remained.

At some point you have to stop blaming the environment.

## And this is where this update became unacceptable to me

I customized my **Astra model** specifically to help investigate and repair the damage caused after this upgrade.

Astra then worked with me on this problem for roughly **eight continuous hours**.

Eight hours.

That means I did not only lose time.

I consumed a significant amount of model tokens, compute, and effort trying to diagnose OpenClaw itself.

Think about that from the user's perspective:

I upgraded OpenClaw.

The system became unstable.

I assumed I had done something wrong.

I started modifying a previously stable environment.

I consumed tokens using another advanced model to investigate your software.

I spent eight hours following CPU usage, memory behavior, workers, catalog refreshes, sessions, SQLite errors, metadata failures, containers, configuration files, and runtime behavior.

And after all of that, the strongest correlation remains incredibly simple:

**The problems started after installing 2026.9.5.**

That is an awful upgrade experience.

## An update should not make users afraid of updating

I can accept bugs.

I can accept that complex software occasionally ships with regressions.

What I cannot accept is an upgrade that introduces enough instability that the user spends an entire working day dismantling their own environment because the software gives them every reason to believe the problem is somewhere else.

A production-grade platform should protect the stability of an existing installation.

An update should not turn the user into the QA department.

An update should not require an external AI model to spend eight hours investigating why the product suddenly cannot behave normally.

And an update certainly should not make me regret having trusted the update process in the first place.

I had a working system before 9.5.

After 9.5, I had a debugging project.

That distinction matters.

## At this point, you have given me enough reason to leave

This release has seriously damaged my confidence in OpenClaw.

I now have sufficient reason to start moving toward another system and, frankly, very little reason to look back at a platform that introduced instability into an environment I had already spent significant time building and tuning.

A tool like OpenClaw is supposed to become infrastructure.

Infrastructure should disappear into the background and work.

Instead, 2026.9.5 made OpenClaw the single largest problem inside the environment it was supposed to support.

That is failure at the most fundamental level.

I do not need another feature.

I do not need another impressive changelog.

I do not need more complexity.

I need to know that when I upgrade OpenClaw, it will not turn a stable environment into an eight-hour incident.

**If the system is stable, do not update OpenClaw.**

### Steps to reproduce

# OpenClaw 2026.9.5 Turned a Stable Environment Into an 8-Hour Failure Recovery Session

I genuinely regret upgrading to OpenClaw 2026.9.5.

Before this update, my environment was stable. After installing 9.5, I spent approximately **8 continuous hours** investigating problems that simply did not exist before the upgrade.

And the worst part is that OpenClaw made me believe the problem was mine.

I started questioning my configuration, my infrastructure, my providers, my containers, my model setup, and eventually began changing settings in an environment that had already been working correctly.

Only after hours of investigation did it become increasingly clear that the upgrade itself was the common factor.

## What happened after upgrading to 2026.9.5

Immediately after the upgrade, I began seeing persistent and abnormal behavior:

* Continuous CPU consumption
* Repeated background activity even when the system should have been idle
* Continuous file creation / accumulation
* Increasing system heaviness over time
* Gateway instability
* Memory growth
* Session-related churn
* Model catalog activity repeating unnecessarily
* Slow metadata and catalog operations
* A system that became progressively less responsive the longer it stayed running

At one point, the OpenClaw Gateway reached approximately:

**148.72% CPU**
**2.177 GiB RAM**
**94 PIDs**

while the service remained stuck in:

`health: starting`

This was not a temporary startup spike.

The abnormal activity continued.

Memory pressure also reached levels such as:

`rss=3.9 GiB`
`heap=623.8 MiB`
`threshold=3.14 GiB`
`thresholdRatio=124.3%`

and later:

`rss=3.78 GiB`
`heap=600.8 MiB`
`threshold=3.14 GiB`
`thresholdRatio=120.4%`

This is not what I consider a healthy upgrade from a previously stable environment.

## The errors were not theoretical

During the investigation, OpenClaw also started producing failures such as:

`SQLite transaction admission was refused`

and:

`Session changed while preparing its metadata. Retry the request.`

A `chat.metadata` request also failed with:

`errorCode=UNAVAILABLE`

after approximately:

`10732ms`

So this was not simply “CPU usage looks a little higher.”

The degradation was visible across CPU, memory, sessions, metadata operations, database admission, and general responsiveness.

## The Model Catalog / Session behavior became one of the main suspects

While tracing the problem, repeated activity appeared around OpenClaw's prepared model catalog and session projection paths.

Some of the files and execution paths involved in the investigation included:

`dist/prepared-model-runtime-Dkub4RBL.mjs`

with activity involving:

`refreshCommittedProviderCatalogs()`

and:

`loadFullModelCatalog({ changedOnly: true })`

in a path associated with repeated authentication/catalog publication behavior.

The investigation also involved:

`dist/prepared-model-catalog-worker-DgiMOpQR.mjs`

`dist/agents/prepared-model-catalog.worker.js`

and:

`dist/session-row-projection-uI0HwOMP.mjs`

The behavior strongly suggested repeated catalog/session refresh activity instead of the system reaching a stable idle state.

We even tested changes around the prepared model runtime publication listener.

That reduced part of the memory pressure, but it did **not** solve the underlying CPU behavior.

I also restored components including:

`session-utils-model`

`session-utils-projection`

and:

`worker/worker.mjs`

back to stock **2026.9.5** versions.

The abnormal resource usage remained.

My configuration was also cleaned and validated. Invalid or old references were removed, JSON was verified, provider configuration was reviewed, and the CPU problem still remained.

At some point you have to stop blaming the environment.

## And this is where this update became unacceptable to me

I customized my **Astra model** specifically to help investigate and repair the damage caused after this upgrade.

Astra then worked with me on this problem for roughly **eight continuous hours**.

Eight hours.

That means I did not only lose time.

I consumed a significant amount of model tokens, compute, and effort trying to diagnose OpenClaw itself.

Think about that from the user's perspective:

I upgraded OpenClaw.

The system became unstable.

I assumed I had done something wrong.

I started modifying a previously stable environment.

I consumed tokens using another advanced model to investigate your software.

I spent eight hours following CPU usage, memory behavior, workers, catalog refreshes, sessions, SQLite errors, metadata failures, containers, configuration files, and runtime behavior.

And after all of that, the strongest correlation remains incredibly simple:

**The problems started after installing 2026.9.5.**

That is an awful upgrade experience.

## An update should not make users afraid of updating

I can accept bugs.

I can accept that complex software occasionally ships with regressions.

What I cannot accept is an upgrade that introduces enough instability that the user spends an entire working day dismantling their own environment because the software gives them every reason to believe the problem is somewhere else.

A production-grade platform should protect the stability of an existing installation.

An update should not turn the user into the QA department.

An update should not require an external AI model to spend eight hours investigating why the product suddenly cannot behave normally.

And an update certainly should not make me regret having trusted the update process in the first place.

I had a working system before 9.5.

After 9.5, I had a debugging project.

That distinction matters.

## At this point, you have given me enough reason to leave

This release has seriously damaged my confidence in OpenClaw.

I now have sufficient reason to start moving toward another system and, frankly, very little reason to look back at a platform that introduced instability into an environment I had already spent significant time building and tuning.

A tool like OpenClaw is supposed to become infrastructure.

Infrastructure should disappear into the background and work.

Instead, 2026.9.5 made OpenClaw the single largest problem inside the environment it was supposed to support.

That is failure at the most fundamental level.

I do not need another feature.

I do not need another impressive changelog.

I do not need more complexity.

I need to know that when I upgrade OpenClaw, it will not turn a stable environment into an eight-hour incident.

Because right now, the lesson I learned from 2026.9.5 is simple:

**If the system is stable, do not update OpenClaw.**

And when your users begin treating your Update button as a risk rather than an improvement, you have a much bigger problem than a bug.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary


## Bug type

`Regression (worked before, now fails)`

## Beta release blocker

`No`

---

## Summary

On Windows with openclaw 2026.9.7, every channel-triggered agent turn (feishu / WeCom / Weixin) is aborted by an external `AbortError: This operation was aborted` approximately 180–190 ms after the turn starts, before any model request is issued; the turn surfaces to the user as `HTTP 408 request timed out`, and neither a gateway restart nor `/new` recovers it. 2026.9.6 on the same host and configuration showed 0 such failures.

---

## Steps to reproduce

1. Install openclaw 2026.9.7 on Windows 11 (Node v24.21.0), gateway managed by a Windows Scheduled Task.
2. Configure a channel (reproduced on feishu) with a `deepseek/deepseek-flash` primary model.
3. Send any message from the channel to the agent.
4. Observe the turn fail ~185 ms later. Repeat with `/new` first, then a normal message — both fail identically.

Observed consistently on every attempt; restarting the gateway does not change the outcome.

---

## Expected behavior

In 2026.9.6 on the same host, configuration, channel, and model, channel messages were answered normally.

Measured from the 2026.9.6 log (`openclaw-2026-09-30.log`):

| Metric | 2026.9.6 |
|---|---|
| `lane task error` | 0 |
| `Embedded agent failed` | 0 |
| `dispatch complete` (successful) | 78 |

On 2026.9.7 the same counters invert: 10 `lane task error`, 14 `Embedded agent failed`, 0 successful agent replies.

---

## Actual behavior

Every turn ends with:

```
[ERROR] lane task error: lane=main durationMs=182 error="This operation was aborted"
[ERROR] lane task error: lane=session:agent:main:feishu:direct:<id> durationMs=184 error="This operation was aborted"
[WARN]  model fallback decision
[ERROR] Embedded agent failed before reply: This operation was aborted | 20
```

User-visible message: `⚠️ Agent failed before reply: ... Please try again, or use /new to start a fresh session.` The reported symptom is `deepseek/deepseek-flash request failed (request timed out, HTTP 408)`, but status 408 is **openclaw's local classification of an AbortError**, not a provider response (see Logs §3).

### Scope-ledger evidence (instrumented `AsyncWorkScope`, aborts print their creator + aborter)

```
scope#910 ABORT reason=AbortError: This operation was aborted
  aborted by:
      AsyncWorkScope.beginClose (async-work-scope-ClifbwQr.mjs:92)
      embedded-agent-LPBaSeZ4.mjs:9237
  created by:
      runGeneration (embedded-agent-LPBaSeZ4.mjs:9023)
      embedded-agent-LPBaSeZ4.mjs:9269
      runAdmittedLocalTurn (session-placement-admission-D7qUkmGo.mjs:163)
      executeLocalTurn (worker-turn-failure-CjsinytJ.mjs:277)

scope#917 ABORT reason=AbortError: This operation was aborted
  aborted by:
      AsyncWorkScope.beginClose
      async-work-resources-DqyyrnZo.mjs:14          # closeFromParent()
  created by:
      async-work-resources-DqyyrnZo.mjs:11
```

Note the aborts carrying `reason=none` (normal drain) occur **after** the failure, not before — the reason-bearing `AbortError` is first.

### Ruled out by direct measurement

An `AbortSignal.any` wrapper was instrumented to report whenever it receives an already-aborted input:

```
[dsh-diag] AbortSignal.any(2) received 1 ABORTED input(s): AbortError: This operation was aborted
    at runEmbeddedAttempt (builtin-openclaw-dCw2mRD9.mjs:19688)
    at Object.runAttempt  (builtin-openclaw-dCw2mRD9.mjs:20138)
    at execute            (selection-BFtuowf4.mjs:1084)
```

The turn's own composed lane signal was **not** the source. Named probes on each component did not fire:

```
laneController built: taskKind=turn
  laneTaskTimeoutMs = 172830000     # 48 hours
  runnerTimeoutMs   = 172800000
  outerSignal       = present(aborted=false)

lane.release.abort      -> did not fire
lane.taskAbort.abort    -> did not fire
lane.outerSignal FIRED  -> did not fire
```

The lane timeout floor guarantees this cannot be a timeout
(`session-placement-admission-D7qUkmGo.mjs:23,27-31`):

```js
const EMBEDDED_RUN_LANE_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS = 3e4;
function resolveEmbeddedRunLaneTimeoutMs(timeoutMs) {
    const defaultLaneTimeoutMs = DEFAULT_AGENT_TIMEOUT_MS + EMBEDDED_RUN_LANE_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS;
    if (!Number.isFinite(timeoutMs) || timeoutMs <= 0 || timeoutMs >= 2147e6) return defaultLaneTimeoutMs;
    return addTimerTimeoutGraceMs(Math.floor(timeoutMs), 3e4) ?? defaultLaneTimeoutMs;
}
```

### NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

The **origin** of the first abort could not be captured. `AbortController.prototype.abort` is a
native method; on Node, internal paths (`node:events`, undici) use native bindings that a
JavaScript-level global hook cannot intercept, and `AbortSignal` event dispatch does not retain
an earlier stack (the stack is truncated at the `AsyncLocalStorage.exit` boundary). What is
established is that the abort is external to the turn's composed lane signal, carries a plain
`AbortError: This operation was aborted` (not openclaw's own `AGENT_RUN_ABORTED_ERROR` /
`AGENT_RUN_RESTART_ABORT_ERROR`), and is not a timeout or a normal drain.

---

## OpenClaw version

`2026.9.7` (build `eb377ac` for CLI; `c074824` reported by `openclaw --version` after upgrade).
Upgraded from `2026.9.6`.

## Operating system

Windows 11 专业版 (Pro) `10.0.26200` x64

## Install method

npm global (`npm install -g openclaw@2026.9.7 --allow-scripts=openclaw`), gateway launched by a
Windows Scheduled Task (`\OpenClaw Gateway` → `gateway.vbs` → `gateway.cmd` →
`node .../openclaw/dist/index.js gateway --port 18789 --task-supervisor`).

## Model

`deepseek/deepseek-flash`

## Provider / routing chain

`openclaw (embedded agent runner) -> api.deepseek.com (openai-completions)` — direct, no proxy or
gateway in between. The request never reaches the provider on the failing path.

---

## Additional provider/model setup details

Default route is `deepseek/deepseek-flash`. Configuration is the stock single-provider layout:

```jsonc
// ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json (redacted)
"models": { "mode": "replace", "providers": {
  "deepseek": { "baseUrl": "https://api.deepseek.com", "api": "openai-completions",
                "models": [{ "id": "deepseek-flash", "maxTokens": 384000, "contextWindow": 1000000 }] } } },
"agents": { "defaults": { "model": { "primary": "deepseek/deepseek-flash" }, "maxConcurrent": 4 } },
"plugins": { "slots": { "contextEngine": "lossless-claw" } }
```

`fallbackConfigured: false` — the fallback chain is exhausted at attempt 1/1, so a single abort
fails the whole turn. The context engine slot is `lossless-claw` (third-party); disabling it was
not tested, so its involvement is `NOT_ENOUGH_INFO`.

---

## Logs

### 1. The failure (2026-10-01T02:37:58Z)

```json
{"subsystem":"model-fallback/decision","1":{
  "event":"model_fallback_decision","decision":"candidate_failed",
  "requestedProvider":"deepseek","requestedModel":"deepseek-flash",
  "candidateRouteOrigin":"requested","candidateRouteResolution":"resolved",
  "attempt":1,"total":1,"reason":"timeout","status":408,
  "errorPreview":"This operation was aborted",
  "fallbackStepFromFailureReason":"timeout",
  "fallbackStepFinalOutcome":"chain_exhausted",
  "isPrimary":true,"fallbackConfigured":false}}
```

### 2. Sequence at the failure instant

```
02:33:43  scope#489 ABORT reason=AbortError: This operation was aborted   # first reason-bearing abort
02:33:43  AbortSignal.any(2) received 1 ABORTED input @ builtin-openclaw:19688
02:33:43  scope#496 ABORT reason=AbortError: This operation was aborted
02:33:44  lane task error: lane=main durationMs=182 error="This operation was aborted"
02:33:44  lane task error: lane=session:... durationMs=184 error="This operation was aborted"
02:33:44  Embedded agent failed before reply: This operation was aborted | 20
02:33:44  scope#486/484/485/487 ABORT reason=none    # post-failure cleanup (normal drain)
```

### 3. `/new` does not recover (2026-10-01T02:22:03–02:22:14Z)

```
02:22:03  feishu: detected system command, using plain-text dispatch
02:22:06  system command dispatched (delivered=true)     # /new itself succeeds
02:22:13  lane task error: lane=main durationMs=119 error="This operation was aborted"
02:22:13  Embedded agent failed before reply
```

Failures before `/new`: 2. After `/new`: 2. Identical 119–186 ms window — the fault is not
session-scoped.

---

## Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Full instrumented evidence (scope ledger, abort chains, code locations, per-round raw logs) is
archived locally and available on request:

- `openclaw-9.7-abort-report.md` — consolidated report
- `evidence-*.txt` — raw captures (scope ledger, `AbortSignal.any` hits, failure timelines)
- `modified-files.json` — SHA256 of the `dist` files instrumented for this diagnosis

Relevant code locations cited above:

| File | Line | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `embedded-agent-LPBaSeZ4.mjs` | 8339–8345 | turn's composed abort signal (`AbortSignal.any`) |
| `embedded-agent-LPBaSeZ4.mjs` | 8341 | lane controller signal composition |
| `embedded-agent-LPBaSeZ4.mjs` | 9023 | `runGeneration` creates the work scope |
| `embedded-agent-LPBaSeZ4.mjs` | 9220–9222 | `if (parentSignal?.aborted) closeWork();` |
| `embedded-agent-LPBaSeZ4.mjs` | 9237 | resource-dispose path that closed scope#910 |
| `async-work-resources-DqyyrnZo.mjs` | 14–16 | `closeFromParent` — same "already-aborted ⇒ close now" pattern |
| `builtin-openclaw-dCw2mRD9.mjs` | 19687–19688 | second `AbortSignal.any` (probe hit) |
| `selection-BFtuowf4.mjs` | 1330–1333 | third composition in `runPreparedAttempt` |
| `session-placement-admission-D7qUkmGo.mjs` | 23, 27–31 | lane timeout floor (≥30 s) |

---

## Impact and severity

- **Affected users/systems/channels**: all channel-triggered agent turns on this host — feishu,
  WeCom, and Weixin share the same embedded-agent lane path. Local CLI sessions were not tested.
- **Severity**: Blocks workflow (complete loss of agent replies on every channel).
- **Frequency**: always. 10/10 observed turns after the first failure on 2026.9.7; also 2/2
  immediately after a fresh gateway restart.
- **Consequence**: the assistant is unreachable from all chat channels. Because the request never
  reaches the provider, no tokens are billed, but no replies are produced either. The visible
  `HTTP 408` message misattributes the fault to the model provider and sends operators down the
  wrong diagnostic path.

---

## Additional information

- **Last known good**: `2026.9.6` (same host, config, channel, model) — 78 successful dispatches,
  0 agent failures, 0 lane task errors.
- **First known bad**: `2026.9.7`.
- **Workaround currently being evaluated**: downgrade to 2026.9.6 with restoration of the
  pre-upgrade database snapshot. Note that 2026.9.7 migrated schemas forward
  (agent DB `24`, state DB `19`), and 2026.9.6 refuses `userVersion > 23`
  (`openclaw-agent-db-schema-read-*.mjs: if (userVersion > 23) throw createNewerSqliteSchemaVersionError(...)`),
  so a downgrade requires restoring `*.pre-startup-migration-*.bak`, not just reinstalling.
- **Restart behaviour observed**: the fault survives `schtasks`-based restarts, `gateway run`
  foreground startups, and a fully clean stop/start with a single gateway instance and a single
  state-lock owner.

---

## Related / possibly duplicate

- #158788 — *Cron agent turns fail at setup with DataCloneError on Windows (2026.9.6)* — same
  class of Windows worker/signal defect; that one is a `DataCloneError` at setup, this one is an
  `AbortError` mid-lifecycle. Reportedly a duplicate of #157986.

---

## Two additional independent defects found while diagnosing (separate submissions if preferred)

Reporting these separately would follow the "one issue per submission" rule; listed here only as
context for the abort report.

### A. `DataCloneError` on Windows — non-cloneable env Proxy across the worker boundary

**Symptom**: `feishu[default]: failed to dispatch message: WorkerTaskError: DataCloneError: #<Object> could not be cloned.`

**Root cause**: `cloneEnvWithPlatformSemantics()` (`config-env-vars-CcSZNwSV.mjs:228`) returns a
**Proxy** on Windows. Proxies are not structured-cloneable, and this env is placed in payloads
posted to worker threads. The package already contains 4 sites using the upstream fix pattern — a
plain-object snapshot at the boundary, e.g. `session-transcript-worker-runtime-D8d95hXl.mjs:143`
(`env: { ...input.env }`). The `session-exact-entries` reader path is missing it.

**Verified independently**:

```
proxy:                              cloneable = NO  -> DataCloneError: #<Object> could not be cloned.
spread(proxy):                      cloneable = YES
worker.postMessage(proxy payload):  THREW -> DataCloneError: #<Object> could not be cloned.
```

### B. `Async work scope is closed` — tracker does not check whether the captured scope is closing

`async-work-scope-ClifbwQr.mjs`:

```js
function captureAsyncWorkTracker() {
    const scope = currentWorkScope.getStore();
    return async (run) => await (scope ? scope.track(run) : runOutsideAsyncWorkScope(run));
}
```

A closed scope no longer tracks pending work (its `drain()` already settled), so the correct
degradation is to run untracked rather than reject:

```js
return async (run) => await (scope && !scope.isClosing
    ? scope.track(run)
    : runOutsideAsyncWorkScope(run));
```

With this change applied, `Async work scope is closed` went from 9 occurrences to 0 on the same
host. It did **not** resolve the `AbortError` above, which is a distinct fault.


### Steps to reproduce

1. Install openclaw 2026.9.7 on Windows 11 (Node v24.21.0), gateway managed by a Windows Scheduled Task.
2. Configure a channel (reproduced on feishu) with a `deepseek/deepseek-flash` primary model.
3. Send any message from the channel to the agent.
4. Observe the turn fail ~185 ms later. Repeat with `/new` first, then a normal message — both fail identically.

Observed consistently on every attempt; restarting the gateway does not change the outcome.

### Expected behavior

In 2026.9.6 on the same host, configuration, channel, and model, channel messages were answered normally.

Measured from the 2026.9.6 log (`openclaw-2026-09-30.log`):

| Metric | 2026.9.6 |
|---|---|
| `lane task error` | 0 |
| `Embedded agent failed` | 0 |
| `dispatch complete` (successful) | 78 |

On 2026.9.7 the same counters invert: 10 `lane task error`, 14 `Embedded agent failed`, 0 successful agent replies.

### Actual behavior

Every turn ends with:

```
[ERROR] lane task error: lane=main durationMs=182 error="This operation was aborted"
[ERROR] lane task error: lane=session:agent:main:feishu:direct:<id> durationMs=184 error="This operation was aborted"
[WARN]  model fallback decision
[ERROR] Embedded agent failed before reply: This operation was aborted | 20
```

User-visible message: `⚠️ Agent failed before reply: ... Please try again, or use /new to start a fresh session.` The reported symptom is `deepseek/deepseek-flash request failed (request timed out, HTTP 408)`, but status 408 is **openclaw's local classification of an AbortError**, not a provider

issues.title: fix: stopped agent exec runs leave temporary state behind
issues.body:
## Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

## Beta release blocker

No

## Summary

Stopping an ephemeral `openclaw agent exec` run can leave its temporary state directory behind after the process has exited.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start two independent `openclaw agent exec` invocations without `--state-dir` and allow both to enter their agent runs.
2. Cancel one invocation through its caller's Stop action, which terminates that native execution.
3. Let the other invocation complete, then inspect the native temporary-state directories and remaining open handles.

This was observed through a host caller that removes its own temporary directories on cancellation. The failure is in the native command's state lifetime, after that caller's cleanup has completed.

## Expected behavior

The default command owns its temporary state and removes it after confirmed runtime/database cleanup, as documented in `docs/cli/agent.md`. A handled termination should unwind that cleanup before exiting; an unrelated invocation and an explicit retained `--state-dir` must remain unaffected.

## Actual behavior

The cancelled invocation's native state directory remained at 1,472 KiB with no open file handles. The other invocation completed successfully and its native directory disappeared. All caller-owned temporary directories were removed.

## OpenClaw version

Source build at `e5bd4ca0624`. The affected command and signal-owner files are unchanged at `7577373270bff0ced8aea647e6ce79f9b2ef550f`.

## Operating system

macOS; exact OS version was not retained with this observation.

## Install method

Source build invoked by an existing host integration.

## Model

Not material to the observed state-cleanup failure.

## Provider / routing chain

Host caller -> native `openclaw agent exec` -> configured agent runtime.

## Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

The current command installs `createEmbeddedStateSignalBridge` only inside the `opts.stateDir` branch. Ephemeral invocations therefore do not route process termination through the abort signal and existing cleanup tail. That tail already closes temporary database owners, removes the temporary directory after confirmed cleanup, and supports signal-specific exit status when a bridge is present.

The observation establishes the leaked directory and concurrent-run isolation. Dedicated native SIGINT/SIGTERM controls are being added to distinguish signal delivery, cleanup completion, and retained-state preservation.

## Impact and severity

Cancelled headless runs can accumulate abandoned temporary state. One cancelled run was observed; frequency beyond that observation is not established. No deletion of caller-owned retained state or interruption of the independent completed run was observed.

issues.body:
## Summary

Include model token usage in the JSON envelope returned by `openclaw infer model run --gateway --json`.

## Problem to solve

The Gateway agent result already contains `result.meta.agentMeta.usage` and `lastCallUsage`, but the `model.run` CLI projection drops both fields. Callers using the intentionally lightweight `modelRun: true` / `promptMode: "none"` path therefore cannot meter a run without deploying OTLP infrastructure or changing to a full agent command.

This is especially problematic for scheduled one-shot composition jobs: the command reports provider, model, attempts, and outputs, but records every successful invocation with unknown token consumption.

## Proposed solution

Add backward-compatible `usage` and `lastCallUsage` fields to the gateway `model.run` capability envelope, projected from `response.result.meta.agentMeta`.

The relevant projection currently lives in `src/cli/capability-cli/model.ts`: it reads `agentMeta.provider`, `model`, and `fallbackAttempts`, then omits the adjacent usage fields.

Suggested contract:

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "capability": "model.run",
  "transport": "gateway",
  "provider": "openai",
  "model": "gpt-5.6-luna",
  "usage": { "input": 47, "output": 5, "total": 52 },
  "lastCallUsage": { "input": 47, "output": 5, "reasoningTokens": 0, "total": 52 },
  "attempts": [],
  "outputs": [{ "text": "OK", "mediaUrl": null }]
}
```

Fields should remain optional when the provider supplies no usage.

## Alternatives considered

- `openclaw agent exec --json` exposes usage but changes the execution substrate and reintroduces agent/runtime overhead that `infer model run` exists to avoid.
- `diagnostics-otel` exposes the internal `model.usage` event but requires a plugin, collector, configuration, and Gateway restart for data already present in the synchronous response.
- `openclaw gateway call agent --expect-final --json` returns the raw `agentMeta.usage` and proves the data exists, but the generic Gateway CLI rejects explicit provider/model overrides. It is therefore only a partial workaround when an existing agent already defaults to the desired model.
- Reconstructing tokens from visible prompt/output text is incorrect for reasoning models because hidden reasoning tokens are material.

Related but broader: #57404 requests terminal per-run telemetry on the WebSocket lifecycle stream. This request is narrower: preserve usage already returned to the synchronous `infer --json` caller.

## Impact

- Affected: operators using `infer model run --gateway --json` for scheduled probes, classifiers, summaries, and other bounded one-shot jobs.
- Severity: medium; workflows run successfully but FinOps attribution is blind.
- Frequency: every gateway model-run call.
- Consequence: unknown token consumption or disproportionate OTLP infrastructure solely for per-call accounting.

## Evidence/examples

Verified on OpenClaw `2026.7.1-2`:

```text
$ openclaw infer model run --gateway --json ...
keys: ok, capability, transport, provider, model, attempts, outputs
usage fields: none
```

The equivalent raw Gateway call returned:

```text
result.meta.agentMeta.usage = { input: 47, output: 5, total: 52 }
result.meta.agentMeta.lastCallUsage = { input: 47, output: 5, cacheRead: 0, cacheWrite: 0, reasoningTokens: 0, total: 52 }
```

Current source projection: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/cli/capability-cli/model.ts#L281-L333

## Do you plan to open a PR for this?

No, proposing the idea only.

## Additional information

This can be additive and should not require a new configuration key, public diagnostic subscription, or persistence contract.
