issues.body:
# RFC: Expose existing InputProvenance / AgentInternalEvent signals to `ContextEngine.assemble()`


**TL;DR.** OpenClaw already has a complete `InputProvenance` model (`src/sessions/input-provenance.ts`) and an `AgentInternalEvent` taxonomy (`src/agents/internal-event-contract.ts`) that distinguishes third-party user messages, inter-session bridge messages, internal system events, and subagent announce / task-completion events. The runtime uses these internally in `shouldSuppressAgentPromptPersistence()` to decide what *not* to write to transcript. The same signals are absent from `ContextEngine.assemble()` params, so durable-store engines that rebuild context from their own DB cannot tell live volatile injections (subagent announces, inter-session bridges, internal-runtime-context blocks) apart from ordinary turns — and have to text-sniff for them. We propose exposing these signals via three optional, non-breaking `assemble` params. Zero changes to `AgentMessage` shape, zero new lifecycle hooks, zero changes to runtime persistence behavior. Engines that ignore the new fields behave identically to today.

---

## 1. Motivation

### 1.1 The contract gap

Current `ContextEngine.assemble()` (`src/context-engine/types.ts`):

```ts
assemble(params: {
  sessionId: string;
  sessionKey?: string;
  messages: AgentMessage[];
  tokenBudget?: number;
  availableTools?: Set<string>;
  citationsMode?: MemoryCitationsMode;
  model?: string;
  prompt?: string;        // added by #50848
}): Promise<AssembleResult>;
```

From inside `assemble()` the engine cannot reliably answer:

1. **Where does pre-prompt history end and the live in-flight turn begin?** (`afterTurn` gets `prePromptMessageCount`. `assemble` does not.)
2. **Which messages were synthesized by the runtime as non-persistent live injections** (subagent announces, retry/overflow re-prompts, internal-runtime-context blocks) **vs ordinary durable user/assistant turns?**
3. **Which messages does the runtime know it will not write to transcript** (i.e. `shouldSuppressAgentPromptPersistence()` returns true), so the engine should not ingest them?

### 1.2 The runtime already has all three signals

This RFC's central claim. We are not asking OpenClaw to invent new metadata. The signals already exist and are already used internally.

**Signal A — `InputProvenance`** (`src/sessions/input-provenance.ts`):

```ts
export const INPUT_PROVENANCE_KIND_VALUES = [
  "third-party_user",
  "inter_session",
  "internal_system",
] as const;

export type InputProvenance = {
  kind: InputProvenanceKind;
  originSessionId?: string;
  sourceSessionKey?: string;
  sourceChannel?: string;
  sourceTool?: string;  // e.g. "subagent_announce", "agent_step"
};
```

This is attached to user messages via `applyInputProvenanceToUserMessage()` (same file) and propagated through `AgentCommandOpts.inputProvenance` (`src/agents/command/types.ts`). At every assemble call site the runtime knows the provenance of the current turn's user message and can recover the provenance of prior turn messages from the transcript / session-context if needed.

**Signal B — `AgentInternalEvent`** (`src/agents/internal-event-contract.ts`, `src/agents/internal-events.ts`):

```ts
type AgentTaskCompletionInternalEvent = {
  type: typeof AGENT_INTERNAL_EVENT_TYPE_TASK_COMPLETION;
  source: AgentInternalEventSource;       // "subagent", "cron", etc.
  childSessionKey: string;
  // ... announce / task metadata
};
```

These travel on `AgentCommandOpts.internalEvents` (`src/agents/command/types.ts`) and are formatted into the prompt body by `formatTaskCompletionEvent()` / `formatTaskCompletionEventForPlainPrompt()`. The runtime knows which exact message in `messages` carries the formatted event because it just inserted it.

**Signal C — `prePromptMessageCount`**: already passed to `afterTurn`. Same number is available at the `assemble` call site; the runtime computes it once per attempt.

### 1.3 Existing internal consumer: `shouldSuppressAgentPromptPersistence`

The runtime's own decision logic for whether to persist a synthesized prompt to transcript reads exactly these signals (`src/gateway/server-methods/agent.ts`):

```ts
function shouldSuppressAgentPromptPersistence(params: {
  inputProvenance?: InputProvenance;
  internalEvents?: AgentInternalEvent[];
}): boolean {
  if (
    params.inputProvenance?.kind !== "inter_session" ||
    params.inputProvenance.sourceTool !== "subagent_announce"
  ) {
    return false;
  }
  return (
    params.internalEvents?.some(
      (event) =>
        event.type === AGENT_INTERNAL_EVENT_TYPE_TASK_COMPLETION && event.source === "subagent",
    ) === true
  );
}
```

This proves the signals are already structurally accessible at the call site. They're just not threaded into `assemble`.

### 1.4 Live consequence: lossless-claw Track 1 hotfix (#688)

Without these signals, [Martian-Engineering/lossless-claw#688](https://github.com/Martian-Engineering/lossless-claw/pull/688) (`fix: preserve unpersisted volatile live input in LCM assembly`, currently open) has to detect volatile-live-input tail messages by:

1. Walking `params.messages` from `prePromptMessageCount` forward (but `prePromptMessageCount` itself is not in params, so the engine computes a guess from its own DB state).
2. String-matching the user-message body for `[Inter-session message]`, `<<<BEGIN_OPENCLAW_INTERNAL_CONTEXT>>>`, `[Internal task completion event]` markers.
3. Doing bipartite occurrence-matching against assembled DB output to avoid double-counting.
4. Evicting from the front of the assembled prefix if budget overflows.

The PR's own description acknowledges this is Track 1 (止血 / hot fix) and that the proper fix is a contract change. The marker strings come from `src/sessions/input-provenance.ts` (`INTER_SESSION_PROMPT_PREFIX_BASE`), `src/agents/internal-runtime-context.ts` (`INTERNAL_RUNTIME_CONTEXT_BEGIN`), and `src/agents/internal-events.ts` (`formatTaskCompletionEvent`) — i.e. the engine is doing inverse text-matching against the same OpenClaw code paths that emitted the messages, instead of receiving the structured metadata that drove the emission.

### 1.5 Other downstream cases

- **#74286** ("Bug: sub-agent announce completion causes parent session to generate out-of-context replies"): the parent session's context engine reassembles from a durable store but the trigger message is a subagent announce. With provenance signals, an engine can detect a subagent-announce trigger and apply different inclusion logic (e.g. retain more recent turns).
- **#75541** ("TypeError at prompt assembly stage when lossless-claw is enabled"): downstream symptom of mismatched expectations between runtime and engine over what's in the assembled messages. Better contract signals reduce surface for this.
- Any third-party context engine that wants to do prefix-aligned RAG, identity-based anchoring, or live-input passthrough faces the same gap. lossless-claw is the example we have, not the only consumer this benefits.

### 1.6 What this RFC is *not* about

- **Not** adding fields to `AgentMessage` itself. The `message.provenance` extension already exists in `applyInputProvenanceToUserMessage` (object-spread, untyped on `AgentMessage`). This RFC does not formalize that — it threads parallel arrays through `assemble` params instead, which is a smaller surface than adding to the cross-package `AgentMessage` type.
- **Not** changing when `assemble` fires (#73437's lane).
- **Not** changing how compaction is triggered (#81164's lane).
- **Not** asking the runtime to enforce persistence on the engine's behalf.

---

## 2. Proposal

Add three optional parameters to `assemble`. All optional, all backward-compatible.

```ts
assemble(params: {
  // existing fields unchanged

  /**
   * Number of messages that existed before the current prompt was issued.
   * `messages[0..prePromptMessageCount-1]` is pre-prompt history the engine
   * has (or should have) seen via prior afterTurn calls; the tail
   * `messages[prePromptMessageCount..]` is the current turn (prompt + any
   * runtime-injected entries that go with it).
   *
   * Same source of truth as the field already passed to `afterTurn`.
   * Optional; omitting it preserves today's behavior (engine cannot
   * distinguish pre-prompt vs live tail).
   */
  prePromptMessageCount?: number;

  /**
   * Per-message InputProvenance, aligned to `messages` by index.
   * Entries with no known provenance are `undefined` at that index.
   *
   * The runtime already attaches provenance to live user messages via
   * `applyInputProvenanceToUserMessage`. For ingested transcript messages
   * the runtime exposes whatever it can recover from `session-context` /
   * stored provenance, or `undefined`. Engines should treat `undefined`
   * as "no signal" rather than "third-party_user".
   *
   * When provided, `inputProvenance.length === messages.length`.
   */
  inputProvenance?: readonly (InputProvenance | undefined)[];

  /**
   * Per-message AgentInternalEvent annotation, aligned by index. An entry
   * at index `i` carries the internal event(s) that the runtime
   * synthesized into `messages[i]` (e.g. a subagent task-completion event
   * whose `formatTaskCompletionEvent()` output is the message body).
   * Entries with no associated internal event are `undefined`.
   *
   * Engines may use this to (a) detect that a tail user-role message is a
   * synthesized announce body rather than a real user input, (b) read the
   * structured event metadata (`childSessionKey`, `announceType`,
   * `status`, etc.) without parsing the formatted prompt body.
   *
   * When provided, `internalEvents.length === messages.length`.
   */
  internalEvents?: readonly (readonly AgentInternalEvent[] | undefined)[];
}): Promise<AssembleResult>;
```

### 2.1 Engine-side semantics (lossless-claw's planned use)

After this RFC lands, lossless-claw can replace its current text-marker sniff with a structured detection:

```ts
function isVolatileLiveInputAt(i: number, params: AssembleParams): boolean {
  // (a) Subagent / task-completion event marker
  if (params.internalEvents?.[i]?.some((e) =>
    e.type === AGENT_INTERNAL_EVENT_TYPE_TASK_COMPLETION
  )) return true;

  // (b) Inter-session bridge from a runtime tool
  if (params.inputProvenance?.[i]?.kind === "inter_session") return true;

  // (c) Tail position past pre-prompt boundary + no DB context_items row
  //     covering this identity → live volatile by elimination
  return false;
}
```

The new code is simpler than the current marker-based logic and is robust against the runtime renaming the formatted-event body or the inter-session prefix.

### 2.2 Runtime-side implementation sketch (~150 LOC excluding tests)

Single call site update on each runner:

1. **`src/agents/pi-embedded-runner/run/attempt.ts`** (`runEmbeddedAttempt`): compute the three arrays from already-available locals:
   - `prePromptMessageCount` — already computed for `afterTurn`.
   - `inputProvenance[i]` — for each message, read `message.provenance` if present (set by `applyInputProvenanceToUserMessage`); for prior turns, look up via the existing session-context provenance store if available, else `undefined`.
   - `internalEvents[i]` — when the runtime inserts the formatted body of an `AgentInternalEvent` into `messages`, it knows the index. Carry an `Map<messageRef, AgentInternalEvent[]>` from insertion site to the assemble call, project to the parallel array. (Sketch: instead of carrying a Map, attach to the message-ref hash; one of several easy implementations.)

2. **`extensions/codex/src/app-server/run-attempt.ts`** (codex harness): same. If `prePromptMessageCount` is harder to compute on the codex side, omit it (engine tolerates omission), keep the other two.

3. **`src/agents/internal-runtime-context.ts`** / **`src/agents/internal-events.ts`**: no change to existing exports; the runtime continues to format prompt bodies the same way. The new arrays are derived from sibling state, not from re-parsing message bodies.

4. **Tests**: extend `src/agents/harness/context-engine-lifecycle.test.ts` with new cases:
   - `assemble` receives `prePromptMessageCount` matching `afterTurn`.
   - `assemble` receives `inputProvenance[i].kind === "inter_session"` for an inter-session-tool-routed message.
   - `assemble` receives `internalEvents[i]` containing an `AGENT_INTERNAL_EVENT_TYPE_TASK_COMPLETION` for a subagent-announce body.
   - Backward compatibility: an engine ignoring the new fields gets identical `messages`.

### 2.3 Plugin SDK surface

- Add the three optional params to the `assemble` type in `src/context-engine/types.ts`.
- Re-export `InputProvenance` and `AgentInternalEvent` from the plugin-sdk barrel so engines can name the types without importing from internal paths. (`InputProvenance` is already in `plugin-sdk/src/sessions/input-provenance.d.ts`. `AgentInternalEvent` would need to be added.)
- Regenerate `dist/plugin-sdk/src/context-engine/types.d.ts` via the existing build pipeline.

### 2.4 What this RFC explicitly does *not* require

To stay narrow and avoid the rejection pattern of #80218 (RAG-in-assemble) / #77714 (pluggable memory backend) / #46234 (re-run sanitizers):

- **No** changes to `AgentMessage` shape itself.
- **No** new lifecycle hook (#73437 owns "assemble per LLM call").
- **No** request for the engine to enforce persistence; the runtime stays the source of truth for transcript writes.
- **No** changes to compaction or intercept-compaction (#81164 owns that).
- **No** runtime-side text re-parsing; signals come from already-classified state.

---

## 3. Precedent

This proposal extends the same pattern that's been growing `assemble`'s contract since #50848:

| PR | Field | Status | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **#50848** | `prompt?: string` | MERGED | Retrieval engines need the user query |
| **#76251** | (filter `OPENCLAW_RUNTIME_CONTEXT_CUSTOM_TYPE` out of assemble) | MERGED | Hide internal-runtime-context custom messages |
| **#81079** | `currentTokenCount?: number` | OPEN | Engines need headroom estimate |
| **#81164** | `interceptCompaction(request)` | OPEN | Engines can replace codex GPT compaction |

All four are non-breaking optional extensions. All follow "expose a signal the runtime already has, gate engine behavior on reading it." This RFC adds three more in the same shape.

---

## 4. Open questions

1. **Naming.** `inputProvenance` (matches existing `InputProvenance` type and `AgentCommandOpts.inputProvenance`) vs `provenance` (shorter at the call site). The current draft uses `inputProvenance` for symmetry; happy to flip.
2. **Type access for engines.** Re-exporting `AgentInternalEvent` from `plugin-sdk` exposes the internal event taxonomy to downstream consumers. That's intentional — it's how engines can use the structured event payload — but it does pin a more public contract for `AgentInternalEvent`. Alternative: expose only the discriminator (e.g. `internalEventTypes?: readonly (readonly InternalEventType[] | undefined)[]`) and keep the full event internal. Trade-off: less power for engines that want the structured fields, but smaller exposed surface.
3. **Codex harness parity.** PI-embedded runner has clean access to all three signals. Codex's `extensions/codex/src/app-server/run-attempt.ts` may have a thinner pipeline. Open to feedback on whether codex should pass through `inputProvenance` / `internalEvents` from day one or whether that's a follow-up.
4. **Should we also pass an `identityHashes` array** for prefix alignment? Speculative; the first three signals already resolve the immediate downstream pain. Happy to defer to a separate proposal if there's a stronger demand signal.

---

## 5. Migration / rollout

- Optional fields, zero behavior change for engines that don't consult them.
- lossless-claw will feature-detect the presence of the new fields. While both old and new OpenClaw versions are in production, the engine keeps its current text-marker sniff path as a fallback. Once the floor OpenClaw version has the signals for a release cycle, the marker constants and bipartite-matching logic are deleted.
- No deprecation needed in the runtime; the new fields are pure additions.

---

## 6. Why this isn't already covered by #73437 / #81079 / #81164

Each addresses a different dimension:

- **#73437** ("assemble per LLM call"): cadence — when does assemble fire. Orthogonal to *what* it gets.
- **#81079** ("currentTokenCount"): one specific token-accounting field for overflow guards.
- **#81164** ("interceptCompaction"): engine participation in codex GPT-driven compaction. Different lifecycle.

This RFC sits on the dimension of *"what context does assemble have about its inputs?"*, between #50848 (added the user prompt) and #81079 (adds the current token count).

---

## 7. Related issues / PRs

- **Concurrent downstream hotfix**: [Martian-Engineering/lossless-claw#688](https://github.com/Martian-Engineering/lossless-claw/pull/688) — text-marker-based volatile-input recovery. Track 1 stopgap; this RFC is Track 2 (the proper contract fix). lossless-claw#688 will be rewritten on top of this RFC's contract when both land.
- **Direct motivating bug**: openclaw/openclaw#74286 (subagent announce → out-of-context parent reply).
- **Related contract-extension precedent**: openclaw/openclaw#50848, #76251, #81079, #81164.
- **Adjacent**: openclaw/openclaw#73437 (assemble cadence), #75541 (downstream assembly TypeError), #67716 (bootstrap/reconcile + hot-cache deferred compaction).

---

## 8. Author notes

Filed by jetd1, maintainer of `@martian-engineering/lossless-claw`. We have shipped Track 1 (lossless-claw#688) to stop production bleeding while this RFC is discussed. Happy to drive the OpenClaw-side runtime patch as a follow-up PR (PI runner side at minimum; codex harness if a maintainer can confirm the wiring there).

---

issues.body:
## Summary

The `[trace:embedded-run] prep stages` line and the `timeline` diagnostic (`openclaw.diagnostics.v1` envelope) both expose `bundle-tools` as a single aggregate duration. On hosts with multiple stdio MCP servers configured, this stage routinely accounts for the dominant share of per-turn prep time — but it's a black box: there's no way to attribute the cost to a specific MCP server, plugin tool registry, or sub-step.

This makes regressions and duplicate-child situations (e.g. #75621) much harder to diagnose than they need to be, and makes proposed fixes like #80131 (tool bundling memoization) harder to verify after the fact.

## Concrete observation

On a Linux/WSL host running OpenClaw `2026.5.7` with 6 stdio MCP servers configured (`filesystem`, `github`, `desktop-automation` via WSL→cmd.exe, and 3× `graphify.serve`), bundle-tools shows a bimodal distribution:

- Fast mode: ~8 s (event loop quiet)
- Slow mode: ~17–20 s (event loop contended by concurrent worker subagents)
- Outliers >50 s (one timeout at the 30 s mark on `filesystem` MCP)

```
[trace:embedded-run] prep stages: phase=stream-ready totalMs=21441
  workspace-sandbox:1ms, skills:0ms, core-plugin-tools:320ms,
  bootstrap-context:27ms,
  bundle-tools:20931ms,            ← black box
  system-prompt:5ms, session-resource-loader:137ms,
  agent-session:0ms, stream-setup:20ms
```

All evidence points at sequential `tools/list` cold-start across the MCP children (re-spawned per prep cycle), with one slow child dominating, but **there is no log signal that names which child is slow**. Diagnosis required ad-hoc `ps`/`strace`/timing experiments.

## Proposal

Emit nested sub-spans inside `bundle-tools` to the timeline diagnostic (`openclaw.diagnostics.v1`), one per MCP server / tool source. Also include a compact summary line in the existing aggregate `[trace:embedded-run] prep stages` log when `diagnostics.flags` includes `timeline` or a new `bundle-tools.detail` flag.

Suggested shape (JSONL timeline):

```json
{"span":"bundle-tools","durationMs":20931,"children":[
  {"span":"mcp.tools_list","server":"filesystem","durationMs":3120,"toolCount":11},
  {"span":"mcp.tools_list","server":"github","durationMs":1840,"toolCount":29},
  {"span":"mcp.tools_list","server":"desktop-automation","durationMs":11420,"toolCount":6,"warn":"slow"},
  {"span":"mcp.tools_list","server":"graphify-orchestrator","durationMs":1505,"toolCount":7},
  {"span":"mcp.tools_list","server":"graphify-trader","durationMs":1490,"toolCount":7},
  {"span":"mcp.tools_list","server":"graphify-openclaw","durationMs":1456,"toolCount":7},
  {"span":"core-plugin-tools.assemble","durationMs":80}
]}
```

Compact one-liner (for the existing log channel):

```
[trace:embedded-run] bundle-tools detail: filesystem:3120ms(11) github:1840ms(29) desktop-automation:11420ms(6,slow) graphify-orchestrator:1505ms(7) graphify-trader:1490ms(7) graphify-openclaw:1456ms(7) core-plugin-tools.assemble:80ms
```

Either format is enough to identify the slowest server at a glance.

## Why this matters now

Two open performance issues would directly benefit:

- **#80131** (per-request auth and tool bundling dominate TTFT) — proposes memoizing bundle-tools. With sub-spans we could quantify the actual saving per MCP server and prove the fix lands.
- **#75621** (duplicate stdio MCP children) — currently diagnosed by inspecting `ps` after the fact. Per-server timing would surface the duplicate (two children responding to the same `(server, config)` key) as duplicated sub-spans or anomalous totals.

It also helps users with many MCP servers decide which servers are pulling weight vs being dead-weight cold-start cost.

## Backwards compatibility

- New sub-spans should only emit when `diagnostics.flags` includes `timeline` (already gated) or a new dedicated flag — no change to default behavior.
- The aggregate `bundle-tools` value in the existing `[trace:embedded-run] prep stages` line stays as-is, so downstream parsers keep working.

## Environment

- OpenClaw `2026.5.7` (`eeef486`)
- Node `v22.22.2`
- WSL2 / Linux `6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2`
- 6 stdio MCP servers configured (filesystem, github, desktop-automation via cmd.exe, 3× graphify.serve)
- Channels: Discord, Telegram
- Gateway up ~52 h, ~300 prep traces/day, no regression — the cost is structural

## Offer

Happy to test patches against this workload — I already have a CSV parser of the prep-stages line and a baseline corpus across two days of bimodal traffic.

issues.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Android and Apple mobile implementations duplicate several deterministic
protocol and business-rule paths while the native UI and device integrations
must remain platform-owned. Existing near-duplicates already differ in edge
behavior, so an unplanned extraction risks a protocol regression.

## Proposed Solution

Create an evidence-backed, contract-first migration record before introducing
KMP. It defines the initial pure-logic boundary, a Swift-friendly SKIE plus
hand-written facade, ABI and Swift-parity gates, required Android/iOS proof,
and a per-PR net-negative production diff gate.

## Alternatives Considered

- Share mobile UI: rejected because platform-native UX and OS integrations are
  first-class requirements.
- Use Kotlin Swift Export as the production boundary: deferred because it is
  currently Alpha.
- Keep duplicate logic: rejected for deterministic protocol and business rules
  where a single source of truth has clear maintenance value.

## Impact

No runtime or UI behavior changes are proposed by the planning PR. The plan
gives maintainers a safe sequence for reducing future Android/iOS business-logic
duplication without exposing generated Kotlin APIs to Swift callers.

## Evidence

- Repository mapping found direct Talk directive and Bonjour parser overlap plus
  behavior differences that require characterization before extraction.
- Official Kotlin guidance supports incremental logic sharing while retaining
  native UI; Swift Export remains Alpha.
- Docs formatting, MDX, glossary, and link validation pass; autoreview reported
  no actionable findings.

issues.body:
### Summary / Problem Statement
During gateway shutdown or restart, the active sessions shutdown tracker maintains references to all active sessions to emit final `session_end` lifecycle hooks. However, the current implementation suffers from memory leak risks, rigid timeouts, and potential resource leakage during cleanup:
1. **Memory Pinning:** The module-level map in `active-sessions-shutdown-tracker.ts` retains full `OpenClawConfig` objects for every active session. In environments with many concurrent/short-lived sessions, this prevents GC of large config snapshots.
2. **Hardcoded Drain Timeout:** The shutdown drain timeout is hardcoded to 2 seconds. When exceeded, pending `session_end` hook executions are abandoned, but their underlying promises continue running unsupervised, which can lead to database write conflicts or background errors.
3. **Orphaned MCP Runtimes & Browser Tabs:** In `session-reset-service.ts`, if an embedded agent run fails to stop within the 15-second cleanup window, the function returns an error without disposing of the session's MCP runtime or browser tabs, resulting in file descriptor and process leaks.

### Detailed Technical Context
- **Memory Leak Vector:** `ActiveSessionForShutdown` preserves the full `cfg` context:
  ```typescript
  export type ActiveSessionForShutdown = {
    cfg: OpenClawConfig;
    sessionKey: string;
    sessionId: string;
    storePath: string;
    ...
  };
  ```
- **Hardcoded Limit:** `SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DEFAULT_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_MS = 2_000` is defined statically in `session-reset-service.ts`.
- **Incomplete Cleanup:** In `ensureSessionRuntimeCleanup`, the early return on timeout skips `retireSessionMcpRuntime` and `closeTrackedBrowserTabs`.

### Impact Analysis
- Long-running gateways can experience cumulative heap exhaustion due to config references pinned by the shutdown tracker.
- Heavy-weight memory plugins or slow logging systems will frequently exceed the 2-second timeout, resulting in lost session termination logs.
- Orphaned MCP runtimes and browser tabs will gradually consume server resources, leading to degraded performance or eventual OOM.

### Proposed Solution / Implementation Plan
1. **Reduce Memory Footprint:** Optimize `ActiveSessionForShutdown` to store only key identifiers (like `sessionId`, `sessionKey`, `storePath`, and `agentId`). Load or resolve the active configuration dynamically at drain time.
2. **Configurable Shutdown Timeout:** Expose the shutdown drain timeout as a configuration option in `openclaw.json` (e.g., `gateway.shutdownDrainTimeoutMs`, defaulting to 5,000ms).
3. **Safe Cancellation with Abort Signals:** Pass an `AbortSignal` to the hook runner and individual `session_end` handlers. Trigger the signal when the drain timeout expires, ensuring pending tasks terminate cleanly.
4. **Resilient Cleanup Schedule:** In `ensureSessionRuntimeCleanup`, even if the agent run doesn't exit within the timeout window, schedule a background task to forcefully dispose of MCP runtimes and close browser tabs.

### Affected File References
- [src/gateway/active-sessions-shutdown-tracker.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/gateway/active-sessions-shutdown-tracker.ts)
- [src/gateway/session-reset-service.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/gateway/session-reset-service.ts)

### Additional Considerations
Ensure that lazy configuration resolution does not fail during shutdown if the config file was deleted or corrupted. Fall back gracefully to a baseline configuration structure.

issues.body:
Follow-up to a forthcoming PR that introduces a typed `WebchatNotDeliverableError` thrown from `resolveMessageChannelSelection` for `delivery.channel: "webchat"` (the internal session-bound surface, not a deliverable channel plugin).

The cron delivery resolver (`resolveDeliveryTarget` in `src/cron/jobs.ts`, calling into `src/infra/outbound/channel-selection.ts`) has a sibling failure family that surfaces the same generic wrapped error string — `"Channel is required (no configured channels detected). Set delivery.channel explicitly or use a main session with a previous channel."` — but for a different root cause:

- `delivery.channel: "last"` (or omitted) when the resolved session key has no prior chat in the session store to anchor against.

Today both failure modes wrap to the same string at `assertSupportedJobSpec` / the cron-runner delivery resolver, which makes them indistinguishable in `task_runs.error` and in `openclaw cron list` output (e.g. `announce -> last (last -> no route, will fail-closed: Channel...)`). Operators have to read `cron show <id>` and cross-reference session state to tell whether they configured a bad channel or just have a fresh session with no chat history.

### Proposal

Add a parallel typed error (working name: `NoPriorChatChannelError`) thrown from the same `resolveMessageChannelSelection` site (or from the cron-side `resolveDeliveryTarget` if that is the cleaner seam) when:

1. `params.channel` normalizes to `"last"` (or is undefined/empty meaning "infer from session history"), AND
2. the resolved session entry has no `lastChannel` recorded, AND
3. there is no `params.fallbackChannel` resolvable.

Message should name the actionable fixes: configure a real channel and switch `delivery.channel` to it explicitly, or use `sessionTarget: "session:agent:<id>:main"` with `payload.kind: "agentTurn"` and `delivery.mode: "none"` so the agent turn output renders in its own session without an announce route.

### Why not include in the original PR

To keep the original diff focused. The webchat case is structurally non-deliverable (a property of the channel constant); the `"last"` case is dependent on session state at fire time (a property of the session store). Different invariants, different message text, and the `"last"` case probably wants its own test fixtures around stale/empty session history.

### Source pointers (paths at the time of filing)

- `src/utils/message-channel-constants.ts` — `INTERNAL_MESSAGE_CHANNEL`, `WebchatNotDeliverableError` (introduced in the original PR; the new error would live next to it).
- `src/infra/outbound/channel-selection.ts` — `resolveMessageChannelSelection`. The webchat check is at the top of the explicit-channel branch in the original PR.
- `src/cron/jobs.ts` — `resolveDeliveryTarget`, where the wrapping happens today.
- Documented contract: `docs/automation/cron-jobs.md` — the "Webchat is not an announce target" subsection added by the original PR.

The original PR link will be added in a comment here once it is opened.

issues.body:
## Summary

Proposing a new `doctor:secret-resolve-preflight` health contribution that walks the user's secret target registry and warns on shape-coverage gaps the CLI's apply path can't handle.

Today, when the gateway emits a secret assignment for a target whose `secretShape` is `sibling_ref` and whose value path doesn't exist in source config, the CLI's `resolveCommandSecretRefsViaGateway` crashes via `setPathExistingStrict` ("Cannot set value at non-existent path"). PR #78555 fixes that specific instance by introducing a `setPathCreateStrict` path for sibling_ref. **This issue asks the orthogonal question: should doctor _also_ catch the general class proactively, so future shape additions don't reopen the same hole?**

## Motivation

The bug class is **shape coverage drift** — the gateway emits shapes the CLI's apply path hasn't grown a handler for. The user finds out by hitting a crash during `openclaw status`, `openclaw channels list`, or doctor itself, not by anything diagnosable from their config.

`sibling_ref` is the first concrete instance, but the same class can recur whenever a plugin registers a new `secretShape` or the gateway introduces a new resolution path the CLI hasn't switched on yet. Doctor is the natural place to surface this — it already loads the user's config and runs diagnose-only contributions for adjacent concerns (`doctor:gateway-config`, `doctor:gateway-auth`).

## Proposed design

A new contribution `doctor:secret-resolve-preflight`, slotted right after `doctor:gateway-auth` in `resolveDoctorHealthContributions()`. For each target returned by `discoverConfigSecretTargets(ctx.cfg)`:

- If `secretShape === "sibling_ref"` and `getPath(ctx.cfg, target.pathSegments) === undefined` → warn. Suggested remediation: upgrade to a CLI build that resolves sibling_ref SecretRefs via `setPathCreateStrict` (i.e. a build including PR #78555 once merged).
- If `secretShape` is anything other than the values this CLI build recognizes (`secret_input`, `sibling_ref`) → warn with the path + the unrecognized shape. Defense-in-depth for future shape additions that ship in the gateway before the matching CLI handler lands.

It does **not** mutate the config — the user's config is correct; the remediation is always a CLI upgrade.

## Draft

A draft implementation is on a fork branch for evaluation:
<https://github.com/octocore-autonomous-systems/openclaw/tree/feat/doctor-secret-resolve-preflight> (commit `27898c0f6f`)

Diff: +51 lines in `src/flows/doctor-health-contributions.ts`, +108 lines in `src/flows/doctor-health-contributions.test.ts`. No framework changes; six new tests covering registration ordering, empty-config, populated/absent value paths for both shape branches, and unknown-shape defense-in-depth. All tests pass locally on `upstream/main`. Happy to convert into a PR if maintainers prefer to evaluate at that surface.

## Relationship to PR #78555

This is **orthogonal** to PR #78555. #78555 fixes the specific sibling_ref crash by changing the apply primitive; this proposal adds a defensive doctor surface for the general class. They don't conflict — merging this without #78555 just means doctor warns affected users while they wait for the fix, and merging both keeps doctor catching any future shape additions where the CLI handler list falls behind the gateway.

If you'd prefer a different remediation entirely (e.g. exhaustiveness-typed `secretShape` at the registry boundary so missing CLI handlers fail at build time), I'm equally happy to abandon this branch in favor of that direction — wanted to surface the proposal while the shape is fresh.

issues.body:
## Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect capability state without a crash)

## Beta release blocker

No

## Summary

The iMessage message-tool discovery omits `edit` on macOS 26 when `imsg` reports the supported `editMessageItemTranslation` selector instead of either legacy edit selector.

## Steps to reproduce

1. On macOS 26.6.1 with `imsg` private API v2 active, run `imsg status --json`.
2. Observe that the bridge advertises `message.edit`, reports `editMessageItemTranslation: true`, and does not report `editMessageItem` or `editMessage`.
3. Let OpenClaw build the iMessage message-tool action list from that cached private API status.
4. Observe that `edit` is omitted from the available actions.

## Expected behavior

OpenClaw should advertise the iMessage `edit` action when the active private API reports any supported edit selector, including `editMessageItemTranslation` on macOS 26.

## Actual behavior

`extensions/imessage/src/message-tool-api.ts` only accepts `editMessage` or `editMessageItem`. When macOS 26 reports only `editMessageItemTranslation`, OpenClaw suppresses `edit` even though `imsg` advertises the `message.edit` RPC method and can perform the action.

## OpenClaw version

Observed on OpenClaw 2026.10.3. Current `main` at `9a8ef35a96ed78d88310c0247b1749aca9fada92` and release 2026.10.4 retain the same gate.

## Operating system

macOS 26.6.1

## Install method

npm global

## Model

Not applicable; capability discovery is deterministic and occurs before model action selection.

## Provider / routing chain

Not applicable.

## Logs

```json
{
  "v2_ready": true,
  "rpc_message_edit": true,
  "selectors": {
    "editMessageItemTranslation": true,
    "editMessageItem": false,
    "editMessage": false
  }
}
```

## Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Current source gate:

```ts
if (
  action === "edit" &&
  privateApiStatus?.selectors &&
  !privateApiStatus.selectors.editMessage &&
  !privateApiStatus.selectors.editMessageItem
) {
  continue;
}
```

## Impact and severity

- Affected: iMessage channel users on macOS 26 whose bridge exposes the translation-based edit selector.
- Severity: medium; message editing is supported by the bridge but unavailable to agents.
- Frequency: every capability-discovery pass with this selector shape.
- Consequence: agents cannot use the native edit action for corrections or low-noise progress updates.

## Additional information

A focused fix should include `editMessageItemTranslation` in the existing selector gate and add positive coverage for the macOS 26 shape plus a negative case where no edit selector is present.

issues.body:
### Summary

The gateway's own WAL auto-checkpoint on `state/openclaw.sqlite` is reported as blocked on every attempt since boot, and has **never completed**:

```
openclaw-state WAL checkpoint PASSIVE blocked by a reader
  state=blocked  checkpointedFrames=866  logFrames=17091
  consecutiveBlocked=14  lastCompletedAtMs=null  never_completed=true
```

The WAL therefore keeps growing (unbackfilled 41.5 MB at 15:33 → 65.7 MB at 19:09) instead of being checkpointed.

### Environment

- OpenClaw **2026.9.7 (c074824)**
- Windows 10.0.26200 (x64), Node v24.18.0
- State DB `state/openclaw.sqlite` ≈ 405 MB, `-wal` 47–73 MB

### What was ruled out

A Sysinternals **handle.exe** scan of all processes for `openclaw.sqlite`:

```
node.exe  pid: 33900  .sqlite  x7
node.exe  pid: 33900  -wal     x7
node.exe  pid: 33900  -shm     x1
```

**No other process holds any handle on the DB** — every handle belongs to the gateway process itself. This is not an external contender; the pin is **in-process**.

The gateway's own telemetry cannot name the holder either:

```json
"candidate_connection": {
  "connectionId": 2, "operation": "sqlite connection", "ownerKind": "worker",
  "threadId": 2, "ageMs": ~25200000, "transactionOpen": false,
  "trackedReaders": 0, "blockingOwner": "unknown",
  "readerCount": 0, "scope": "current-thread", "nativeStatements": "unobserved"
}
```

Note the internal inconsistency: it reports "blocked by a reader" while also reporting `readerCount: 0` and `blockingOwner: unknown`.

### Reproduction pattern

1. Maintenance stops the gateway, checkpoints cleanly, restarts:
   `[checkpoint] PASS | [('openclaw-agent.sqlite',(0,0,0)), ('openclaw.sqlite',(0,0,0))]` (12:00:01)
2. After restart (~12:03) the block immediately re-forms and **never** clears for the rest of the uptime (observed 12:03 → 19:05, 71 blocked records, `never_completed=true`).
3. Only another full gateway restart clears it.

### Correlated (NOT proven) impact

- `Agent run failed: the Gateway state database was busy (SQLite: database is locked)`
- repeated `cron: isolated agent setup timed out before runner start`

Same DB, same subsystem. Timing supports a link; no controlled reproduction was done, so causation is **unproven**.

### Suggested directions (guesses)

- Likely a long-lived connection or unclosed read snapshot inside the worker pool (threadId=2, `ownerKind=worker`) — a single un-reset statement pins the WAL.
- `blockingOwner=unknown` + `readerCount=0` + "blocked by a reader" suggests the reader-tracking path does not cover all connection kinds.

---
*Reported from a self-hosted single-user deployment. Paths sanitized.*

issues.body:
## Summary

On OpenClaw 2026.9.9, stranded-reply recovery retried an older provisional final after a later inter-session report had successfully reached the originating Telegram chat. The retry returned `already_delivered` / `delivered:false`, without a new Telegram message ID, but runtime delivery-mirror handling subsequently emitted:

> I generated a reply but could not deliver to this chat. Please try again.

The actual report had already been accepted by Telegram and observed by the user.

## Environment

- OpenClaw: 2026.9.9
- Main: Codex runtime, message-tool-only delivery
- Orchestrating peer: ZeroCool, returning through `sessions_send`
- Originating channel: Telegram direct conversation

## Observed sequence

This was a bounded synthetic delivery test, not an upgrade or service-change test.

1. Main handed work to ZeroCool; the handoff returned accepted/queued.
2. The original Main turn ended with a provisional “test incomplete” final while the report was still queued.
3. ZeroCool's envelope-bearing report arrived as inter-session `sessions_send` input in a later Main run.
4. Main stripped the internal envelope and explicitly sent the synthetic version-1 report. Telegram returned an accepted message receipt at 2026-10-16 00:13:45.108 UTC. The user independently observed the report in Telegram.
5. A subsequent recovery run explicitly attempted to send the **old provisional “test incomplete” final**. The recovery prompt supplied that prior final text.
6. Source-reply suppression returned **`already_delivered` / `delivered:false`**, with no new Telegram message ID. This was intentional suppression, not a recorded Telegram transport attempt.
7. A runtime `delivery-mirror` record at 00:14:02.296 UTC produced the misleading “could not deliver” notice.
8. A separate status-only ZeroCool handoff arrived afterward. Main handled it with `NO_REPLY`; that run made no Telegram send. It did not trigger the earlier failure notice.

## Expected behavior

Recovery should account for the later accepted delivery before attempting an older provisional final. An intentional `already_delivered` suppression should settle without a delivery-failure notice or stale-status resend.

## Evidence and limitations

The original provisional final, later report send/accepted receipt, stale-text send call and suppression result, delivery-mirror diagnostic, and subsequent status-only input are present in retained records.

The sanitized history does **not** expose the recovery enqueue's internal cause or ownership flags. Identification of stranded-reply recovery and stale-final selection also relies on inspection of the installed 2026.9.9 implementation; the exact scheduling edge is not proven by a lower-level branch trace.

The successful synthetic report was delivered once with its envelope removed. The defect reported here is the subsequent stale-final recovery and misleading failure notice, not failure to deliver that report.

## Related work

Related: #170534 (terminal-reply classification, deliberate silence, and undelivered-final retry behavior). This report isolates the receipt/suppression sequence above; it does not assume that PR fixes it.

No local runtime patches, configuration changes, restart, or resend were made to address this defect.

prs.title: fix(codex): defer plugin approvals for gated MCP tools to Codex's MCP approval
prs.body:
Fixes #173073.

## What Problem This Solves

Under the Codex runtime, a `before_tool_call` plugin that returns `requireApproval` for an **MCP** tool call had no viable wait path. Codex injects OpenClaw's native `PreToolUse` hook, and the `mcp__*` payload generated by Codex never carries `openclaw_approval_mode: "report"` (the field does not exist in the pinned `@openai/codex 0.160.1`). The relay therefore performed the human wait **inside the short-lived hook subprocess**, bounded at ~9 s (default hook timeout 10 s minus a 1 s parent margin), so every gated MCP call failed closed with `Tool call blocked by PreToolUse hook: Native hook relay timed out` while the approval card stayed interactive.

Measured on the real binary: the ~9 s fail-closed comes from OpenClaw's relay CLI deadline, not from Codex. Codex is **fail-open** on a PreToolUse hook timeout (a hook sleeping past its timeout still let the MCP tool execute), so returning "no decision" or letting the hook time out would execute the tool **without any human decision**.

## What Changed

Codex already gates MCP tool calls through its own in-process approval surface, `mcpServer/elicitation/request`, raised for every approval mode except `approve`; OpenClaw's elicitation bridge already handles it.

1. `runNativeHookRelayPreToolUse` treats an `mcp__*` call like report mode when Codex will gate it: the plugin approval requirement is recorded on the relay and the hook returns **no native decision**, moving the human wait to Codex's elicitation instead of the 9 s hook subprocess. `mcpToolApprovalDefersToCodex` reuses the existing `requiresMcpCodexToolApproval` / `resolveProjectedMcpCodexToolApprovalMode` projection, so servers projected to `approve` (no elicitation) and unresolved native server names keep the hook in custody — no widening.
2. While a plugin approval is parked on the relay for the active MCP tool call, the elicitation prompt is restricted to `["allow-once","deny"]`, refusing Codex's `session`/`always` persistence that would otherwise widen a plugin's per-call consent into a durable MCP grant. The relay handle exposes `hasPendingPreToolUseApproval(toolUseId)` for this check, so no new public Plugin SDK export is added.
3. `docs/plugins/codex-harness-runtime/hooks.md` documents the MCP deferral contract and its `approve`/unresolved-name exceptions.

## Evidence

Reproduced against the real `codex-cli 0.160.1` (offline mock Responses provider + local stdio MCP server + the actual native `PreToolUse` hook):

| # | Fact |
|---|---|
| E1 | MCP PreToolUse payload has no `openclaw_approval_mode` |
| E2 | PreToolUse is the MCP execution gate: `deny` blocks execution |
| E3 | Codex is fail-open on PreToolUse hook timeout (tool still executed) |
| E4 | No `item/mcpToolCall/requestApproval`; MCP approval only via `mcpServer/elicitation/request` |
| E5 | `default_tools_approval_mode` ∈ `auto｜prompt｜writes｜approve` |

App-server matrix (real `codex app-server`): `approve` → no elicitation, tool runs; `auto`/`prompt`/unset → elicitation raised and `decline` blocks execution.

Tests:
- `src/agents/harness/native-hook-relay.test.ts`: defers a plugin-gated MCP tool to Codex's gate; guard truth table.
- `extensions/codex/src/app-server/elicitation-bridge.test.ts`: per-call restriction when an approval is parked; none otherwise.
- Suites: relay trio = 110 passed; elicitation-bridge = 60 passed. `plugin-sdk:surface:check` and `plugin-sdk:check-exports` pass; `oxfmt` clean.

## Impact

Fixes the always-fail-closed behavior for plugin-gated MCP tools under Codex; the human can answer within the configured approval window. No change for `approve` servers, non-MCP tools, or deployments without a `before_tool_call` policy. Approval boundary is preserved: deferred decisions are never auto-approved and cannot be escalated to a durable grant.

## Follow-up (not in this PR)

- Surface the plugin's exact approval payload through the elicitation instead of OpenClaw's generic MCP prompt.
- Settle the parked deferred handle once the elicitation resolves, avoiding a redundant `CANCELLED` bookkeeping notice at relay teardown.

prs.title: feat(claws): prepare private drafts for reviewed publication
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

An agent workflow has no private proposal and explicit human publication path to a personal ClawHub account.

## User Impact

An administrator can create a private draft, have the normal agent author portable instructions and files, inspect the exact package, and explicitly publish it under their personal ClawHub identity. Drafts currently require a workspace on the Gateway host and a ClawHub login there.

## Why This Change Was Made

```text
private authored proposal → isolated package build → exact-file review → explicit Publish
```

Only authored proposal text enters the package; the source workspace is never copied. Known private paths and credential-like text are rejected. Review binds the draft revision, archive, publisher, and registry. Publication rechecks the current human connection and permissions, and reports pending scanning accurately. Creators must still inspect the draft for personal facts that automated checks cannot recognize.

Companion Control UI: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/173377.

## Evidence

- **Before:** there was no draft/review/publication API; copying a source workspace would include private context.
- **After:** the real package build excludes synthetic memory, identity, and credential sentinels. Tests compare reviewed files with the bytes sent to the publication endpoint and reject changed drafts, publisher accounts, and authority before any upload.
- Package/publication tests cover private-file exclusion, exact reviewed bytes, stale reviews and rejected authority. Existing HTTP client tests cover the shared bounded transport. The POST is never automatically retried after an uncertain response.
- Affected core and test typechecks passed, including the Gateway method fixtures. Formatting and targeted lint passed.
- The full protocol gate passes: schema registry, generated schema, Swift/Kotlin contracts and determinism, and release-train metadata for the five new methods. The registry guard now accounts for the added draft schema owner.
- Real local UI/Gateway integration completed on combined stack commit `16029c078424` (includes API head `b0be8e0b8d8`): normal agent authoring/write, creator review, explicit personal publication, fresh credential-free discovery, Add, and ordinary-agent chat. [Companion Add proof and inspected screenshots](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/173345).
- The 847-byte archive contains only the two reviewed files, byte-identical to reviewed contents, and excludes all four synthetic private markers and private source files. SHA-256: `6d91eff0ed17172d05a522947986b111ed99f07565c15657c5cf662696bd1432`.
- The model required a creator-side format-only Python-literal-to-JSON edit after correction attempts; every authored value was preserved. External scanner receipts are simulated in the local registry; auth, storage, publication, finalization and artifact delivery are real. Pending scanning and the consumer acknowledgement gate remained enforced. No production publication or deployment.

### Review repair: drafts above 256 KiB

Before the repair, reading and creating drafts accepted up to 1,000,000 bytes, but saving an existing draft inherited the shared file updater's 256 KiB read limit and failed. The real filesystem/Gateway-handler regression fails at both 262,145 and 1,000,000 bytes before the repair and passes afterward; a stale revision still rejects without overwriting the saved file.

The draft handler now supplies its existing size limit to the shared conflict-safe updater. Other callers retain their default limit. This adds one optional read-bound parameter to the existing owner; it does not add another writer or weaken revision checks.

Author simplification pass: draft artifacts are explicit user-authored files; the existing workspace writer owns safe updates and the existing publication client owns transport. Private preparation, exact review and explicit publication are one coherent backend stage, separate from discovery and the UI. Whole-PR delta: production +661/−1, tests +350/−0, tooling +2/−2. Remaining growth supplies the five new draft operations and tests their privacy, revision and authority boundaries.

### Current-build publication authority proof

Run on `853e003fb4988d4759e36027874d396533bf9a69`, build `2026.10.4-853e003fb498-2026-10-16T03-21-06.275Z`. The publication, caller-admission, device revocation, paired-device cache, dispatcher and HTTP-client sources match API head `2f5e81e5097b`. This rerun includes main’s updated device-authority cache behavior.

| Actual Gateway caller | Actual package POSTs |
|---|---:|
| Authorized administrator (positive control) | 1 |
| Connected operator without admin scope | 0 |
| Production plugin synthetic caller | 0 |
| Administrator disconnected in flight | 0 |
| Operator device-role credential revoked in flight | 0 |

The test uses real signed WebSocket requests to the built Gateway and a real local HTTP counter server. For disconnect and revocation, publication first reaches a held `/api/v1/whoami` response. It then closes the actual socket or successfully calls `device.token.revoke(role=operator)`, releases the HTTP response, waits for terminal Gateway dispatch, and checks zero `/api/v1/packages` POSTs. The revoked connection closes with code 4001. The synthetic case calls production `api.runtime.gateway.request`; it does not fabricate a GatewayClient. The positive control sends the reviewed 935-byte artifact once and reports pending publication.

Limits: the counter server is a controlled publication-transport fixture; real ClawHub storage and discovery are covered by the separate end-to-end proof above. Revocation here removes the device’s operator credential; it does not claim named-user policy-demotion coverage. Driver exit 0, all five assertions pass, both listeners are verified closed, and personal/OCM state is unchanged.

### Current revision validation

On combined stack head `853e003fb498`: 59 focused source/disclosure/draft/filesystem tests, 252 UI unit tests, and 7 browser scenarios pass. UI and Gateway-method typechecks, formatting and targeted lint, the runtime build, and the protocol gate pass. The stack is rebased onto main `49ecf70827307`, after its Add prerequisites merged.

Broad `check:changed` checkpoint: inherited failures in unchanged files: a max-lines suppression in `ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-message.test.tsx`, and TS2540 (assignment to readonly `text`) in `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/model-request-body.test.ts:69`. Both files and the suppression baseline have identical Git blobs at base and head. Targeted checks above pass.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** two-way for code; an explicit Publish creates a public immutable package version. **Blast radius:** administrator-only Claws draft methods behind the existing Labs flag. No database migration or deployment is included.

prs.title: docs(config): warn about Windows environment snapshot serialization
prs.body:
Closes #164702

## What Problem This Solves

The environment snapshot helper does not warn contributors that its Windows result cannot cross a worker serialization boundary.

## User Impact

User impact: no runtime behavior changes. Contributors see the Windows serialization constraint at the producer and can find the existing session-worker capture helper before adding another worker call site.

## Why This Change Was Made

Windows snapshots intentionally use a Proxy to preserve case-insensitive environment access. Proxies cannot be structured-cloned or sent through worker `postMessage`. The function documentation now names that constraint and directs session transcript callers to `captureSessionTranscriptStorageEnvironment`, which captures plain storage-routing facts. This addresses the remaining documentation request without changing the accepted Proxy design.

## Evidence

### Shipped Windows Gateway session flow

The requested shipped-entry-point proof now ran successfully on a native **Windows Server 2025** GitHub runner with **Node v24.21.0** and the published npm package **OpenClaw 2026.10.3 (`59cb447`)**. The script invokes the package's `openclaw.mjs` CLI, starts a real loopback Gateway with fresh temporary config/state/workspace, and issues authenticated `gateway call` commands. It creates an explicit non-main durable session, resolves that session, confirms it appears in the session list, and reads its transcript through `sessions.get`. Assertions verify the returned session key/id and list membership. No runtime helpers, worker calls, or platform values are mocked, and no model turn or provider API request is made.

Terminal output from the successful job, with runner prefixes omitted:

This is a smoke run of the published release, not a source build of the PR head. It demonstrates the existing Windows session/worker contract documented by this comment-only change; the exact PR head is additionally covered by the integration results below. An earlier proof attempt stopped at config validation because the proof script used a retired memory-search config key; the linked successful revision uses the current `memory.search` configuration.

### Static validation and review

- Inspected the producer, `captureSessionTranscriptStorageEnvironment`, its session-worker callers, and the existing Windows Proxy regression in `src/cron/isolated-agent/session.preparation.storage-env.test.ts`.
- `git diff --check` passed.

- Canonical `autoreview --mode local --max-priority P3` completed with no actionable findings, with the capture helper and existing regression supplied as context.
- No local runtime tests or build were run. The integration proof below was executed by PR CI on the current head.

### Executed session-worker regression

PR CI executed the existing regression at head `6762648cd5c66b3e29c2cc80f74206e4a2d1b2b4` in [checks-node-changed-3, Run Node test shard](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/38749671328/job/116473496670#step:18:1). The job succeeded. The following excerpt is from that job's terminal output; runner prefixes and color escapes are omitted:

Both cases first call the actual `cloneEnvWithPlatformSemantics` implementation with Windows semantics and [assert that `structuredClone` throws `DataCloneError` with code 25](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/6762648cd5c66b3e29c2cc80f74206e4a2d1b2b4/src/cron/isolated-agent/session.preparation.storage-env.test.ts#L43).
