prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`. Current signed head `453b50229bd056e6d82118159670aafad7db384c`, tree `9a099481b45ba773267d2dd75564c939e5c2830c`, is a normal successor of `130519fd2b94b3ce044232a95b8eb5746ab50759` on the original fork/topic. This successor also corrects generated-config defaults; the namespace repair is retained.
- **What changed and why:** New installations start with eleven everyday built-ins in Chat and eight in Code/ACP. The single `[tools].optional` selection adds individual extras or full eligible availability. Existing files without `[tools]` retain full availability in v0.8.6; explicit empty selections remain minimal. Selection still requires compiled support, prerequisites and policy.
- **Latest correction:** Resolve late `tool_search` ownership at actual native creator sites, then remove the conflicting Wasm object from every captured executable/context/parent/pipeline/skill view and its eligible hidden schema. Fixing only the final vector leaves callable captured copies behind. Native helper creation is not inferred merely from configured MCP: all eight no-host cases retain the actual guest.
- **Scope boundary:** The latest two-file correction records canonical minimal defaults in newly generated documents and strengthens existing tests. The preceding construction-time namespace repair is retained. No live policy cache, generic role normalization, second selection setting, blanket new namespace catalog or authority grant. Other late extension names, progressive disclosure and adapter dependency removal remain separate work.
- **Blast radius:** Native tool preparation, scoped/captured registries and hidden specs; original feature also covers configuration, CLI/ACP/delegation and distribution feature contracts.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #8310, #6165, #8754, #11305, #11308, #11306, #11327, #11442, #11473, #11475 and #7432. No replacement PR.

### What this does, simply

Chat starts with `shell`, `file_read`, `file_write`, `file_edit`, `glob_search`, `content_search`, `memory_recall`, `memory_store`, `memory_forget`, `web_fetch` and `git_operations`. Code retains its memory exclusion, leaving eight. Configured extensions and policy still affect the effective catalog.

```toml
[tools]
optional = ["*"]
```

That selection restores eligible built-ins; it does not install prerequisites, provide credentials, activate integrations or grant permission. Canonical `dist` downloads include `tools-compat`; `dist-compat` is the identical alias. Custom Cargo-default builds need the relevant features first. Packaging keeps the existing ten-target archive matrix and names; Android remains experimental.

Existing omitted-section configs preserve full intent through migration and unrelated saves. New installations persist `optional = []`; malformed or explicit selections are not silently promoted. A v0.9.0 migration of existing installations to minimal is separate and is not implemented here. Generated documents now explicitly record the canonical minimal selector for every supported schema version, including encrypted generation, so loading a newly generated file preserves that intent.

The latest build registry keeps original object identity and one final pipeline object. Actual creator claims retire conflicting guest captures and narrow existing schema winners without replaying getters or promoting an earlier loser. The consuming `PipelineTool::retain_context_tools` method removes existing children only; creator-owned `ToolSearchTool::NAME` supplies its canonical name. There is no new grant or dispatch API.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes, using isolated config/HOME/workspace and synthetic fixtures. Review current source and official receiving CI before integration.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** Runtime tool assembly and real WIT guest execution with a granted synthetic MCP server. Earlier real Chat/ACP tasks remain historical evidence below.
- **Setup / preconditions:** Rust 1.98, locked dependencies, the existing Cranelift feature and reviewed two-variant `wasm32-wasip2` fixture. No production service/provider/credential is needed for the namespace controls.
- **Steps to run:** The existing required Cranelift admission step builds the fixtures, verifies the exact 23-name list and runs the original selectors plus `tools::r5_namespace_tests::late_tool_search`. Compare fresh/explicit-empty/named/wildcard configs separately for original selection behavior.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** All 23 current namespace controls pass. When a real native helper claims the name, no retired guest is callable through captured views or a promoted schema. When no helper is created, the guest remains usable; caller/principal/policy and one shared MCP registry remain intact.
- **Prior behavior (before):** The public original behavior and a final-vector-only mutation both leave real guest paths callable after top-level handling. Actual failures, not setup or zero-selection errors, are counted below.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** [Current Quality Gate 38797960526](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38797960526), on signed `453b50229bd056e6d82118159670aafad7db384c`, completed with 40 successful jobs, 2 failed and 3 skipped. The only failed prerequisite is Security: inherited Rustls 0.23.45 is denied for RUSTSEC-2026-0346 through 0349; the aggregate gate correctly fails. Current logs individually record 99 migration integration PASS results, including all nine generator methods, 12 compatibility/save/omission PASS results, and all 23 required Cranelift namespace PASS results with 23 cleanup receipts. Format, Lint, MSRV and selected Windows checks pass. All 41 source checkout receipts pin the same synthetic merge; all 36 inspected relevant blobs match the public head. Shared #11755 still needs a second independent non-author Core vote and protected landing. A fresh receiving gate is required after dependency adoption; these results do not claim a full gate or release pass.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** Stable archives, optimized size, full platform, Code/ACP acceptance and release qualification remain separate. Current required Security, non-author owners/Core and holding-crate placement remain held.
- **Commands run and tail output:** Exact current tree `9a099481b45ba773267d2dd75564c939e5c2830c`, Rust 1.98 on the isolated Linux dev-box, jobs 8/incremental 0, task-local umask 022 and separate target:

```text
cargo fmt --all -- --check                              PASS
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-config --test migration   99 PASS
12 selected legacy/explicit/malformed/save controls      12 PASS
cargo clippy --locked -p zeroclaw-config --all-targets
  -- -D warnings                                        PASS
real CLI generate 1/2/3, plain and --encrypt              6 combinations emit and load []
original-generator inverse, same new tests              6 PASS / 2 intended missing-selector failures
real original CLI generate 3 / load                     section absent / ["*"]
restored fixed generator / rebuilt CLI                  8 PASS / emits and loads []
```

- **Optimized current-source check:** The canonical generator emitted the expected 29 distribution features. The isolated Linux dev-box completed the locked x86_64 GNU `--release --no-default-features` build with that vector in 570 seconds. The uncompressed main binary is **75,991,816 bytes (72.47 MiB)**, below the 80 MiB cap; repeated SHA256 is `d0744e8b9833cc1f380485b862bd41188be1677cf83ec6242134dd219d91c4b0`. The compiled source tree equals current public `453b502`, and source/index/lock remained unchanged. Ubuntu 22 ABI, ARM64, archives/runtime, Core and full release qualification remain separate.

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** The real CLI trials use private config and key directories. Existing documents without `[tools]` still load full selection; generated documents explicitly preserve minimal selection. Removing only the production generator fix reproduces the omission and full-on-load behavior. Restoring it reproduces the initial fixed executable hash. Both owned source files, the lockfile and all 2,279 outside entries are preserved; generated documents and keys are not exported.
- **Visual interface evidence:** This correction changes generated config output. The observed selector/load values above cover that command boundary; no screenshot claim is made.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** Signed `453b50229bd056e6d82118159670aafad7db384c`, tree `9a099481b45ba773267d2dd75564c939e5c2830c`; real `config generate` and `config get` plus the existing migration tests. The current official run is linked above.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** Fixed generation and actual loading return `tools.optional = []`; the original-generator comparison returns `["*"]` after loading its omitted section. Plain and encrypted output were checked for versions 1, 2 and 3. The two baseline test failures stop on the first loop version; the separate real CLI comparison specifically covers version 3.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** Generation serializes `BuiltinToolsConfig::default()` after the historical schema chain, before optional encryption. Existing-document normalization is unchanged, preserving full tools for upgrades that omit the section.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Optimized release/size, full platform and application/live qualification are outside these config checks.

**Retained namespace qualification:** Parent `130519fd` has 23 individually named official Cranelift namespace PASS results, 23 cleanup PASS receipts and 33 other selected PASS controls in [run 38786159045](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38786159045). Its full gate failed only shared Security and the aggregate gate. Separate source-bound dev-box controls produced F:23 PASS; original behavior B:13 PASS / 9 namespace FAIL / 1 uncredited observer FAIL; weakened final-vector-only retirement M:14 PASS / 9 namespace FAIL. All 69 cleanup receipts, executable/component hashes and the 17 fixture inputs were verified. B's extra missing baseline observation is not credited as a namespace or order failure. Namespace production/support/CI blobs are unchanged by this two-file generator correction; current hosted execution remains separate.

**Retained failures:** The namespace fixture's initial direct Tokio spawn was replaced with the attributed macro after lint rejected it. Earlier fixture stack, mode and cumulative no-host deadline failures remain associated with their original sources; individual case budgets and assertions were preserved.

**Historical selection/migration evidence:** QG38149015910 passed its twelve migration/save cases and selection/deferral/Matrix/Notion contracts. On `63d3a8f`, QG38572272395 failed shared Rustls Security; both corrected channel fixtures and 26 contract / 80 broader names passed on that older source. Earlier thirteen real Chat/ACP tasks exercised all core tools, optional calculator, restricted-shell refusal and private Code Git effects. Those used an older debug executable, not current source or an optimized size measurement. Its failed intermediate Git call and other retained failures remain historical. These results do not replace current receiving validation.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or filesystem access scope? **No.** Selection and namespace handling preserve approval, sandbox, path/network and lifecycle checks; supplied/native code remains trusted according to its existing boundary.
- New external network calls? **No new production path.** Current tests use an isolated granted loopback MCP fixture.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? **No production change;** fixtures use synthetic data.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? **No.**
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? **Yes in the original selection feature:** minimal reduces descriptions and selected extras restore eligible descriptions. No new input surface in this successor.
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: Selection is not authority. Actual native ownership must also remove captured guest paths; real metadata and counterfactual controls cover this correction. The risk remains high and needs current independent non-author Core/path-owner review.

## Compatibility (required)

- **Backward compatible?** Existing omitted-section configs retain full eligible tools in v0.8.6; explicit selections and schema 3 remain. New installs use minimal. No automatic v0.9.0 reset occurs.
- **Config / env / CLI surface changed?** Original `[tools].optional` only; no additional setting in this successor.
- **Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed?** No.
- **Upgrade steps:** For explicit full selection set `optional = ["*"]` under `[tools]`, or run `zeroclaw config set tools.optional '["*"]' --no-interactive`, then recreate/reload the registry. Custom builds add compatibility/concrete features first. Migration records omitted-section full intent and ordinary saves retain it.
- **Rust API:** The original public `AllToolsResult.reserved_host_names` addition requires external exhaustive literals to add that field; external consumers are not qualified here. This successor adds the consuming removal-only pipeline method and creator-owned name constant, not mutable dispatch or grant access.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Operator recovery:** Select `optional = ["*"]` or individual extras; add missing build features on custom builds.
- **Code rollback:** Revert through the normal PR path while preserving user data and coordinating dependent callers. Reverting this namespace correction restores the captured-view defect; it is not a safe security workaround.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** Existing tool selection only; no new authority toggle.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** Unexpected optional construction, missing expected schemas, compiled-out diagnostics, captured guest calls after native ownership, schema loser promotion or changed policy/refusal behavior.

## Supersede Attribution (required only when `Supersedes #` is used)

N/A. Original PR, fork, branch, authorship and history retained.

prs.title: feat(release): ship the WASM plugin host in supported release artifacts
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `test/10994-plugin-artifact-smoke` (stacked on #11311; retarget to `master` once it merges)
- **What changed and why:**
  - Integrate the current public minimal-tools distribution profile from #11221 and the landed Wasmtime 48.0.6 / Rustls 0.23.46 security update from #11755. Distribution builds retain compatible tool implementations; existing configurations without `[tools]` retain full availability, while newly generated configurations start minimal.
  - Root `Cargo.toml`: `plugins-wasm-cranelift` joins `dist_extra_features`, so the standard distribution artifacts carry the WASM plugin host with the compiler that loads `.wasm` components, the only form the plugin registry publishes. `dist_target_exclusions` removes it for `armv7-unknown-linux-gnueabihf` and `arm-unknown-linux-gnueabihf` (Cranelift has no native ARM32 backend, and no native ARM32 runner can prove wasmtime's Pulley fallback) and for `aarch64-linux-android` (experimental, not a required asset). The Pulley feature comment now describes what the feature does.
  - Generated surfaces regenerated with `cargo generate installers` (source container builds, AUR package, Nix flake, `setup.bat`, container tag registry); the base-image digest refresh the generator also performs is left out on purpose.
  - `release-stable-manual.yml`: `plugin-smoke-packages` builds the fixture plugin packages once on Linux; `plugin-smoke` downloads each of the seven 64-bit desktop and server archives on a runner of its own platform and runs `scripts/ci/plugin_artifact_smoke.sh` against the packaged binary; the legs set up no toolchain and compile nothing. `publish` and `docker` need it. Both jobs run with `permissions: contents: read` and a checkout that persists no credentials. `BINARY_SIZE_HARD_LIMIT` rises from 64 MiB to 80 MiB.
  - `cross-platform-build-manual.yml`: the same two jobs against the binaries it builds, so one dispatch both measures sizes and proves plugin execution for a distribution change.
  - Tests and docs: an xtask test ties "this target carries a plugin backend" to "the release has a smoke leg for it" in both directions; the architecture suite pins the wiring (needs, artifact names, least privilege, the whole smoke invocation, no `continue-on-error`, no condition on the smoke step); generator tests match feature names as whole tokens; the dist parity test reads the build job's matrix. Every page that said prebuilt binaries lack the host now says which artifacts carry it, which do not, and where the proof is recorded; the protocol page gains a per-artifact table and the limits that hold for all of them; the operator page gains the release-binary walkthrough and rollback; the Nix module and README explain `MemoryDenyWriteExecute` against plugin loads.
- **Scope boundary:** The artifact changes preserve plugin enablement/discovery/signature defaults, the WIT contract and desktop bundle behavior. The normal public #11221 integration also carries its tool-selection and CLI/config changes, including the existing-config versus new-install behavior above. The normal master integration carries the reviewed security and supporting fixes. Existing external actions remain pinned; the Stable build step now uses the local shared release recipe. No release asset is added, renamed, or removed. The `v*` tag trigger of docker-publish.yml is unchanged.
- **Blast radius:** the seven 64-bit desktop and server CLI archives; the GHCR `latest`, versioned and `debian` images, repackaged from two of them; source builds from the generated distribution list (the GHCR `dist` variant, the AUR package, the Nix flake package, `setup.bat`); the stable release and manual cross-platform workflows; the plugin documentation; consumers of `/api/plugins`, the dashboard Plugins page, and `zeroclaw status` output, which change what they report; the cron database, where any plugin-host binary that opens or creates it adds an empty `plugin_outbox` table; and, with `skills.install_suggestions.enabled = true` (default off) and a registry index cached by `plugin search` or `plugin install <name>`, a release binary now answers a matching turn with a `zeroclaw plugin install` suggestion instead of calling the model, whatever `plugins.enabled` says. Not affected: the ARM32 and Android archives, the desktop bundles, `cargo install`, and `install.sh` source builds.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #10994; the issue closes after the v0.8.6 run posts downloaded-artifact evidence on #10994, #7432 and #10999. Depends on #11311 and #11310.

### What this does, simply

ZeroClaw can load WebAssembly plugins, but until now the prebuilt release binaries were built without that plugin host: `zeroclaw plugin ...` was not even a command, and outside the amd64 `all-features` container image a plugin needed a source build. This PR puts the plugin host, with the compiler that loads ordinary `.wasm` plugins, into the release binaries for the seven 64-bit desktop and server targets. For an operator who does not use plugins, what is off stays off: the plugin system is disabled by default, a plugin is instantiated only by the operator's own `plugin install`, `plugin info` or `plugin list --verify` commands, and it is offered to the model only after the operator enables the plugin system and turns discovery on. What such an operator does see change on a release binary: `zeroclaw plugin` exists as a command, `zeroclaw status` lists a `Plugin` channel row, `/api/plugins` reports `wasm_plugins_available: true`, and the dashboard's Plugins page says the plugin system is disabled instead of unavailable in this build.

What was missing was proof. A binary can carry the host and still fail to run a plugin, so the release now checks itself: one job builds a small test plugin, and one job per archive downloads the archive that is about to be published, installs the plugin through the normal commands, and makes an agent call it. On a dispatched release, the GitHub Release and the container images are created only if every one of those checks passes. The manual cross-platform build runs the same checks, so a change to what ships can be rehearsed before a release.

Limits: the two 32-bit ARM archives and the experimental Android archive still have no plugin host. The binary size cap grows because the host adds about 4.7 MiB. Plugins are experimental: a plugin must be built against the WIT contract shipped with the release that runs it.

Decisions taken here and flagged for maintainers (from the plan on #10994):

| # | Decision | What this PR does | Needs sign-off |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | Size cap | 64 MiB to 80 MiB. The v0.8.5 x86_64 Linux binary was 61,537,880 B against 67,108,864; the host adds 4,909,008 B measured on aarch64-apple-darwin with this machine's stable toolchain, rustc 1.97.1 (36,802,864 to 41,711,872 at master 4f93bf5399). | Yes. An estimate until a Cross-Platform Build dispatch on this branch reports the x86_64 Linux sizes. |
| D2 | Backend per target | Cranelift on the seven 64-bit desktop and server targets; none on ARM32 and Android. | Yes |
| D3 | Package formats | `.wasm` only; no artifact ships a deserialize-only backend. | Follows from D2 |
| D4 | Smoke plugin | The in-tree `tool-fixture` packages (eight variants) for the blocking gate. `redact-text@0.3.0` from the registry was verified by hand on a release-profile build while planning. | No |
| D5 | Gate strength | `publish` and `docker` both need `plugin-smoke`; the images repackage two smoke-gated archives. | Yes, for `docker` |
| D6 | Nix hardening | `MemoryDenyWriteExecute` stays on; comments and README say plugin loads fail under it and how an instance overrides it on its own unit. | No |
| D7 | Authority | FND-001 section 4.4.2 plus `status:accepted` on #10994 cover artifact-only inclusion with defaults unchanged. FND-001 says every binary carries the plugin host; after this PR the ARM32 and Android archives do not, and the desktop bundle sidecars never did. Both are recorded gaps, not edits to the protected document. | Yes |

### Current receiving source and validation

Signed `4d08d6bb821acec5690b4f0bc587e38da35c401f`, tree `2ea3a363bbe477fa76a9b6841204f4d52cafbe93`, preserves the original topic, draft and #11311 base. Its single parent is `7ab574822f1d267725a9913737c6d08aba5ce830`, whose normal parents are `74b9a8ed697ee88fda2d8818a1cc63fc30982ce2` and landed master `be354a7ac9d5af1f822728c445acbd41a53ac11a`. The preceding normal integration retains exact public #11221 `453b502` as a parent. No contributor history was rewritten.

The distribution feature selection remains target-specific and includes a compiling WASM plugin host on the seven supported native legs. The workflow readers now preserve outdented generated comment sentinels while still stopping at the next real job. Stable and the GNU qualifier retain the same original cache namespace. Existing build recipes, profile choices, target exclusions, canonical feature resolution, resources, budgets, permissions, 80 MiB cap and acceptance gates are preserved.

Supplemental Linux dev-box validation ran on preceding receiving tree `4086479` / public `74b9a8e`: official Rust 1.98 formatting, all 22 generated surfaces, 58 individually named generator controls and three static whole-file architecture controls passed. Three inverse changes each failed their intended retained assertion; each restored positive passed again with exact source/stages/lock. The architecture methods linked real existing locked dependencies; this was not the full root architecture suite. The later eight-path master import is byte-identical to the separately reviewed public-source integration and preserves every other receiving entry. Those selected results remain tied to that preceding tree. The current one-literal correction updates the architecture test's expected full-workflow digest for the four intentional, generated target/distribution matrix lines. Removing those four lines reconstructs the prior Stable workflow byte for byte; the 324-byte Build release wrapper is unchanged. On the exact current tree, a separate isolated Linux dev-box run passed formatting and both controlled recipe methods. Reverting the expected digest or changing the actual cap by one byte each caused the retained assertion to fail; both normal reversals restored exact source/stages/lock and passed again. These fixture methods intercept cargo/cross and do not build production payloads.

Current [Quality Gate 38824352184, attempt 1](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38824352184/attempts/1) **passed: 43 successful jobs and three declared skips**. Required Gate `116731550780` accounts for all 36 needs (33 success, three skips). All 42 source checkouts pin `6903a8d683b9a9a5d8f075f8bb79337bdbc6b71b`, merging the actual #11311 base `6b05d5c` with this head; its entire tree equals the public tree. All 51 scoped named controls pass: 27 generator-spec methods and 24 release-workflow architecture methods, including the two recipe methods, four baseline methods, six qualification methods and the comment/cache controls. The workspace passes 18,865 tests with 40 skipped. Current Security, locked fetch/audit, Format, Lint/rustdoc, Docs, MSRV 1.96.0, generator drift, opt-in tools and selected Windows/Cranelift jobs pass. The current debug x86_64 Linux plugin smoke has 18 actual named checks and matching PASS rows; its opposite-expectation control correctly refuses the host binary. This is ordinary debug-binary evidence, not packaged-release qualification.

Historical GNU Ubuntu 22 qualification remains incomplete. [Run 38540320215](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38540320215), attempt 1 on prior `7e9bf80`, delivered its bounded initial baseline, three archives and nine input/ABI pairs, then failed after ARM64 received shutdown signal/exit 143 at 26m46.043s. Both native suites were NOTRUN and completeness correctly refused. The shutdown cause remains unknown. Earlier successful archive/native runs retain their own heads and provide no current artifact credit. No new retry, resource/runner alternative or causal repair is claimed.

Successful ordinary CI does not settle required parent landing, current human/Core review, Stable archives, Ubuntu 22/ARM64, companion runtime, size or full-platform/release acceptance. The binary demo and earlier local size reports are supplemental evidence on their own sources, not release-artifact acceptance.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes, optional: an A/B run of the smoke against a release-profile build takes about twenty minutes of compile time on a laptop plus a minute for the checks.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `cli`

All 46 selected named controls passed, including the four baseline methods, six retained qualification methods and 24 generator-spec tests; the workspace ran 19,534 tests successfully. That run’s tested merge tree equals its own prior public tree; its execution remains historical. Current `4d08d6b` qualification is recorded above.

The bounded initial baseline uploaded successfully, but it does not establish the shutdown cause. Three of four archives and nine input/ABI pairs were verified; both native suites did not run and completeness correctly refused with exit 2. Full GNU artifact qualification remains incomplete. Earlier runs and contributor-local reports below retain their own revisions and provide no current-head execution credit.
- **Current receiving CI:** [Quality Gate 38824352184, attempt 1](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38824352184/attempts/1) passed on exact signed `4d08d6b`; the actual checkout/source and named-result scope are recorded under “Current receiving source and validation.” Historical contributor reports below remain tied to their named revisions.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** the seven release legs, the musl archives built through `cross` with wasmtime, and the Windows leg run only in Release Stable or the manual Cross-Platform Build; a dispatch of the manual workflow on this branch is the planned proof before this PR leaves draft.
- **Commands run and tail output:** Historical contributor report on aarch64-apple-darwin with rustc 1.97.1. The release workflow pins 1.98.0; these local outputs do not measure the current release candidate or satisfy D1:

The same list without the plugin host measured 36,802,864 bytes at master 4f93bf5399. (2) The `run:` bodies of both new smoke steps, extracted from the workflow YAML with the matrix target substituted, executed locally against that binary: the release step against an archive packaged like the build job's output (binary plus `web/dist`), the manual step against the raw binary with its executable bit cleared; both exit 0 with 18 PASS rows and write the evidence file and the step summary. ## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? `Yes`. The 64-bit desktop and server release binaries now contain a code-loading runtime (wasmtime with Cranelift). Compiled-in effects that do not depend on config: the `plugin` CLI, the gateway plugin webhook routes, `/api/plugins`, a status row, and the empty `plugin_outbox` table added when the cron database is opened or created. Instantiating a component calls no export but does run any start function its core modules carry (for example a reactor's `_initialize`). `plugin install` (unless `--no-verify`), `plugin info` and `plugin list --verify` instantiate the component whether or not the plugin system is enabled, in a store with no preopened files, no network or egress authority, and the per-call fuel, memory and time limits. Exports run only after the operator opts in. With `plugins.enabled` and `plugins.auto_discover` set, every build of the tool registry compiles, instantiates and queries each admitted tool component for its metadata under the package's declared permissions and egress policy, and the tool is offered to the model; each `execute` then needs approval unless pre-approved (`auto_approve` by name or `*`, `level = "full"`, or an Always grant). A skill package needs `enabled` and `auto_discover`. A channel package needs `enabled`, a `[channels.plugin.<alias>]` declaration, and an enabled agent that lists `plugin.<alias>`. The smoke proves the closed defaults per archive: install leaves the plugin system off, discovery without enabling offers nothing, enabling without discovery offers nothing, a discovered tool waits for approval, and payload digests, the WIT world and the signature policy are enforced at install.
- New external network calls? `Yes`. `plugin search` and `plugin install <name>` fetch the registry index, operator-initiated. A plugin granted `http_client` or socket permissions can make policed egress from a release binary once enabled, including during the metadata probe; egress is deny-by-default through the per-instance allowlist. The release smoke itself talks only to a local stub provider.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? Application interfaces remain unchanged. The incorporated Rustls security patch includes upstream TLS/secret-handling fixes. No new secret collection or export is introduced. The new jobs receive no secrets, hold `contents: read`, and check out with `persist-credentials: false`. The added diagnostic reads only whitelisted public identity/resource/package fields and writes two private runner-temp files. It adds a bounded upload to the existing GitHub artifact service, with no new permission or destination; no environment, argv, process, kernel, network or credential dump is collected.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? `No`.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? `Yes`, in reach rather than mechanism: once a plugin is enabled, its tool name, description, parameter schema and results are model-visible text supplied by the plugin. Source builds have this today; this PR makes it reachable from release binaries once the operator enables the plugin system and discovery: the name, description and schema reach the model at registration without any approval, and results only after an approved call. A plugin skill package injects package-supplied skill text once the plugin system is enabled and discovery is on, and a channel plugin feeds inbound text to the model.
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: covered in the answers above. wasmtime advisories become release-relevant; `cargo deny` and the daily audit already gate them.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? `Yes`
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? `Yes`: the 64-bit desktop and server release binaries gain the `zeroclaw plugin` subcommand and the gateway's plugin webhook route. `/api/plugins`, present in every gateway build, now answers `wasm_plugins_available: true` and lists installed packages; the dashboard's Plugins page shows the plugin system as disabled rather than unavailable; `zeroclaw status` gains a `Plugin` channel row; any plugin-host binary that opens or creates the cron database adds an empty `plugin_outbox` table. The incorporated #11221 prerequisite adds explicit tool selection: existing configurations without `[tools]` retain full availability, new installs start minimal. Plugin enablement remains opt-in; no new environment variable is introduced.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? `No`

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** revert the four commits together (`git revert` of the merge commit, or of the four SHAs in reverse order); they restore the policy, the generated surfaces, the workflows, the tests and the docs as one unit. A partial rollback has to go further than the policy line: remove `plugins-wasm-cranelift` from `dist_extra_features` and from the three `dist_target_exclusions` entries (the resolver rejects an exclusion that names a feature outside the selection), remove the two `plugin-smoke` jobs from both workflows and `plugin-smoke` from the `publish` and `docker` needs, update the xtask and architecture tests and the docs, then run `cargo generate installers`. Rolling back one target is smaller: add it to `dist_target_exclusions` and drop its leg from both workflows; the xtask test holds the two in step.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** runtime `plugins.enabled` (default `false`) and `plugins.auto_discover` (default `false`); operators pin an older release with `zeroclaw update --version <previous> --force` (musl and package-manager installs reinstall the previous archive or package instead).
- **Observable failure symptoms:** a `Check binary size` failure on a build leg (`Binary exceeds 80MB safeguard`); a `Plugin Smoke <target>` leg failing, with its step summary naming the failed check, which skips `publish` and `docker`; `zeroclaw --help` listing no `plugin` command on a 64-bit desktop or server archive, which is the smoke's first check.

## Known risks

- The Windows smoke leg is the first blocking Windows plugin check. The harness handles MSYS paths and `.exe` but has run only on macOS and Linux so far.
- The musl archives build through `cross`; wasmtime's C helpers in that container are unproven until the manual workflow runs.
- `ubuntu-24.04-arm` runners execute the aarch64 archives; the glibc one links glibc 2.35 (built on 22.04) and runs on 24.04. The manual rehearsal cross-builds on `ubuntu-latest`; once that label moves past 24.04 the binary may need a newer glibc than the runner has.
- The 80 MiB cap is an estimate until the manual workflow reports x86_64 Linux sizes.
- A release started by a tag push also triggers Docker Publish on its own `v*` trigger, which does not wait for the smoke; the dispatch path is the gated one.

## Follow-ups, not in this PR

- ARM32 with the Cranelift feature and wasmtime's automatic Pulley target: a compile check in CI, then an emulated smoke.
- A `plugin sign` command (proposed in RFC #8135, which is deferred and not accepted).
- A way to ask a binary which backend it carries; `--version` lists no features.
- Registry CI that instantiates published artifacts (#9624), and registry signing.
- Size figures in generated release notes; a smoke inside the published container image.
- The plugin crate setup snippet clones the WIT from `master`; now that release binaries are the documented host it should pin the release tag (`--branch vX.Y.Z`).
- #11335 and #11336, found while building the harness.

prs.title: fix(channels): honor Telegram 429 retry_after via shared per-token flood gate
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - Telegram Bot API 429 responses were treated like formatting failures: `sendMessage` retried immediately as plain text (a markdown→plain double-hit), draft edits kept their cadence, and the typing loop never noticed — so a rate-limited token got hammered, its penalty escalated, and finalized replies were lost (issue #11615).
  - This adds a flood-control gate (`TelegramRateLimiter`) shared **by the clones of one channel instance** (channel fields, spawned typing loop, approval paths) — it is *not* a registry keyed by bot token: separately constructed channels on the same token, including repeated one-off announcement factories, keep independent windows. Gated surface: the channel's text traffic — `sendMessage` (final answers, draft creation, approval prompts), `editMessageText` (draft updates, finalize), and `sendChatAction` (typing). Media uploads, `deleteMessage`, `answerCallbackQuery`, and the model picker's markup edits still post directly and are not covered by this gate.
  - Droppable calls (typing, draft edits) skip silently while the window is open. Deliver calls wait the window out bounded by a caller-side budget (`rate_limit_max_wait_secs`), **re-check the shared gate after sleeping**, and stop with a distinguishable budget-exhausted outcome if the window is still active — the budget bounds how long the caller waits, never the server deadline, so nothing is sent into an active window. On a fresh 429 a Deliver call retries once; a second 429 contributes its own (possibly longer) `retry_after` to the shared window and stops the formatting/resume/resend fallbacks — a 429 is not a formatting failure.
  - The recorded deadline keeps the later of the active and new values, so out-of-order concurrent 429 responses cannot shorten the window; an unrepresentable delay is rejected rather than clamped into permission to send sooner.
  - Honors `retry_after` from the JSON envelope (`parameters.retry_after`), with a `retry after <N>` description fallback and a 5s fallback when nothing is parseable.
  - Partial deliveries still suppress the orchestrator's full-answer resend via `FinalizePartialDelivery`, and flood-control exhaustion now stops the chunk-resume path as well instead of burning the wait budget twice. The pending-narration loop in multi-message finalization also stops on the terminal gate outcome: instead of burning three narration retries plus a final-answer wait on fresh budgets, it propagates the gate error, so the outer resend is suppressed without reporting an undelivered final answer as delivered.
  - Two new optional telegram channel config keys: `rate_limit_max_wait_secs` (default 60; `0` restores the default — it is not a disable switch) and `typing_refresh_interval_secs` (default 4, previously hardcoded). Both resolve from the live config authority at each use, including per-tick in the typing loop, so a published change applies to a running channel without a rebuild.
- **Scope boundary:** adaptive draft throttling and any listener-side changes are explicitly out of scope (per maintainer triage on #11615); no behavior change when no 429 occurs — the pre-send gate is a no-op on `Clear`.
- **Blast radius:** Outbound paths of the Telegram channel only (`send_text_chunks`, `send_draft`, `update_draft`, `finalize_draft`, `start_typing`, approval send) plus one guard in the orchestrator's finalize-fallback arm. No change to inbound/listener logic, other channels, or the agent loop. Defaults keep today's behavior for well-behaved tokens.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #11615. Related #11608.

### What this does, simply

Telegram tells throttled bots exactly when to come back (`retry_after` in the 429 body), but the channel ignored that and fired again immediately — markdown attempt, then plain attempt, then more draft edits and typing ticks. Each ignored window made the next one longer, and when the final reply finally hit the limit it was dropped: users saw drafts vanish mid-sentence. Now the channel records "blocked until N seconds" per channel instance (shared by its clones) the moment any call sees a 429, keeping the longest active deadline. Cosmetic traffic (typing indicator, live draft edits) stays silent during the window; user-visible sends wait out the server-directed window up to a bounded caller budget and try again once. When the window clears within budget, the reply is late instead of dropped. When the window outlasts the budget, nothing is sent into it: the answer is held and an error is returned — this slice has no durable delivery queue or automatic later redelivery, so such a reply can go undelivered (WARN-logged) until the sender retries; what the gate guarantees is that the token stops digging itself deeper and no message is duplicated by a blind resend.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `N/A` — the rate-limit interaction is fully covered by mock-server tests (429-then-success, repeated limiting with escalating deadlines, blocked-window skipping, budget expiry without resend, mid-wait window extension, cancelled waiter, cross-chat window sharing, gated draft creation, live-config resolution, pending-narration finalize stop with zero and nonzero accepted prefixes); a live 429 cannot be induced reliably without flooding a real bot token.

### How I tested

```sh
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-channels --all-targets --no-deps -- -D warnings
env -u HTTP_PROXY -u HTTPS_PROXY -u ALL_PROXY cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels telegram
env -u HTTP_PROXY -u HTTPS_PROXY -u ALL_PROXY cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels finalize
```

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** channels/config unit and integration tests cover the changed surface (telegram channel + config schema).
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` at workspace level shows pre-existing warnings in platform-conditional code outside this diff (unix-gated code on a Windows host, Windows-only service code); none originate from this change, and the channels crate itself is `-D warnings` clean. Two pre-existing `zeroclaw-config` test failures reproduce on unpatched master (`agent_bundle::…outside_shared_is_dropped_with_its_content`, `platform::native::…powershell_full_scripts_execute_with_native_semantics`).
- **Commands run and tail output (head `fe42c5d30`):** `cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels telegram` → `test result: ok. 429 passed; 0 failed`; `cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels finalize` → `test result: ok. 23 passed; 0 failed` (including the two new `finalize_stops_on_flood_gate_with_{zero,nonzero}_accepted_narration_prefix` regressions and the retained transient-retry controls).
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Author-reported live observation (distinct from CI signals): ran an earlier revision of this change as a production Windows service against live Telegram for 24h — 3 real 429s observed (previously 7+ per incident), zero `failed to reply` events, every post-429 turn delivered after the gate window. This predates the review-round semantics tightening; the current head's budget/no-resend and pending-narration-stop behavior is covered by the mock-server regressions above, not by live observation.
- **Visual interface evidence:** `N/A` — no presentation change.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `fe42c5d30` on branch `fix/telegram-429-retry-after`; terminal test output above.

prs.title: fix(cron): prevent shell diagnostics from leaking to channels
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:** A scheduled shell command (`cron` with `job_type = "shell"`) forwarded the raw `status/stdout/stderr` envelope to the delivery channel. A failing command — or a successful one that prints to stderr — could therefore leak command text, file paths, and stderr diagnostics to the end user. This closes that leak.
- **What changed and why (mechanics):** `run_job_command_with_runtime_and_timeout` now returns bare stdout on success (logging any stderr internally at WARN with a sanitized diagnostic), and on failure returns the wrapped envelope only to a new `render_job_output` helper, which replaces it with a localized user-safe message and logs the sanitized failure. `execute_job_now_with_runtime` and `execute_and_persist_job` route their results through `render_job_output`, so both the channel and the persisted run history see only safe text. `cron run`'s tool-level policy rejection is likewise localized.
- **Scope boundary:** Shell jobs only. Agent jobs and non-shell outputs pass through unchanged.
- **Blast radius:** Cron shell job result rendering. No change to scheduling, retry, delivery routing, or command execution itself.
- **Linked issue(s):** None.

### What this does, simply

A cron shell job that prints `internal-warning` to stderr and `public-output` to stdout now delivers only `public-output` to the channel; the stderr is recorded in the server log. A cron shell job that fails no longer sends its `status=`/`stdout:`/`stderr:` dump to the channel — the operator sees "The scheduled command failed. Check the server logs for details." while the sanitized details are logged server-side.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `N/A`; output-rendering change covered by unit tests and required CI.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** Required hosted CI covers the changed `zeroclaw-runtime` surface via `Test`, `Lint`, `Format`, and `Parallel Runtime Test`.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** The output assertions do not capture emitted diagnostic log attributes or verify credential scrubbing in those attributes.

- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
(no output; formatting clean)

$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 4m 42s
(no warnings)

$ cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib cron::
test result: ok. 228 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5224 filtered out

$ cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib cron_run
test result: ok. 20 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5432 filtered out

$ git diff --check
(no output)
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** `execute_job_now_hides_shell_failure_diagnostics` and `execute_job_now_shell_success_returns_only_stdout` drive the real `execute_job_now` entry point and assert the failure output is the localized message (with no `wecom-leak-repro`, `status=`, or `stderr:` substring) and the success output is exactly `public-output`.
- **Visual interface changed?** Yes — cron shell failure/block messages are now localized; success output is bare stdout.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? Yes. Shell diagnostics move from returned results to WARN log attributes. The sanitizer removes known token prefixes and URL credentials, but ordinary credential-bearing key/value text can remain in those logs.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No — this *reduces* what untrusted command output can reach the channel

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? The config remains parseable, but shell result text changes. Both `wrapped` and `raw` now return trimmed stdout on success and a localized message on failure; empty success returns a completion message. The accepted `shell_output_format` setting no longer selects execution output formatting.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No new fields or flags. Existing `shell_output_format` values remain accepted but are ignored during output rendering.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

Revert the eventual merge commit to restore the previous shell output and logging behavior. No config or database migration is introduced.

prs.title: feat(zerocode): rename provider aliases in Config
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`.
- **What changed and why:**
  - Add a rebindable Rename action to provider alias lists and the open alias's settings in ZeroCode Config, with `e` as its default key.
  - Capture the selected alias or derive the open alias from its settings path, edit its replacement name, and require a second confirmation before calling the existing `config/map-key-rename` RPC.
  - Clicking a Config sidebar section returns to its starting view from nested alias or field screens, cancelling unsaved input. Parent breadcrumbs navigate back to their existing screen. Field and Aliases/Costs tab clicks focus the detail pane. Valid detail-row clicks also move keyboard focus there; double-clicking [+ Add] opens the existing creation form for aliases and Costs without saving. Group headers, blank space and breadcrumb separators stay inactive.
  - Reload the alias list after success. Keep explicit method/parameter refusals editable and show returned warnings. A timeout or other uncertain outcome closes the editor and clears stale aliases before attempting a reload. If a reload fails, the stale rename cannot be resubmitted. The Keybindings row resolves its displayed Rename label through Fluent.
- **Scope boundary:** Rename covers provider models, TTS, and transcription only. The adjacent section-click repair applies to the shared Config sidebar. Channels, agents, bundles, Costs rows, and Add rows do not gain rename here. No new RPC, dependency, config schema, or persistence mechanism.
- **Blast radius:** ZeroCode Config key handling, transient editor state, English strings, help, provider alias rendering, shared Config mouse navigation, RPC error propagation, and the Keybindings row label. Existing daemon validation, reference rewrites, persistence, and live-session refresh remain the mutation owner.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #7468. This implements the provider slice; the issue remains open for other alias types.

### What this does, simply

ZeroCode Config is the terminal editor for ZeroClaw settings. Provider aliases are the names used to select a configured model, text-to-speech service, or transcription service. The daemon already knows how to rename those entries and update their references, but the Config editor has no way to ask it to do so.

This PR adds that control. Select an existing provider alias, or open its settings, press `e`, enter its new name, then review and confirm the old and new names. Escape cancels without changing settings. When Rename starts from settings, Escape returns to the same tab and field selection. The daemon checks and saves the rename using its existing machinery. The editor reloads the list and selects the new name after success. If the reply is lost, it reports an unknown outcome, closes the editor, and rereads aliases. It clears stale names before that read, so a failed reload cannot offer the old rename for retry.

If you open an alias or its fields, clicking its sidebar section now takes you back to that section's starting view. You can also click an earlier label in the breadcrumb to return to that level. Clicking a settings tab or detail row makes that pane respond to the keyboard. Double-clicking [+ Add] opens its name form, including on the Costs tab. A filtered alias list opens the alias you clicked.

### Scope and maintenance tradeoff

The three provider categories share one editor and confirmation path. Keeping reference discovery and persistence in the daemon avoids a second implementation in the terminal client. Most of the added lines are boundary tests for cancellation, retries, rebinding, navigation and failed refreshes. The navigation repair stays in the existing Config module, reuses its root/back loaders, and derives clickable regions from the existing renderer. It adds no separate navigation store or settings mechanism. Extending this control to channels and bundles is separate work under #7468. My earlier note on that issue also requested a cascade preview. This slice shows the old and new names for confirmation; it does not list the references a rename will affect. Rename-preview support remains follow-up scope under #7468.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `surface=tui`, ZeroCode Config.
- **Setup / preconditions:** Connect ZeroCode to a daemon with a disposable provider alias in Models, TTS, or Transcription. Use a spare alias with a valid lowercase destination that does not already exist.
- **Steps to run:** Open Config, choose the provider category and family, focus its Aliases list, and select the existing alias. Press `e`, replace the name, and press Enter. Repeat from inside the alias's settings; the same Rename key should target that open alias, and Escape should restore the settings tab and field selection. Review the confirmation showing the map path and old and new names. Escape should cancel. Repeat and press Enter again to apply. Reopen the list and inspect any settings that refer to the alias. From its alias list or fields, click Model providers in the sidebar and verify that the provider family list returns. Clicking a group header or blank sidebar space should keep the current screen. Open an alias field editor, change its input without saving, then click the family breadcrumb to return to its alias list without saving. Click Connection, Model, and Advanced; keyboard navigation should follow the clicked tab. Click a detail row and press Down; the detail cursor should move. Double-click [+ Add] in an ordinary alias list and a Costs list; each should open its name form. Type a draft and Escape to cancel. Border and blank-area clicks should leave the screen and focus unchanged.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** The first Enter opens confirmation without a mutation. The second Enter sends the rename. Success selects the destination; validation errors remain editable and require confirmation again. A real section-row click returns to the starting view and clears the filter and unsaved input without a mutation. Earlier breadcrumbs navigate to their existing screen. Clicking the current breadcrumb only focuses the detail pane and preserves input.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** Provider alias lists have no Rename action or confirmation screen. Clicking the already selected sidebar section leaves its nested detail screen open. Breadcrumbs are display-only. Settings-tab and detail-row clicks do not move keyboard focus out of the sidebar, and double-clicking [+ Add] does nothing.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** Required Test includes the ZeroCode binary and its input/RPC regressions; Lint and Format cover Rust; ZeroCode RPC Boundary checks client dependencies. [Current CI](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38693624389) runs at `fd2b7128b7bb8f1c20211e553bbfd349e9e79b8c`. Format, Lint and ZeroCode RPC Boundary passed; Test is still running. Security failed on RUSTSEC-2026-0346 through RUSTSEC-2026-0349 in rustls 0.23.45. Cargo.lock, Cargo.toml and deny.toml match the merged master; this repair does not change those dependencies. The local focused checks below passed.
- **Known CI coverage gap:** CI does not capture the running TUI. The posted captures cover the alias-list hint, name editor and confirmation. The settings entry is covered by production input/RPC tests; its new footer hint has no separate capture.
- **Commands run and tail output:** `cargo test --locked -p zerocode --bin zerocode provider_alias_rename`: `16 passed; 0 failed; 1465 filtered out`. `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `git diff --check`, `bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh`, and `bash scripts/ci/zerocode_no_zeroclaw_dep_gate.sh` passed.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Source inspection confirms all three provider categories use the existing rename RPC. The user confirmed the earlier sidebar return path. The posted captures show the list hint, name editor, confirmation and renamed alias. The settings-entry extension is covered by production input/RPC tests.
- **Visual interface evidence:** [Posted Rename sequence](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/11460#issuecomment-6160808412). The settings-view footer has no separate capture.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** Automated validation at `fd2b7128b7bb8f1c20211e553bbfd349e9e79b8c`, ZeroCode Config input/RPC boundary. The user posted captures during verification of `15c87bc4a3141a9db9e11c0ba86c934024428bad`; those images omit revision and terminal-cell dimensions. The name editor and confirmation rendering are unchanged by the settings-entry extension.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** See the posted Rename sequence and the focused test result above.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** Automated tests exercise both list and settings entry across all three provider categories, settings-derived targeting with a different remembered alias selection, settings-context restoration on cancellation, excluded settings paths and search input, confirmation, errors, warnings, rebinding, section return, breadcrumb navigation, tab and detail-row focus, Add by keyboard and double-click in empty and populated alias/Costs lists, filtered alias targeting, inactive borders, a committed rename followed by a failed reload, and a committed fixture rename whose response is suppressed until the production client times out. That lost-reply test covers both successful and failed reconciliation and checks that a stale mutation cannot be sent again. A separate-process French catalogue fixture verifies the actual Keybindings pane row uses translated text. Mouse tests use production draw geometry and exact read-only RPC responses. Opening or cancelling Add sends no mutation. The new Add hint follows the configured Enter binding.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** No local broad workspace suite; fresh required CI supplies that coverage.

### Visual evidence

[The posted real-interface captures](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/11460#issuecomment-6160808412) show the alias-list `e=rename` hint, name editor, confirmation of `providers.models.openrouter: ox` to `ox2` with confirm/cancel controls, and the resulting `ox2` list entry and success message. The final picker crop shows `openrouter.ox2`. These frames establish the visible states; the input/RPC tests establish confirmation and mutation ordering.

The settings entry uses the same name editor and confirmation shown above. Its targeting, cancellation and confirmation behavior is covered by the production input/RPC tests.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No. The UI calls the existing config mutation RPC under its existing authorization.
- New external network calls? No. The existing daemon connection carries the RPC.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No. Tests use synthetic aliases and responses.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? Yes. ZeroCode adds the `config_tab.rename_alias` keybinding action, default `e`. No daemon schema or CLI command changes.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No.
- **Upgrade steps:** None. Existing keybindings retain their defaults. The new action can be rebound through the existing keybinding settings.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** Revert the provider-rename feature, its test-only lint follow-up, and the section-click, breadcrumb/tab and detail-row/Add repairs, then rebuild ZeroCode. This removes the UI control; it does not undo previously saved aliases. To reverse a successful rename, rename the destination back to the original name through the supported provider rename control after checking for a collision.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None. Rebinding or removing the shortcut does not disable the underlying daemon RPC.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** Wrong source/destination in confirmation, alias missing after reload, references retaining the old alias, or a visible rename/reload error in Config. A reload error after a successful mutation requires inspecting the saved alias before retrying.

prs.title: feat(cli): add zeroclaw plugin update with verified replacement
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`. Stacked on #11261, which is stacked on #11236. #11581 has landed on `master` as `ea4a54bb5b`: this branch merged its head first (`0ba2b77343`) and now carries the landed commit through `277aeabb0e`'s merge of `master`. `2f3409e9ba`, `bd2d4e5eea`, `f94508dc69` and `2ec36c26dc` merge #11261's head, now `369fb21334`, which carries #11236's `7a3ad81ed5`. Until they merge, this PR's diff also contains their commits. Please review the eight commits after `0ba2b77343`, up to `bab70cc225`, the follow-ups from `75116ac28a` to `a1d212eca1`, and `f3d0a59844`. `6354484051`, `2f3409e9ba`, `bd2d4e5eea` and `f94508dc69` only merge the base, `2ec36c26dc` with the adaptation described below; `277aeabb0e` and `2b3c93631d` merge `master`, with the resolutions described below.
- **What changed and why:**
  - **The command.** Adds `zeroclaw plugin update`, the missing lifecycle operation from #10995 (#7432 R3, Phase 2 D3). It implements the contract posted on the issue for review: https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/10995#issuecomment-5894198515.
    - Syntax: `plugin update <name>[@<version>]...`, `plugin update --all`, and `plugin update <name> --from <dir>`, with `--registry <url>` as for install. Update never installs a package that is not installed.
    - Version selection is install's rule: the last entry the registry lists for a bare name, the exact entry for `name@version`, compared only for equality. An equal version is "up to date" and nothing is downloaded. A different version, even an older one, is installed, so pinning the previous version is the way back. When both are semantic versions and the selected one is older by SemVer precedence, the result line says so (`Replaced 'x' 2.0.0 with 1.2.5, an older version than the one installed.`) instead of reporting an update. A `--from` package always replaces, so a rebuilt plugin can be reinstalled at the same version.
    - Verification is the existing path, reused: the registry download, with its digest when the registry entry lists one, then `PluginHost::admit_update` from the stacked host PR, then the install-time load check with the operator's `plugins.limits`. There is no `--no-verify` for update.
  - **Authority gate.** The runtime grants every permission a manifest requests. So an update is refused, before its component is compiled, when its manifest adds a permission, a capability, or a new `provides` id, or names a different publisher key than the installed version (or none where the installed version named one).
    - The refusal prints the exact command that accepts the difference, with one `--allow-token <item>` per added item, such as `--allow-token permission:<name>`; `--allow` still takes the same items as a comma-separated list. It is pinned to the reviewed version and quoted for the host shell by the egress ceremony's `ShellDialect`, because versions, `provides` ids and keys are publisher-controlled text. Every output line that carries manifest text escapes control, format, line separator and paragraph separator characters (Unicode Cc, Cf, Zl, Zp), line breaks and invisible characters included, so manifest text cannot rewrite, rearrange or disguise the prompt, including an approval block a batch printed earlier, or print a line of its own.
    - `--allow` and `--allow-token` apply to one plugin, and a registry update that uses either must be pinned as `name@version`.
    - The publisher key is a verified identity only under `signature_mode = "strict"`; the docs say so.
  - **Preserved state.** Config rows, secrets, `egress_hosts`, `egress_allow_private`, TLS profiles, durable state, and instance keys are never modified.
    - Missing rows are created without a grant and saved before the package changes, so nothing after the replacement can fail.
    - Egress keeps the never-extend rule: update seeds nothing, even into a row it creates, and prints the same declared-versus-granted difference install prints for an existing row.
    - When preserved config fails the new version's schema, the update still completes and names the instance and the schema location. A missing required property is named, since the name is the schema's own. A configured value, or a configured key the schema does not declare, is never printed, because either could hold a secret.
    - A package whose config row still uses the pre-1.0 package-name key is refused with the same guidance `plugin install` prints (its rename steps, or a deployment-wide egress refusal in their place), one line each under the result; the docs say so.
  - **Results and recovery.** Each plugin gets one result: updated, reinstalled, up to date, skipped (with `--all`, not listed in the registry), needs approval, or not updated with the version kept.
    - A failure does not stop the others, and the command exits 1 when any plugin was not updated.
    - A command that updated anything ends with one restart-the-daemon note, and a batch ends with a summary line.
    - A package an interrupted update displaced is put back by the next `plugin update <name>`, before the registry is consulted, so recovery works offline. Names that are not installed are answered before the registry too, with the install command for the source the update named. `plugin list` and `plugin update --all` point at the recovery with two complete commands (a plugins directory this process cannot lock, such as a read-only one, simply gets no such note in `plugin list`), one from the registry and one from a package directory, rendered for the selected configuration as the approval, install and not-installed commands are, and `--all` never restores a displaced package unasked. An update interrupted mid-swap points back at its own source, so a `--from` run is retried from the same directory; authority the update adds is asked for again.
    - A restored copy the host does not admit is reported with where it now is, and with `plugin list --verbose`, which prints discovery's reason.
  - **Pointers keep the source.** `plugin install` on an installed package now fails with the update command for the same source: `--from <dir>` after a local install, `name@version` after a pinned one. Likewise, `plugin update <name> --from <dir>` for a name that is not installed points at installing that directory. Neither ever offers the registry for a local build, and exit statuses are unchanged.
- **Scope boundary:**
  - No new registry, installer, config key, or on-disk format.
  - No version ordering for selection. Semantic versions are compared only to report an older one.
  - No daemon signalling: channel instances keep their component until restart, and tool sets built afterwards load the new version.
  - Channel-instance config and grant seeding stays with #10996. Install's own `<already-installed>` semantics stay with #10162; this PR only adds the pointer.
  - Registry-side compatibility metadata (#9624) does not exist yet; the load check is the compatibility gate.
  - Known limits, documented where operators read them:
    - no `fsync` around the renames, as for install
    - a tool set built at the instant of the swap can be inconsistent once
  - A process killed between publishing the replacement and marking the replaced version for deletion leaves that version claimed in its hidden transaction. Recovery deletes it while the plugin is installed; after a later `plugin remove`, `plugin list` shows it as displaced until a named `plugin update` restores it, and `--all` never does. `plugin remove` leaving such a claim alone is a follow-up.
- **Blast radius:** `zeroclaw plugin install`/`list`/`update`, the root plugin CLI, and five runtime Fluent catalogues.
  - `seed_plugin_config_entries` is split. Its row-finding first half becomes `ensure_plugin_config_entries`, shared with update, and install's behavior and output are unchanged.
  - A batch fetches the registry index once and compares versions before downloading, through `download_registry_entry` from #11581, which this branch merges. This PR no longer defines that function itself.
  - In `zeroclaw-plugins`, `validate_config_instance` names a missing required property in its `InvalidConfig` message, so every surface that reports that error, such as a daemon load failure, names it too. The existing test that config errors expose no secret values or undeclared keys still passes unchanged.
  - `ci.yml` adds the new component test to the root CLI plugin step, and the plugin backend change filter now selects the plugin CLI component tests. The advisory Windows workflow runs the update tests in `src/main.rs` in its plugin CLI group and the `plugin_update_cli` and `plugin_info_cli` component tests in a step of their own, and the selector contract pins both.
  - The host PR builds update and its recovery on #11236's package lock and leased transactions, so updates, installs, removals and recoveries are serialized across processes, and a claim a running update holds is never touched. #11236 now carries #11232 merged in, and the stack is restacked onto it, so it holds one revision of each. Merge order: #11236, #11261 and #11581, then this PR. #11232 has landed.

### What this does, simply

Until now the only way to move a plugin to a new version was to remove it and install the new one, with nothing checking the new version first or keeping the old one working if something went wrong. `zeroclaw plugin update` does it in one step.

It fetches the new version and runs every check a fresh install runs, including that the component actually loads on this host. Only then does it swap the package in. If anything fails before the swap, the old version is untouched; if the swap itself fails, the old version is put back. If the process dies mid-swap, the next update puts the old version back, even without network access.

A plugin's settings, secrets, network grants and stored data are keyed by its name, not its version, so they carry over. If a new version asks for more than the old one had (a new permission, a new capability, or a different publisher key), update stops and prints the exact command that accepts that difference. So an update can never quietly give a plugin more power. Update also never widens a plugin's network allowlist; it prints the command instead.

    - `--allow` without a pin accepted → `allow_for_a_registry_update_needs_a_pinned_version`
    - the batch stopping at its first failure inside the update loop → `one_plugin_failing_does_not_stop_the_update_of_the_next`
    - a local install's pointer aimed at the registry → `installing_an_installed_local_package_points_at_updating_it_from_that_directory`
    - outcome lines printed without escaping → `update_lines_print_manifest_control_characters_as_escapes`
    - the other update lines printed without escaping → `update_output_never_carries_a_control_byte_from_the_manifest`
    - a local update's not-installed pointer aimed at the registry → `a_local_update_of_a_name_that_is_not_installed_points_at_installing_that_directory`
    - the pre-1.0-row refusal folded into a one-line failure, and that row not refused at all → `update_refuses_a_package_whose_config_row_uses_the_pre_1_0_key`
    - the refusal's steps joined into one line → `a_legacy_row_refusal_prints_each_step_on_its_own_line`
    - the `--from` alternative appended to the registry command, the `plugin list` note built from a default configuration, the `--all` note built without the run's registry, and the note's commands built without the selected configuration → `all_points_at_a_displaced_package_instead_of_putting_it_back`, and for the first and last also `the_displaced_note_offers_two_commands_for_the_selected_configuration`
    - the older-version line folded back into "Updated" → `an_update_to_an_older_version_says_so` (this round)
    - `printable` escaping only the bidirectional marks again → `separators_and_invisible_format_characters_are_printed_as_escapes` (this round)
    - a missing required property left unnamed → `a_missing_required_property_is_named_and_no_value_is_repeated`, `config_rejections_name_the_instance_and_never_the_value`, and `update_output_never_carries_a_control_byte_from_the_manifest`
    - The host guards were checked the same way in the host PR.
  - **Not verified:** the plugin CLI on Windows (the advisory job covered the host crate; see the coverage gap above). Also, no test outside the host crate can make both renames of a swap fail, so the interrupted-update pointer is covered at its rendering and by `update_command`'s own tests, not end to end; the host PR tests the interruption itself.
- **Visual interface evidence:** `Exact plain-text output`
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `0e8c7938d7`, `cli`, a debug `zeroclaw` built with `--features plugins-wasm-cranelift`, `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 LANGUAGE=en`. The messages are Fluent strings; terminal width does not shape them. Paths are shortened to `<tmp>` and the registry port to `<port>`; the `'<dir>'` in the displaced-package note is the program's own placeholder.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:**

